en: We pay homage to that Bhavānī, who is skilled in destroying the afflictions brought about by worldly existence;
to Śāradā, the autumnal one, whose lion-throne is the expanse of the sky.
Without depending on the words of a teacher, she correctly shatters all knots;
her own power of discernment triumphs, revealing the supreme secret.
Homage to the peaceful radiance, whose form is infinite pure consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and which is known solely through its own self-experience.

They speak of him whose twinkling eyelashes constitute the effort in the process of creation and dissolution, and whose desire to bring forth the world is the very act of opening and closing his eyes.
Homage to that Supreme Being, the highest of all.
Homage to Viṣṇu, the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds; the bridge for crossing over to the further shore of the boundless saṃsāra.
Homage to Hari in the form of a lion, the Lord of the three worlds, whose feet are adorned by the luster of the crest-jewels on the heads of gods and asuras.
Homage to that Boar who effortlessly lifted up the earth,
upon whose hoof the Mount Meru, situated in the midst of his hooves, seemed to tremble with the sound of his trampling.
Homage to Śambhu, who is beautiful with the moon-knife and the chowrie kissing his lofty head,
and who is the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.
Homage to that Lord of the Gaṇas, who is worshipped even by the gods for the sake of accomplishing desired aims, and who cuts through all obstacles.
Homage to that Manmatha, for whom women— with their hips moving languidly and their breasts full and elevated— are the very temple.
Homage to the one whose name is infinite, who manifests in all forms, who is expressed by all mantras, and who is the sole lord of the universe.
Oṃ, homage to Śambhu, whose sole form is the ultimate truth, who is the supreme self, and who manifests the divisions of the unreal according to his own will.
The mountain ranges are its petals, the golden mountains its pericarp, and the infinite stalk supports this lotus-seat.
Namaste!

Homage to that supreme radiance which, though undivided, is present within all things that are divided— just as gold is in its ornaments such as the *karṇikā*, or as water is in the oceans and other bodies of water.

Homage to the Supreme Lord, whose greatness transcends speech and mind, who is the embodiment of the three qualities, the eightfold qualities, and infinite qualities, yet remains devoid of all [conditioned] attributes.
Homage to Śiva, who is adorned with the complete pacification of all afflictions,
and who severs the bonds of existence that are difficult to break due to the knots of the three qualities.
Homage to that certain divine Śambhu, whose defining characteristic is precisely the absence of all marks.
Homage to Śambhu, who has the form of saṃsāra yet is free from saṃsāra, whose sole purpose is saṃsāra and whose sole adversary is saṃsāra.
In whatever manner, whoever is worthy of worship, wherever they may be,
and whoever they may be— that deity, to you (or him) be homage!
Homage to the wondrous Śambhu, who transcends that twofold state of existence— both being and non-being— which belongs to all phenomena, and who abides in a third state.
Homage to that certain embodiment of mantra, whose nature is both unmanifest and manifest, and who possesses his own sovereign glory sealed by the independent power of consciousness.
Homage to Śambhu, who is both near and far, hidden and manifest, easily attained and exceedingly difficult to reach, and who is wondrously varied.

Homage to the Self, whose nature consists solely in the pervasive radiance of the entire world of moving and unmoving beings, and whose secret is difficult to comprehend even for those endowed with reason.
Whether it be Viṣṇu, the destroyer of Tripura, Brahmā, or the Lord of the Gods;
whether it be the Sun, the Moon, the Blessed Buddha, or a Siddha—
one who is free from the affliction of passion, hatred, and delusion, and who is exerted in compassion for sentient beings.
Homage always to him who, together with all [beings], is conditioned by virtues and the possessor of virtues.
This verse, composed by Svāmidatta as a memorial for him and characterized as poetry,
bears the name of the poet and is titled *Cakrapāṇiyaya*.
Homage to him— whether he be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, or the Jina— in whom the clouds that nourish the sprouts of the seed of existence, such as passion and the rest, have come to an end.
A musk-tilaka on the surface of his forehead, the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, a fresh pearl at the tip of his nose, a flute in the palm of his hand, a bracelet on his wrist,
pure yellow sandalwood paste upon all his limbs, and a string of pearls around his neck— [all these adorn him].
Surrounded by women, the crest-jewel of cowherds reigns in victory.

May the body of the Self-born (Brahmā), with its hair standing on end from the joy of creating beautiful things, protect you— appearing as if covered by a profusion of filaments clinging to his constant association with unceasing lotuses.
May the tree-like arms of Śauri protect you— arms radiant with the lovely leaf-vines reflected upon the cheeks of Lakṣmī, providing dense shade and bearing great fruit.
May the tusk of the Great Boar protect you— its radiance eclipsing the moon and the sun, serving as a lamp for the dwelling place of the netherworld, and acting as a swing upon the earth.

May that Kṛṣṇa, who is endowed with valor and who descended into the Yamunā— a river difficult to cross for those intoxicated by pride— grant me delight, preceded by the pacification of the insults of the immortals.
May he protect you, at the sight of whose remaining followers— even those who are as dark as him and smeared with black collyrium—
those who are endowed with self-restraint tremble with fear.
The Daityas [rested] upon the lotus-like eyes of their own beloveds.
May the body of Viṣṇu, who assumed the form of a cowherd boy— adorned by the circle of the staff-like arms of the fierce Cāṇūra— protect you all.
To him whose mind was humbled upon hearing the various praises of all the cowherds who rejoiced at the lifting of Govardhana,
and who remembered his form as a boar, radiant as the crescent moon—
May the smile of Hari, who lifted the earth with his tusk, protect you.

The gods and asuras, their skin bristling with joy, were seized by a sudden agitation as the tender sprouts of the Goddess Lakṣmī’s limbs emerged, shimmering amidst the waters of the ocean tossed by the churning mountain, while they drew near to the enemy of Madhu.
May their words, which are uttered with repeated emphasis, protect the world by bringing all activity to rest.

May the breath-winds of the Blessed One, who takes the form of a tortoise and is drowsy from the scratching of his head against the jagged peaks of Mount Mandara as it revolves behind him, protect you—
those winds by whose force the waters follow the movement of his subtle physical constituents under the guise of the ocean tide.
The coming and going of the ocean, unwearied, does not rest even to this day.
As he drinks from one [breast], his eyes slightly narrowed,
and immediately wipes with his hand the other, from which drops of milk are flowing,
his face smiling as it is caressed by his mother’s single finger at the chin— his mouth [is like] a lotus.
May the luster of the teeth of the thief, falling like a string of milk droplets, protect you!
"O Hari, drink the milk of Karburikā while Musalī has gone to play upon the banks of the Kālindī; your crest-lock will grow,"—
hearing these words of Yaśodā, which were intended as a deception due to her [childish] innocence, [the boy drank].
May Hari protect you, joyful as he touches his own crest-lock while half-drinking milk.
Ānanda rejoiced with Yaśodā; the cowherd women gazed long with longing;
Indra, the enemy of Bala, looked on with apprehension; the *siddhas* showered flowers; the earth was agitated;
the cowherd boys looked on with envy; the citizens grieved with compassion; and the gods smiled.
May that Madhuripu, who was seen lifting up Govardhana, purify you.
"Mother, Kṛṣṇa has gone off to play; he has eaten earth at his own will.
"Is it true, Kṛṣṇa? "Who said so? "The wielder of the mace [Balarāma]! "Lie, Mother! Look at my face! When he opened his mouth wide, the Mother saw the entire world within it.
May that Keśava protect you—he at whose sight [the world] fell under the sway of wonder.

"Alas! Is it right for you now to cast aside me—who dwell upon your chest with undivided mind, even though I am but your devotee—and instead take a thousand beloveds? Having spoken thus, she perceived her own body reflected in the jewels on the hoods of the serpent king as being [another] woman.
May the bashful smile of Lakṣmī, which cuts through the sleep of Hari, protect you.

O Hari, since you were made aware [of my state] by the side-long glances cast from the corners of the eyes of the mistress of my life— who, out of affection, showed me her own palace with respect— and even by the tears that fell upon this [palace],
why indeed is there this reversal of the proper order? That I must now be convinced by you!
"May the woman of Vraja protect you"—these words, uttered by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, caused him shame.
Affectionate in her gaze as she looks down with humble devotion, rivaling the blue lotus,

she is brought by those devoted to meditative concentration to the state of being an object of meditation for the sake of attaining welfare; she manifests a state of aesthetic delight in the eyes of Lakṣmī, which are a great treasure-house of loveliness.
May the eyes or the body of Hari bring about for you the removal of the suffering of existence.
By whom the body of the conqueror of Bali was formerly turned into a woman by the one who has destroyed the mind-born [Kāma];
by whom the Gaṅgā was held, he whose arms were raised with necklaces and bracelets like serpents;
and of whom the immortals speak, saying "Hara" because his head bears the moon—and whose name is worthy of praise.
May that Mādhava, who himself brings about the destruction of the darkness of evil, protect you at all times.

May the two eyes of Murāri, composed of the moon and the sun, protect you— eyes which, as they slightly open like the sky at dawn, surpass with their own radiance the mass of jewel-lamps on the heads of the lord of serpents, who are like clouds in a theatrical sleep. For by their splendor, [the world] is illuminated.
Of this lotus, one half remains blooming with splendor, while the other half succumbs to sleep.

To the Mallas he was like the king of mountains; to all people he was a child; to women he was the flower-bowed god of love; to cowherds he was an ordinary soul; in heaven to the wielder of the thunderbolt he was the immeasurable Viśvarūpa;
to Kaṃsa he was the wrathful Time (Kāla); to those whose eyes were startled by fear he was the form to be meditated upon by yogins.
May Hari, seen entering the arena and bringing joy to the immortal people, protect you all.
May the hollow of the belly of Hari, its interior made resonant by the breath of the enemy as he was being torn apart, purify you—
[the belly] which served as the dwelling place for the seven rivers that had entered its cavernous interior.
Like a conch shell, it quickly produced a sound even more terrible than the clashing of weapons.
May that conch shell of Hari—white as the water-lily, the *kunda* flower, and the lotus fiber; the full moon in the sky of Viṣṇu’s palm—protect you all;
by its sound, the playful movements of the wives of the enemies of the gods [are brought to rest].
The girdles become loose upon the regions of their hips.
The form of him who was seen by Hari at the forefront of battle, with the unbearable radiance of his splendor spreading forth in all directions from his eyes—
which contained the reflection of the sun— was such that...
May that [teaching], which shines forth like the sun dispelling the circle of rays, be for your benefit.
May the noble discus of Hari, its crimson stream gushing from the severed throat-pit of the haughty lord of the Daitya hosts, fulfill all your desires.
May it bring you the splendor of a sky made terrible by the conflagration of the quarters.

Having contemplated the discus— which is like a battle-axe for the communal clearing of the dense forest of his arms that are like trees bearing rising arrows, its edge strewn with the thick sparks of fierce, blazing fire—
he conceived the resolve to swallow [the world], amidst the flowing streams of the sun’s shimmering, fleshy rays.
Even now Rāhu is bewildered; may that destroyer of the Daityas quickly burn away your misfortunes.
Having found openings by tearing through the skeletal cages of the Daityas,
they have become thick with the mud formed from the rivers of blood flowing from the gods;
curved like the crescent of the young moon, they possess the luster of a parrot’s beak.
May the claws of the lion-bodied Hari protect you.
"Are these ten suns that cause the fear of universal dissolution, having occupied the entire expanse of space? Or are they masses of meteors risen up to burn the three worlds?"— thus thinking,
the hosts of immortals, out of fear, beheld the hand of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow as he assumed the body of the Man-Lion.
Having seen this, may your nails—red with the blood gushing from the chests of the arrogant asuras that they have torn open—protect you.

By him, the blue lotus was gracefully uprooted from the water— its stamen the Mount Meru, its petals the vast reaches of the quarters, and its stalk the trembling body of Śeṣa hanging from its very root.
May that Boar protect you as if he were wearing it as an ornament upon his head.
How could the earth, though soft, not be crushed by the pressure of his hooves?
How could the Golden Mountain, so vast, not melt away under the flames of fire from his mouth? And how could the seven oceans not dry up by his very breaths?
May the Boar protect you—he who is equipped with vast and profound contemplation.
O Lord of the three worlds, why have you been brought to such a state of transformation by begging?
Or rather, since that which was not created by you, the Creator of the universe, how could it be given to you? This gift is for you, the most excellent one, yet it is a bond for us, not a liberation.
May Hari protect you—he who was humbled by the peerless power of Bali’s request.
When a portion of the auditory ether has dissolved, when the light of the eyes has vanished somewhere,
when the vital air has been consumed by the intake of breath, and when the ocean has been drunk half-way through the anus,
as the wielder of the Śārṅga bow searches for [the breath] within the cavity between a single hair at the tip of his trunk—
May the majesty of the Earth, whose form is like a lap and whose domain is unassailable, purify you!
Where now are those arrogant lords of the quarters, reeking with the thick intoxication of pride?
O Meru, Mandara, Malaya, and Himavat, well done for you who are true upholders of the earth!
O Śeṣa, you are praiseworthy with your many heads, so fierce and capable of bearing the vast weight of the world.
May that Boar protect you, who, with a loud and mocking laugh, proclaimed himself the "Bearer of the Earth."
May Vāmana protect you— he in whose reflection within the Kaustubha gem the three worlds became as if born within his belly, gazing upon him with curiosity.

O Lord of Life, when You are present, we behold the essence of the entire world gathered in one place; our gaze falls upon this dark-hued body of Yours, for it does not enter the sight of a man of meager merit.
Who else but You could possess such exceedingly vast delight? Your very glance is indeed nectar.
May Hari, who was thus addressed by the Daityas and even by the sages, protect you with his form that captivates the hearts of women.
Wandering about, he had fallen into a deep sleep, feeling a momentary pleasure from the scratching of his back produced by rubbing against the great mountain;
with a long, rattling, and terrible roar, he slept soundly.
May that tortoise, who supported the ocean overwhelmed by his breath, protect you.
May that mass of matted hair of Śiva bring you victory—
upon which even the Ganges, though she has appeared, creates the illusion of being a single grey strand.
May he protect you, upon whose mass of matted locks the moon rests, white as a shimmering pearl necklace,
like a cluster of stalks amidst blue lotuses.
Sleeping like a swan in autumn.
May he who is adorned with the moon grant you auspiciousness—
he upon whose head the shimmering waves of his hair flutter like a female swan upon a lotus-stalk, while the stainless crescent of the moon rests there like a swan.
Seeking water, she fell from the sky onto the celestial river.
May he grant you prosperity, whose crest-garland— white as a pale cloud—
is resplendent with the celestial river [Gaṅgā],
which melts from the heat of the blazing upward-glances [of Śiva].
Like a river carrying the nectar spread from the moon's ambrosia.
Having slowly joined together the crescent moon fallen from the sky and the bracelet broken during a lovers' quarrel, the Daughter of the Mountain, with a smiling face,
said: "May that Śiva and that Girijā protect you, whom she beheld."
And that Krīḍācandra had his body filled with the rays of his teeth.
O Hara, O fair-limbed one, which of these is yours? What stands upon your head? Are they matted locks? Does a swan resort to matted locks? No; the moon does not frequent the water.
This is a cloud; where is there water here? The cloud surges like a wave.
May that Śaṅkara, who thus conceals the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā), protect you all.
Let alone the pleasures of embracing, kissing the bimba-like lower lip, conversation, and smiles;
even this mutual gazing at one another’s faces has become difficult to achieve. Thus, for us two, the proposal of uniting into a single body has been rendered futile.
"Who is this mockery of love?"—may the smiling Ardhanārīśvara protect you.
"Mother, live! What is this that Father hides in his cupped hands?
"My child, it is a sweet fruit; do not give it away. Go yourself and take it from my house.
When the mother had thus sent him, he opened the joined palms at the twilight, drawing them apart.
May the outburst of laughter from Śambhu, which possesses the impetuosity of a burst samādhi, protect you!

One half of his body throbs from the power of his muttering, while the other half quivers from agitation; one hand is placed upon his head to offer salutation, while the other is raised to strike it away;
one eye closes in meditation, while the other finds it unbearable to look at [the deity]—thus he remains.
May that body of his protect you, which, though equal in its lack of desire, is beautiful at the conclusion of twilight.

May the remaining lotus-faces of that house— the pair of whose mouths was occupied by the breasts of the daughter of the Mountain King— remove your impurity, though they were distressed by drinking milk.
May that unprecedented web of rays from the sun, which bestows desired objects, grant liberation from the bonds of existence to those who bow down and serve it.
By means of this [web], liberation from the fetters of worldly existence is achieved for those who have prostrated themselves.
O Sun, may those first rays of yours,
which possess the glow of their rising, bestow auspiciousness;
for they bring about the great festival of the birth of day.
The quarters of the sky appeared like celestial women whose faces were flushed rosy-red with vermilion.
With the tips of their arm-circles raised high, their chests armored,
hot with passion, wounded yet crushing the hearts of their enemies, and harsh;
having cast off their garments, they display the full weight of their physical forms— he whose foremost warriors are such as these.
Neither the warriors nor the breasts of beautiful women could cause agitation; such was the power of that Conqueror.

Could it be the sun? Yet the sun does not possess rays that drip with the essence of ambrosia. Could it be the full moon? For nowhere is the cool-rayed moon entirely free from blemish. Could it be the wish-fulfilling gem itself? But whence could such exquisite delicacy belong to a jewel of vast fruit?
May that form of the Sage, first beheld by those of deluded intellect out of doubt, protect you.
May the drawings of Caṇḍī’s bow protect you— drawings that for a long time have inspired both joy and fear in her enemies, mingled with the sound of the bowstring as it rings around her wrist.

May the lotus-stalks of the rays from the swaying rows of her toenails, with the flickering, restless bees of Caṇḍī’s shimmering anklets, grant the fulfillment of desires to the lake-like heads of the great asuras.
May your pair of lotus-feet, captivating with their resonant tinkling, [protect you].
She is modest before the face of her beloved; compassionate toward the elephant hide for her garment; terrified of the serpent; filled with a sense of wonder at the moon that drips nectar;
envious when looking upon the daughter of Jahnu (Gaṅgā); and dejected within the hollow of the skull.
May the gaze of Pārvatī, full of affection at her first union, be for your welfare.
As she rose at the end of their dalliance, supporting the weight of the Lord of Serpents with one hand and holding her garment with the other— her shoulder bearing the burden of her loosened tresses—
may Śauri, his love for amorous play redoubled by her beauty at that moment, protect you.
May that body, led away while embracing its bed, with its arms languidly drooping, purify the world.
May he whose face is that of the lord of elephants protect these three worlds— he by whom, with his great trunk raised up in the sky,
the white sprout of a lotus-root is grasped at its base.
The stalk-like form of the lotus that is the sun’s orb.

When the Lord of Serpents, terrified by the sound of the *mura* drum struck by Nandin’s hand amidst the joyful dance of the Trident-Bearer, contracts his coils and enters the nostril-aperture, while the quarters of the sky resound with swarms of bees flying up from his temples— [in that moment, the world is filled with the fragrance of the sandalwood paste applied to the forehead of the God of Gods].
May the long, sighing movements of the faces of Vaināyaka protect you.
The bow is a garland, the bowstring is a swarm of humming bees, and the target is a frail woman; the mind is the object to be pierced, and these five—beginning with sound—are the arrows.
He who possesses such power to conquer the three worlds, though he is bodiless—[to him I bow].
May that desire, which dwells in the side-glances of beloved women, grant you all your desires.
Brahmā, Dakṣa, Kubera, Yama, Varuṇa, the Maruts, Vahni, Candra, Indra, and Rudra;
the mountains, rivers, oceans, the hosts of planets, humans, Daityas, Gandharvas, and Nāgas;
the continents, the lunar mansions, the stars, the sun, the Vasus, the sages, the sky, the earth, and the two Aśvins.
May that Blessed One, whose universal form contains all things withdrawn within his body, protect you.
"O charming one, abandon your despondency here; let this heavy trembling before the Conqueror of Strength be cast off.
O lotus-eyed one, resort to sincerity and honor these venerable ones.
By means of the artful words of Dhanvantari, who himself awakens Lakṣmī during the rite of self-choice—"
May Hari protect you—he who, hearing elsewhere only a prohibition regarding the self, heard therein an injunction.
May Narahari, the sole hero of the world, grant happiness; he who,
when intent on the destruction of the sons of Diti in battle,
was such that [the gods] were unable even to look upon his face, which was uplifted by fury.
I know that they do not bow even before their own nails.
"Welcome! I am worthy; speak, O Lord, what may be given? 'The earth.
'How much is my portion? 'Three paces of ground have been given. 'I have accepted it. 'Do not give! said Uśanas. 'Why? This is Hari (Viṣṇu). What recipient could be greater than him?"
May that Vāmana, who was thus honored by Bali at the opening of the sacrifice, protect you.
O Discus, speak! O Lord, O Mace, O Conqueror, O Hari, O Kamboja, give your command!
O Nandaka, live on, O King of Serpents! O Lord, has anyone been slain by me?
Which demon is this? Who is Hiraṇyakaśipu? I swear it to you all in truth.
May the face of Viṣṇu, who asked, "By what weapon? and "By my claws," protect you!
Alas! When the Discus-bearer [Viṣṇu] was filled with anxiety, when the Discus itself was seized by fear, when the Lotus-seated One [Brahmā] sat hunched over,
when the Radiance was perishing, when the Hot-rayed One [the Sun] was held in apprehension, when the Moon was greatly distressed,
when the Mind was failing, and when the Lord of the Dead [Yama] was exhausted with grief— [he who remained steadfast].
May he protect you from the act of swallowing the fierce and deadly *kālakūṭa* poison.
Eternal, with its own self-experience as its sole measure, the abode of bliss, the unique seed for the sprout of the world,
[it is] beyond the reach of all calculations of direction, place, time, and so forth.
May the great Mardāsaha bestow great auspiciousness and protection upon you.
Like a mass of clouds in the sky, like a multitude of waves in a lake,
or like the radiance of the moon in its thousandfold light—
that in which this world arises and dissolves.
May that power of Śambhu lead to your prosperity.

He who performs the playful sport of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the three worlds, and through his own activity assumes the forms of Hari, Hara, and Dhruhiṇa— that God transcends the reach of the speech and mind of all people.
May that power grant you eternal and imperishable auspiciousness.

It is said that this entire collection of causes— the body, atoms, karma, and so forth— is devoid of autonomy; it is only through his favor that it attains the skillful capacity to fashion the manifold diversity of the universe.
May he, the sole Great Lord of the three worlds, protect you!

That immeasurable Lord, whose majesty is insurmountable, who sports with the daughter of the Snowy Mountain— just as Purandara plays with the thunderbolt and the Lord of Lakṣmī with his lotus-residence— is he whom the likes of Brahmā and others cannot reach.
May he, the beloved one who crushes the end-maker (Death), diminish your suffering.
Liberation indeed is the supreme goal of human endeavor;
those who know the inner truth perceive that it is hindered by obstacles.
What more need be said? Let that very liberation be like the moon composed of nectar.
May your devotion to the ornament of the crest-line be unbroken.
May the form of Śrīkaṇṭha—joined with Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, and Bharaṇī; always with Rohiṇī;
with Jyeṣṭhā, Bhadrapadā, and Punarvasu; conjoined with Citrā and Viśākhā;
accompanied by the unbroken hand (Aśleṣā) and Mūla; and adorned with Āṣāḍhā and Maghā—grant [auspiciousness].
It is better for you to be accompanied by Vaiśravaṇa, like the Blessed One’s Nakṣatrapālī.

The Lord is the protector of those who bear fear, the master of both the conscious and the unconscious, the destroyer of the affliction of the virtuous who praise Him, the bestower of equality with Himself upon the devoted, and the undoer of the wicked.
He is the God who is the ground for the arrangement of enjoyment and liberation for His servants—the source of the three worlds: Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.
May Mṛḍa, who displays his divine play through the manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal of emanations, protect you all.
The king [of kings] honors the feet of him whose hair has not yet reached maturity, for whom the serpents serve as a crest-jewel;
whose body, white with ashes, the Nāgas adorn with half of the daughter of Gaṅgā;
and by whom Māra was led away from the self-restrained, lest their minds become enamored of Rāmā.
May he who possesses three eyes protect you, bearing those seven arrows impelled by seven horses, which resemble the rays of the rising sun.

As he was about to go from Candrāvalī’s palace to the temple of Rādhāmohana, Candrāvalī, having heard her beloved’s words, “Is Rādhā well? said: “Is Kaṃsa well? Thereupon her beloved became enraged and asked, “Where have you seen Kaṃsa?”
"Where is Rādhā?"—may the outburst of laughter from those two, their minds filled with joy, protect you.

When the bow was drawn in battle, his left hand joined the right. "O, O right hand! While you were performing great acts such as giving food and alms, it is improper for you to go behind now. Then he (the left hand) spoke again, running forward.
He quickly asked Rāghava: "Are you able to shatter the multitude of Rāvaṇa's heads?"
"Has that Keśava been seen anywhere? He has gone away taking some cowherd maiden;
indeed, we have all been deceived. O Khula, he must be searched for! Having said this, she suddenly took Rādhā by the hand and cried, "Go two by two!"
May Hari, who assumed the guise of a cowherd girl and reached the bower-dwelling, protect you all.
"Mother, I will not go to the banks of the Yamunā to guard the calves.
"Why so, my child? For the cowherd women grind me with the weight of their full breasts.
"Even though I have been repeatedly forbidden by the knitting of their brows, I continue to prattle on before Yaśodā."
May that Keśava protect you, his face sealed by the lotus-hands of the cowherd maidens.
That you prostrate at twilight before the world with palms joined in supplication,
and that you carry the river on your head without shame— indeed, I have endured all this.
But if Śrī was obtained by Hari during the churning of the nectar, why then did he swallow the poison?
"O you who are obsessed with women, do not touch me!"—may Hara, thus addressed by Gaurī, protect you.
"Who are you, O spear-bearer? Seek a physician. "I am Nīlakaṇṭha; I love this single cry of the peacock. "Speak! I am Paśupati; the two horns are not seen at all.
"O simple one, he is a pillar (sthāṇu). How can he be the lord of life for Śivā?"
May the Moon-crested Lord protect you, he whose voice was heard saying, "Go to the forest."
"Who is this Hari at the door? Go to the grove; what does a monkey have to do with it here?
"I am Kṛṣṇa, my beloved. I am terrified of Kṛṣṇa—that monkey!
"O charming one, I am Madhusūdana! Drink that very vine, for its leaves are as dark as his."
May Hari, thus made to confess by his beloved and thereby put to shame, protect you.
"O shameless Hari, what is this? Why do you constantly wander about following young women?
"O innocent one, what is so surprising about the fact that joy arises from contact with you?"
"O rogue, I describe for you that your affection for women is excessive.
Why do you prattle such nonsense? For whom does love exist toward enemies?"
Why do you thus confuse me by speaking of your attachment to Rāma?
How could there be any attachment toward one's own elder brother, Rāma?
"Why do you thus bewilder me? I grieve only for your own misfortune.
Tell me, what small misfortune could there be when you are angry without cause?"
May the embrace of Śauri protect you— he who, having surpassed the cowherd women with these crooked words, drew them close as their heavy breasts were rounded.
O Pārvatī, be gracious! Even Śiva has prostrated himself at your feet. How can you still call him "Śiva" (the Auspicious One), when he is clothed in the bloody hide of an elephant?
If, when "Śiva" is uttered by you, I become a Sthāṇu with redoubled anger, then it is true that you are indeed a Sthāṇu;
yet there is nothing at all in your mind.
"Abandon your anger, O proud woman; know me to be the Lord worshipped by the three worlds!
If you, O Three-Eyed One, are the Lord, why are you naked and grey with dust?"
"Now, what will you say here, O you with pale cheeks? 'I am Pāśupati.
Since you do not even consider what is logical or illogical, you are indeed Pāśupati himself."
"O deluded one, why do you wander thus? Know me to be truly Bhava.
O rogue, you are truly Bhava, since you possess such exceedingly diverse forms."
If you are refuted by the wise here in this world, then this [claim] that I am Tryambaka is known;
for you do not even speak of one mother, so how could there be three?
Know me, O Anaṅgahana, as one who has been burned right here by this great dispute;
for every single limb of mine has been consumed by you through such conduct.
May he who, having conquered the faults such as the failure to pay homage at the twilight hours,
is impetuously embraced by Pārvatī with her breast, remove your misfortunes.
"Become free from affection for me; do not be as you have spoken.
O Queen, from where has this desire for freedom from affection arisen in you?"
Enough with these wicked stratagems! For what purpose is this river standing above you?
What is this garland of hell-guardians standing over my head? Take them!
Thus you torment this person who loves you by acting falsely;
you shall certainly have to stand above the rows of hell-wardens.
"Why are you angry? Abandon your wrath and let go of this dispute with me;
for a conflict with you shall never again cause us any distress."
May that Śiva bring you prosperity— he who, having mocked Gaurī with words such as "the Gaṅgā is turbid with a body," won her over when she remained speechless.
"Vijaya, you are skilled with three dice, but I am not able to play with him. Vijaya, I am skilled [with dice], yet these two dice are not in my hand."
"What is the use of this gambling for me, if Gaṇapati is not pleasing to you?
Who in the world hates Vināyaka? Do you not know?"
"What kind of play is this with you, who are devoid of wealth? Are you not ashamed? Look before you at these very gods and asuras, who are separated from their riches."
"Without a lunar eclipse, I find no pleasure; why do you speak thus?
If this is pleasing to the Queen, Nandin, let Rāhu be summoned."
Alas! When the white-toothed Rāhu, the cause of terror, stands nearby, who could find delight?
If you do not desire it, then this Rāhu has been abandoned by you this very moment.
"Why do you vainly attribute this to me? Do I not possess the supernormal knowledge of your lap? Having remained here for a divine thousand years, it is only fitting that I speak thus."
May the face of Bhavānī protect you— her pupils trembling with joy at these crooked words uttered by Paśupati in his playful sport with the noose.
"Who strikes the door-panel with his finger? Is it the crooked Mādhava, or is it Spring?
Is he not the potter Cakrī, nor the mountain-bearer Praṇīndra, nor the double-tongued serpent?
O simple girl, is he not the lord of birds who slays the terrible snake, nor Hari, nor the lord of monkeys?"
Thus, having his words thwarted by Lakṣmī, may this husband of Pāṭu-lakṣmī protect you.
"O beloved, why this distress? Do you not know that the solar disc is well-known to the world?
You must not be angry; we have never seen a water-dweller above it."
Anger is fit to be abandoned by one for whom thirst does not arise; O proud woman, cast away your pride—what is the use of this pride of mine now?
Of what use indeed is that poetry for one who is being crushed, from whom those successions of the nectar of aesthetic flavor do not flow forth, as they do from the ocean?
What is the use of that poet’s poetry, or what is the use of the arrow of the archer,
if it does not strike the heart of the enemy and cause his head to reel?
Some poets, like children, have many words but lack confident expression; they are the cause of passion in their mothers.
What is the use of that poetry now, which has been flooded by torrents of rasa,
if even dull-witted people do not become sprouted with longing for it?

A novel theme, non-vulgar diction, wordplay that is not obscure, clear aesthetic flavor, and a composition of complex syllables— all these together constitute a complete work that is difficult to achieve in one place.
A person who lacks heart produces poetry merely with his mouth,
just as Rāhu casts a dark shadow even over the pale moon.
Those seized by envy are not awakened; those corrupted by pride lack prosperity;
others are struck down by ignorance; and thus the well-spoken word withers away within their limbs.
Wicked people indeed lack the eloquence to join together even two words;
yet they remain undaunted even when faced with the difficult compositions of others.
Thinking in his mind, "Where can I find a fault here?
the wicked man proceeds to listen to the works of the virtuous.
Not withered by successive rebirths, nor distressed by mere instructions,
these words of those with true insight have as their essence that which is to be realized through personal experience.
In some, eloquent sayings reside only in their speech like parrots; in others, they remain silent within their hearts like mute men;
but in yet another, these beautiful words leap gracefully from the heart to the mouth.
Many human heads, hairy and large, were suspended from their necks; among them, some still possessed ears.
The speech of the great poet shines like a virtuous woman, practicing the noble vow of eloquent expression; it remains aloof from contact with vulgar matters and subjects.
They are to be revered, they are great-souled ones, and their fame remains firm in the world— those by whom poems have been composed, or those who have been celebrated in poems.
Through the merits of someone, there arise in their mouth words that are clear, captivating in their luster, and skilled in various forms of expression, and in their home there are women.
How might there not be pain for people whose ears are pierced by the well-spoken words of great poets, which indicate other hidden meanings?
It will fall into the hands of a virtuous person, it will delight him, and it shall remain faultless;
yet even by its production, the poet grows weary of the narrative, as if by a daughter.
Everything recited at the appropriate time attains the status of well-spoken words, even if it is merely a clever saying;
just as even poor food becomes exceedingly delicious to one who is hungry.
The gold of poetry, heated by the fire of wicked people, attains purity;
therefore, one should strive to show it to those whose minds are free from envy.
They do not notice a corrupt word, nor a break in meter, nor even a loss of meaning;
for they are distracted by their own sensuality, like the paramours of courtesans and bad poets.
The dull-witted person feels distress when confronted with poetry requiring a vast heart, yet not in his own ignorance;
like a woman with withered breasts, she generally blames only her bodice.
A virtuous person brings about renown, while a skilled poet merely composes a poem;
the lotus nourishes itself with water, but the sun endows it with splendor.
Some are skilled only in explaining, while others are capable of composing treatises; the tongue presents the food, yet it is the palate alone that knows the flavors.
As long as the arrival of consciousness— which brings about the opening of the eyes— does not occur, the poet’s suffering remains like a beautiful verse caught in the throat.
Furthermore,
in the works of great poets,
there exists another very real entity that is being perceived, which transcends the well-known constituent parts.
It does not shine, like the beauty of women.
The poet’s intention, which lies beyond the reach of words and manifests solely within the moist verses,
is expressed by those whose limbs undergo a transformation of horripilation.
This salutation with palms joined is from the people who have become silent.
Those few who possess hearts attuned to the compositions of poets are not unrestrained;
they are like bees among creepers filled with aesthetic flavor.
They delight in the essence of the heart, not in that which touches the mouth.
Kings have become renowned by relying on poets,
and poets have attained fame by relying on kings;
there is no one who provides greater assistance to a king than a poet.
And for the king, there was no companion equal to a poet.
Producing clarity of mind for those who have awakened to the highest state, gladdening and imbued with every aesthetic flavor,
this most serene poetry finds no place in the heart of the wicked.
It was like drinking nectar emerging from the mouth of Rāhu.

How could those meanings, which were previously bound by the essence of the mirror and then rubbed, not immediately yield their original forms? For the exceedingly soft [words] of great poets are like thieves.
For words forcibly convey even meanings other than their own.

What is the use of that poetry which, like honey not drunk in sufficient measure, does not reach the heart? For those whose minds are shrouded by envy, it fails to cause even a bristling of the hairs on their bodies through the power of its aesthetic flavor,
nor a trembling of the head, nor a reddening of both cheeks, nor eyes clouded with tears.
Or rather, speech has as its support the verbal expression of things that have been superimposed.
For those whose intellects are nourished by their own virtues, the entire world is a forest;
yet those who are full of envy do not wish for the virtues of others even in a dream. As for others who are full of affection, their minds are tender toward anyone at all and find peace.
May the great forests of asceticism now be considered as mere dwellings for the well-spoken words of the great ones.
That vision of the wise which does not loudly proclaim even the stingy as virtuous, despite their being eloquent with words of praise for the good, is not the reality; whereas that which,
upon suddenly coming within the range of hearing, causes the necks of the virtuous to quiver with joy— [that alone is real].
Even the beasts of prey do not leave mouthfuls of young grass untouched; how much less so the words of poets?
Fortunes, like lightning from clouds of luck that crumble at will, cannot be restrained;
the drum for the constant departure of life-breaths never rests. Therefore, protect this body of yours, which consists of fame, with the nectar of poetry.
O lords of the earth, having propitiated those poets, bestow upon them positions free from pride.
O King, abandon your hostility toward the bond of affection for good poets;
surely, through their favor, pure fame will radiate from you. For the heavy and noble life-story of the Lord of the Raghus has been composed by those who are well-pleased.
Enraged, they brought the ten-faced one, conqueror of the three worlds, to a state of ridicule.
Homage, repeated homage, to that essence of poetry,
by even a mere drop of which poured within,
the face of the virtuous man attains a golden luster.
And the ill-natured person comes to possess an ugly complexion.
Those who harbor pride regarding the path of poetry, yet do not know the secret seal of true scholarship, are like those who have not studied the mantras of the *Garuḍa*.
They begin to taste the hālāhala poison.
How could he, who for a long time was not the suckling infant at the thick breasts of Sarasvatī’s mother— consisting of poetic skill and scholarship—
be one whose every limb has not attained excellence?
Day by day, it attains a special degree of maturity.
Those who, like royal swans— the vehicles of Sarasvatī dwelling within the lotus-heart— are as if masters of the training,
and are skilled in discerning the separation of milk from water;
Those poets who possess discernment are victorious.
The nectar of poetry, seized by the Rāhu of wicked men, would not be attainable by those of noble character; yet it shines forth through the unfeigned assembly of the virtuous.
Even if there were no such thing as the excellence of whiteness.
Without a knowledge of poetics (*sāhityavid*), the merit of poets does not manifest in any way elsewhere;
it vanishes in that very instant, like [a reflection] in water.
The drop of oil does not spread elsewhere.
What is the use of that which is exceedingly crooked, meaningless,
and empty, yet reveals all other qualities—
though it is itself defiled by its own intangibility?
Speech is like the flick of a dog's tail against something empty.
Let her low breast shed tears of extreme blackness,
sharing its likeness with collyrium;
for how else could that [blackness] have arisen without it?
Through this refinement, there is the clarity of vision of Sarasvatī.
If there is meaning, yet there is no purity of words; or if there is that purity, yet there is no style—if such a composition exists, from where does it come?
If it does exist, then this is not a new or crooked path.
Alas, without rasa, poetry is a dense thicket; it is utterly useless.
Praiseworthy indeed is the curved course of that bow-staff of the eloquent verses of the best of poets, which possesses a bond of dense firmness,
since its string reaches as far as the tip of the ear.
The minds of those possessed by stinginess are instantly shattered.
Those few who in the past, having repeatedly squeezed the sugarcane-stalk of the essence of speech, extracted the refined juice and thereby touched the ultimate reality—
those poets are now being born again in their respective ways, and they continue to weave their compositions therein.
By which [the mind] is stripped of the scales consisting of upamās, prāsa, kaṭhora, citra, yamaka, śleṣa, and so forth.
Indeed, there are many poets here who, by practicing even a few verses of others day after day, could compose a four-line stanza;
yet they are no friends to the manner of the ocean’s waves rising in an unbroken succession.
Indeed, the words of some friends truly bestow clarity upon them.
Where are those hundreds of loads of gold or those herds of rutting elephants bestowed today by Śrī Harṣa upon the virtuous Bāṇa?
But where are the glories carved out by Bāṇa through the profusion of his elegant compositions?
I consider that even at the dissolution of an eon, they do not undergo even the slightest withering.

Fortunate are those who, having gathered the well-spoken flowers from the creepers of speech that have grown in the garden of their own mouths— flowers that are pure, fragrant, and woven with virtue— remain in the solitude of the virtuous.
They place various colored flowers as ear-ornaments upon the lobes of their ears.
Victorious are the great poets, who, like seafarers, have seen the further shore of the vast ocean of literature;
for by means of the delicate cloves of their well-spoken verses, I feel—
The virtuous always endure the pleasant words of the assembly.
The jewel that adorns the three worlds, the kinsman of the assembly of the virtuous, he alone shines as a second creator of poetry;
they praise his extraordinary greatness with their heads bowed low.
Even for those who bear the earth, they perform the act of grasping his feet.
Even those who do not understand even the mere meaning of the words become as if their entire range of sensory faculties is blocked, like deer drinking in a melody with their ears.
We pay homage to that speech of the lords of poets, which stands as if variegated with diverse forms.
When the Goddess of Speech is directed toward an improper object by those of impaired intellect,
she leads to reproach, defeat, great distress, or even sin;
but when employed in a proper place among the virtuous, she brings about renown and prosperity.
For the sake of the mind's tranquility, for the benefit of others, and for the attainment of ultimate peace in the remote forest.
King Rāma was explained by Vyāsa, who emerged from an anthill;
King Vikramāṅka by the poet Kālidāsa;
Bhoja by Citta, Pabhi, Blaṇa, and others; and Karṇa by Vidyāpati.
They attain renown through the expansive works of eminent poets, not by the sounds of kettledrums, for they are devoid of a creator god.

Those of great majesty who, having resorted to the shade of the forest of their arms, made this earth— girdled by the oceans— free from fear from any quarter; even the memory of those kings does not persist without the favor of that [Buddha].
We pay homage to that one of great primordial nature, whose work is poetry.
This world regards those who were once as radiant as a jar of fresh butter, who attained sovereign glory,
and in whose houses young women dwelt by day as if they were moonlight— even those ornaments of the world— as if they had never existed, even in a dream.
O brother, what is the use of hundreds of praises for a good poet, when the world is blind without you?
With its vast abundance of fragrance, even the essence of that musk-deer’s navel is rendered utterly worthless;
even a garland of jasmine does not produce such delight.
If the goddess who bestows the flow of honey moves forward, she grants the gift of liberation.
It bestows a sense of wonder upon the mind through its method of composition;
when recited in assemblies, it brings about incomparable acclaim; and having attained renown, it spreads exceedingly noble fame.
Like what wish does the wish-fulfilling gem of poetry not fulfill?
He who, like a clear poetic nectar situated on a beautiful pedestal,
steals away the splendor of another while spreading his own lotus within;
he is like a swarm of ants produced by the fault of misplaced syllables.
The dark line of inscribed letters upon it shines forth.

If one who delights solely in the characterized and the characteristics, who is untouched by the contact of logic, whose intellect is not made beautiful by the investigation of ornaments, and who is devoid of the training of those who know poetry—
should from him arise a poem rich in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it would be exclusively beautiful.
Then, because of the blackness of the crow, the palace of the king would appear white.
Like a certain master poet using the key of his own wisdom, [he opens] that treasury of words and meanings, which possesses the winding turns of Sarasvatī’s speech.
Having uncovered it, he makes it his universal ornament.
Some fulfill the divine words,
while others, being utterly deluded, merely blunt them;
those [words] which are like drops at the mouths of oyster shells— divine.
Those very pearls [exist], but they do not exist in the cātaka birds.
Even eloquent men observe the vow of silence without people who recognize their exertion; there are those who remain silent even without living in the forest.
Even the male cuckoos are skilled in the fifth note.
The serpent Vyāla and Rāhu, because of their devotion to the nectar,
suffered the terrible restraint of their tongues and heads;
thus, indeed, do the malicious become fearful.
They turn their backs on the nectar-like essence of poetry.

Speaking with intent of that reality which is the sole object of one’s own self-awareness, a person of intelligence will surely incur ridicule in the presence of those whose intellects are deluded by ignorance; therefore,
it is fitting for a wise person to remain silent like one who is dull-witted.
What is this futile effort regarding the description of form and color for one who has been blind from birth?
Victorious are those who have conquered envy, who are exerted for the sake of the welfare of others,
who are firmly established in the prosperity of others, and who are distressed by the misfortunes of others;
they possess a keen curiosity born from hearing the noble discourse of Great Beings.
The virtuous are manifest bridges across the entire ocean of misfortunes.
Mute when slandering others, blind from birth even at the sight of another's wife,
and lame when seizing the wealth of others— he is the Great Man who triumphs in the world.
In times of prosperity, the minds of the great become as delicate as a blue lotus; yet in times of adversity, they become as hard as a mass of solid rock from a great mountain.
Like a cluster of blossoms, there are two possible fates for a wise man:
either he stands at the head of the entire world, or he withers away in the forest.
They are pained by the kindness shown to them and cannot endure being pitied; even in times of calamity, these high-minded ones are difficult to propitiate and are perpetually sorrowful.
Trees grow by the sprinkling of water, but heaps of stones do not;
for that which is capable attains the state of a substance upon encountering such an action.
For the lowest, there is fear of non-existence; for the middling, fear of death;
but for the highest beings, the supreme fear is of being held in contempt.
It dispels suffering, gives birth to happiness, and makes fame radiant;
this meeting with the virtuous is a form of nectar, difficult to obtain.
Whom indeed does the moonlight of association with the virtuous not delight— that which consists of an elixir, is cooling, and bestows supreme bliss?
Those great-souled ones who protect the auspicious flower of discernment, born from the tree of association with the virtuous, are the vessels for the glory of its fruit.
The empty becomes crowded; even death turns into a festival;
and misfortune appears like prosperity in the company of wise men.
Victorious in this world is the singular, virtuous encounter with the good— a wind that dispels the mist of delusion for the lotus-pond of the mind that has fallen into frost.
Know that association with the virtuous is the supreme increase of wisdom, the felling of the tree of ignorance, and the complete removal of mental afflictions.
For one who has bathed in the Ganges of association with the virtuous— cool and pure—
what need is there for gifts, what need for sacred fords, what need for austerities, or what need for sacrifices?
It is my conviction that the hearts of the virtuous alone are firm;
for they are not pierced in the slightest by the sharp arrows of the words of the wicked.
"Alas! For what reason is this mind of the virtuous so difficult to fill, like the ocean?"—as if in anger at this thought, the Creator filled it with the sufferings of others.
Those embodied beings for whom glass is a jewel and a jewel is glass are indeed others; those wise ones who recognize glass as glass and a jewel as a jewel are truly wise.
A debater who is capable of turning faults into virtues and virtues into faults is not speaking the truth; for faults are indeed faults, and virtues are indeed virtues.
If the virtuous, whose inner selves are filled with the heavy burden of a mass of qualities,
show reverence there, what is so wonderful about that?
Let such a quality of the virtuous dissolve back into its own very self—
that quality which, even when being proclaimed by oneself, does not consider it as much as a blade of grass.
Through association with virtuous people, even something insignificant attains dignity;
by being attached to a garland of flowers, even a blade of grass is carried upon the head.
To whom would the fall of a virtuous person— well-conducted, uniform in nature, and held high for the sake of pleasing others—
not cause distress, much like the falling of a pair of breasts?
The sun rises red and sets red as well;
in both prosperity and adversity, the great remain uniform in nature.
The noble one, even when falling, springs up like a ball due to his upward momentum;
however, the ignoble one falls just like a lump of clay.
Even when struck down by blows of the hand, a ball always springs back up;
for generally, the misfortunes of those who lead virtuous lives are transient.
The wise person, though fallen, rises up again, but not so the one of dull intellect;
a ball bounces when it falls, but not so the pair of breasts of a beloved woman.
They have no regard for affection, nor for a worthy recipient, nor for their own circumstances;
always engaged in the welfare of the world, they are supreme like jewel-lamps.
Virtuous people show compassion even toward beings devoid of merit;
for the moon does not withhold its moonlight from the house of a candāla.
Light is not produced in the sun, nor is the earth held up against its course;
for among the virtuous, there is no expectation of a reciprocal favor.
Even when doing harm, one generally attains great merit;

the ocean calms even the submarine fire that seeks to burn it. For some, there are those with good wings—upright, pure, fruitful, and devoted to virtue—who, having seen what is to be seen, see again, and having heard what is to be heard, hear once more.
Truly, no redundancy is seen in one who conducts themselves virtuously.
The virtuous have good wings, are straight, pure, fruitful, and devoted to excellence;
yet, though their qualities are equal, the virtuous and arrows are diverse—the virtuous being truly virtuous, and arrows being merely arrows.
The base, seeking gain, and the high-minded, desiring honor;
the greedy one in the lake seeking fish, and the clarity of the swan’s nature.
When a person who is naturally straightforward hears of the suffering of another,
they experience pain in their heart because they are unable to provide assistance.
They are worthy of homage, they are accomplished, and their birth is indeed praiseworthy— those who,
having abandoned their own interests, accomplish the welfare of their friends.
If Fortune does not take refuge in a man who is free from deceit, greed, and crookedness, who is generous, devoted, and discerning, then Fortune herself is indeed the one deceived.
Health, wisdom, friendship with the virtuous, birth in a noble family,
and self-mastery— these constitute great sovereignty for men, even in the absence of wealth.
Even a very small amount of the excellence of the virtuous is enjoyed by the great, whereas even the entire earth is not the wealth of the wicked;
only water that possesses essence removes thirst, never that from the ocean.
It does not come to pass, or it comes to pass but not for long; even if it comes to pass after a long time, it fails to bear fruit.
The anger of noble beings is equal to the affection of the base.
For those possessed of virtue, even a great fault becomes a merit; for those possessed of vice, even a good deed becomes a fault.
It is like grass for cows, which turns into milk, yet like milk for snakes, which turns into poison.
Even when fallen into adversity, the wise do not desire prosperity mixed with humiliation;
these *cātaka* birds do not drink the water of the earth that is full of dust.
By their very nature, the virtuous among the noble rarely meet with destruction;
for parrots, though capable of clear speech, must endure confinement in a cage.
Even by seeing a person but once, the wise weigh their worthiness and worthlessness; even with a mere touch of the hand, the skilled discern the measure of its weight.
A virtuous person, devoted to the welfare of others, does not harbor enmity even at the time of their own destruction;
even when being cut down, a sandalwood tree perfumes the blade of the axe.
The virtuous generally do not abandon one who is devoted to them, even if that person lacks merit;
the moon carries its dark spot as well, which shares in its own growth and decline.
Even in his final state, the Buddha does not abandon his own qualities due to the purity of his birth;
a conch shell does not lose its whiteness even when consumed and regurgitated by a peacock.
Those who delight in virtues do not become despondent even when they see faults in a person possessed of virtues;
the world looks upon even the spot on the moon with affection.
Friendship formed by walking seven steps together arises naturally among those whose minds are pure;
how much more so between those whose hearts are bound by mutual trust and the recounting of each other's virtues?
To whom would those noble beings not be objects of longing, they who possess upright intentions and a straightforward mind? For them, these three—heart, speech, and conduct—are all in perfect accord.
One who stays near a person of virtue is honored by the world even if they themselves are devoid of virtue;
through association with clear vision, the blind eye receives collyrium.
It is natural for the great to have no attachment to wealth, yet to be miserly toward virtues;
to be cowardly in the face of others' suffering, yet to possess great fortitude in their own sufferings.
Even those of noble character who are deeply provoked become gentle through the application of skillful means, but the base do not; there is a means for melting even hard gold, but none for grass.
Out of their generosity and courage in doing good, those possessed of virtue do not even count a loss;
for indeed, the flames of a lamp produce light by burning their own bodies.
The redness of lotuses, the altruism of virtuous persons,
and the mercilessness of the wicked— this triad in these three things is established by their very nature.
To provide assistance unasked, to forgive those who are inferior, to give without being solicited,
and to inspire others with virtues— only a few among hundreds understand how to do these things.
One who knows virtues delights in the virtuous; one of unvirtuous character finds no satisfaction in the virtuous.
The bee goes from the forest to the lotus, but the frog does not even leave its own dwelling there.
In the beginning they are very slow, in the middle they are of equal flavor,
and in the end they become affectionate when associated with the wise.
This is a certain kind of hard-heartedness found in great beings who possess exalted natures; having performed a service, they keep themselves at a distance.
Out of apprehension that there might be a reciprocal favor expected from others.

If compassion were directed only toward a benefactor or one free from envy, then its limit would be reached there; but when it is felt even for one who is harmful and has suddenly committed an offense, that is the true measure.
He whose mind is compassionate toward the virtuous is the leader among the worthy.
Good people maintain benevolence toward one another from beginning to middle to end,
but not so toward others;
even through cutting, beating, grinding, and heating—
Gold does not undergo the state of being something else.
Lamps illuminate objects that are present;
some, however, are family lamps,
illuminating even those ancestors who have long since passed away.
They manifest [themselves] through the excellence of their own qualities.
Those who are lofty in nature and even loftier are capable of destroying the mental anguish of others, not those who are base;
only clouds can extinguish the fires of the mountains.
Rivers do not remove the heat of summer or the flood of a forest fire.

Virtues flourish among those who recognize virtue; yet, upon encountering one devoid of virtue, they become faults. For rivers that originate from water of excellent taste [may turn bitter] as they flow.
Having reached the ocean, they become undrinkable.
The wind does not uproot the grasses that are soft and bent low in every direction;
it strikes down only those trees that stand tall.
The great undergoes transformation only among the great.
A self-possessed person whose mind has long been purified by association with the virtuous does not fall into the company of the wicked,
even though he ranges within the groves of captivating blue lotuses.
A bee never alights upon a corpse.
Even if he is destitute of wealth or has been driven from his own country,
a man of noble spirit does not seek the service of the base;
even when tormented by hunger, a lion does not consume a mere blade of grass.
He generally drinks the warm blood of elephants.
Generosity when wealthy, forbearance when powerful, freedom from despondency in suffering, and sincerity in virtuous conduct— this is the natural disposition of great-souled beings.
Indeed, a base person wallows in debility when even a mere fragment of pleasure brings joy;
he stumbles and suffers the cholera-like affliction of despair at the slightest hardship.
The minds of the virtuous, however, are neither arrogant and unrestrained nor filled with wretchedness.
The state of being difficult to overcome regarding profound matters, as well as regarding pleasures and non-pleasures.
Gentleness toward one's master, affection toward virtue, lack of arrogance in joy, secrecy regarding counsel, wisdom in learning, generosity upon the rise of wealth,
reverence for the virtuous, aversion toward the wicked, and extreme fear of sin; [these are the marks of a noble person].
Great beings endure suffering and affliction while longing for what is auspicious.
Fortitude in adversity, forbearance in prosperity, eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle,
delight in fame, and devotion to sacred learning— these are the marks of a great man.
For this is indeed established by nature for those of great soul.
For the wise declare that this is the mark indicating the excellence of greatness among the great:
that their minds remain equanimous when pleasure or pain arises.
He does not fall under the sway of either joy or dejection.
Delight in well-spoken words, lack of pride despite prosperity, actions highly effective in accomplishing the welfare of others,
insatiable longing for virtues, and reverence for those who possess virtues.
This conduct of the Great-Souled Ones is hidden.
It is true that for those possessed of virtues, due to the adversity of the times, even qualities acquired through great effort become fruitless in the Kali age;
yet, this very fact is what makes their fruitfulness all the more certain.
For they once again cause the hearts of the wicked to burn with distress.
When a base person, intent on his own ends, speaks with a mind set on deception and full of many flattering words, the virtuous do not fail to recognize it; indeed, they do recognize it. But...
They are unable to fulfill his request in vain.
The base man, devoid of compassion, commits evil;
the man of middling intellect, however, feels compassion even when facing calamity;
but a person of virtuous conduct does not abandon his noble behavior even at the cost of his life.
He is capable of transgressing the boundary, just as the ocean overflows its shore.
He alone is pure, he alone is of noble birth,
and he alone is steadfast who, even in calamities, does not abandon his true nature—
just as the heat produced by the network of the sun's rays [remains constant].
One may even cast off the body, but not its coolness.
Having experienced the pain of begging as if it were the suffering of death,
what indeed can be gained even by giving in great abundance? Here, the virtuous seem to mock even the wish-fulfilling trees.
That which is given away excessively, having been deprived by what was previously intended for oneself.
Those virtuous ones are the crowns of the world’s circle who demonstrate goodness even toward those who offer no benefit;
they have mastered their own purposes and do not weary their bodies [for such ends].
For even a wicked person feels compassion toward those who have previously done him a kindness.
A virtuous person does not harbor even the slightest ill will within; though unprovoked, they do not perceive evil in a slanderer,
for even the rays of the sun that fall upon the mouth of one who hates it are still its foremost part.
The rays of the moon, the lord of stars, scatter nothing but nectar.

Even when provoked, one born of noble family does not speak what should not be said; even when squeezed, sugarcane only yields sweet juice. A base person, even when served with hundreds of virtues, [remains as he is].
In jests or in quarrels, he says that which ought to be said.
Let those skilled in policy either censure me or praise me;
let fortune come or depart as it pleases;
let death occur this very day or in another age.
The wise do not falter from the path of what is right.

For what reason? Because noble people, who are by nature weighty, clearly undertake even a most important task that is incomparable to any other cause. Having risen, why would the Lord of the Ocean not [fill] even a jar?
The Blessed One Agastya drank even the ocean, whose crest was its surging waves.

A righteous livelihood is dear; even in the destruction of life, it is not easy to commit an impure act. The wicked are not to be petitioned, nor should one beg from a friend who possesses little wealth. In adversity, one should stand firm and follow the path of the great.
By whom was this perilous vow, which is like the edge of a sword, taught to the virtuous?
Giving when a guest has arrived at one's well-covered home; acting with prompt hospitality; being free from pride even in the face of prosperity; not disparaging the accounts of others;
maintaining silence after having done a kindness; and speaking only of one's own deeds in an assembly.
Excessive attachment to learning indicates that a man is of noble birth.
By whose command does the seven-horsed sun dispel the darkness of living beings?
By whom has the salutation with joined palms been offered to the trees along the path for the sake of shade? And by whom are the clouds that shed drops of water entreated for the sake of rain?
By their very nature, these [beings] are firmly girded for the task of accomplishing the welfare of others.
The accumulation of its own fruit causes the breaking of the branches of the tree;
the shaking of its tail feathers causes the sluggish movement of the peacock; and that noble horse which is swift in its fourfold gait is driven like an ox.
Indeed, these qualities are generally enemies to a person who possesses virtues.
Where virtues find no renown, how can there be respect for the possessor of those virtues?
What can even a highly learned man do for people who are like stone—
a man whose throat-chanting is turned away by the intoxication of a beautiful woman mounted upon his love?
For even a charming whistling sound can do nothing for one who is deaf; what indeed could it accomplish?
There are thousands of insignificant beings intent solely on the activity of sustaining themselves; but that man alone whose own interest is the welfare of others is the foremost among the virtuous.
To fill a belly so difficult to satisfy, the submarine fire drinks up the lord of rivers.
But Jīmūta [arose] for the sake of dispelling the torment of the world scorched by the summer heat.
Exalting themselves through humility by praising the virtues of others, they proclaim their own merits; while constantly exerting great effort for the sake of others' welfare,
they cause those with foul faces— whose mouths are noisy with insults and harsh words— to suffer by means of patience alone.
Who would not desire those holy ones, whose conduct is wondrous and who are highly esteemed in the world?
Only virtuous people proclaim the abundance of the qualities of the good;
generally, it is the winds that spread the fragrance of flowers in all directions.
Only the virtuous person is truly skilled in relishing the nectar of excellent qualities;
it is said that the cuckoo alone is expert in tasting the fresh sprouts of the mango tree.
Generally, those who are wise are worthy of instruction, not those of dull intellect;
sesame seeds may absorb the fragrance of flowers, but barley never can.
The heart of a wise person attains clarity through very harshness;
indeed, a mirror generally gains its brightness through ash.
The supreme one is able to endure the agitation of the afflictions, but not the other;
just as a gem alone, and not a clod of earth, can withstand being ground upon a great whetstone.
Generally, suffering falls upon the dull-witted, while the virtuous bear it;
when the moon has risen, the lotuses bear the distress of closing.
Generally, only one who knows the subject can discern the difference between qualities; no other can.
The sense of smell perceives the fragrance of jasmine and Arabian jasmine, but the eye does not.
The virtuous do not abandon their own nature even through association with the wicked;
cuckoos do not cease their melodious song because of contact with crows.
The mind of a virtuous person is tender in prosperity but firm in adversity;
the leaf of a tree is delicate in spring but becomes hard in the summer heat.
A virtuous person does not abandon their inherent nature even when fallen into adversity;
camphor, though scorched by fire, retains its fragrance all the more.
Even a time of adversity for a virtuous person attains a state of praise;
even the period of misfortune caused by the assault of Rāhu upon the moon is beautiful.
Having witnessed the wickedness of the evil, a person takes delight in the virtuous;
like a traveler who has climbed a mountain, he attains complete relief.
The noble do not take delight in wealth that is momentary, perishable, and fraught with danger;
having abandoned the filaments of the lotus, swans feed upon the water-moss.
The onset of suffering afflicts the inferior person more severely, but not the superior;
the touch of cold quickly causes pain in the hands and feet, but not in the eyes.
One endowed with virtue who remains for a very long time cannot be endured even by fate;
the glorious moon, its orb full, stays for but a single night.
A person endowed with virtue shines everywhere and excels even more;
like a gem, it is beautiful whether placed upon the head, the neck, the arm, or even on a footstool.
For one who has attained the supreme state, calamities can never truly overcome them for a very long time; it is like the momentary loss of luster in the moon caused by its being swallowed by Rāhu.
The superior person is satisfied with praise, while the base person is satisfied with great wealth;
the gods are pleased by recitations, and the spirits and demons by offerings.
The minds of the virtuous never incline toward evil deeds;
even as clarified butter quickly poured into water may yet become solidified within it.
In this world, it is said that some men are worthy of refinement because they are virtuous;
even when birth, age, and intellect are equal,
this distinction arises here from repeated practice through clear familiarity.
A parrot is able to recite verses, but a crow is never able to do so.

Even wealth given by another becomes a source of suffering in the hearts of those who possess a sense of propriety, yet it brings joy to others; a drop of sandalwood paste causes pain to the eye, though it refreshes the body.
And that very same [feeling] produces delight in another part of the body.

Even if a flaw has arisen by fate in a virtuous person— one born of a noble lineage, who dispels distress, whose conduct is excellent, whose soul is pure, and who is an ornament to the entire world— [it should be concealed].
It will certainly lead to virtue, just like a pearl from a string of gems.

He avoided the home because of impoverished kinsmen, the teacher’s house because of arrogant students, the marketplace because of swindlers from the city, and hermitages because of sages intent on cursing;
he avoided the forest because of lions and the like, the royal court because of villains, and even the horizons because of thieves.
Having observed these confusions, where can the virtuous man, who is truly upright, find rest?
Those exalted by their virtues do not speak with pride, nor what is improbable, nor what deviates from propriety, nor what is unpleasant, nor what is miserable, contemptuous, or dejected.
The good person who has extensively proclaimed the virtues of others attains a superior state of good fortune;
the radiance of the moon, causing the night-lilies to bloom, carries a twofold splendor.
Even for those possessing qualities, the realization of their own true nature occurs only through another;
for it is by means of a mirror's surface that the vision of one's own majesty arises for the eyes.
What is a mountain of a burden for the capable? What is distant for those who are industrious?
What is a foreign land for those possessed of knowledge? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly?
A horse, a weapon, a treatise, a lute, speech, a man, and a woman—
these become fit or unfit depending on the particular person they encounter.
One who is endowed with enthusiasm, not procrastinating, knowledgeable in the methods of action, unattached to vices,
brave, grateful, and firm in friendship.
Fortune herself desires to dwell there.
Even when a person of great character is treated with contempt,
their innate quality of excellence cannot be wiped away;
it is like fire, which cannot be extinguished even if turned downward.
The crest never goes downward at all.
Logic has indeed been abandoned by the wicked, and the Dharma has fallen away; the age of Kali has set in with its supreme turbidity,
and for the most part, evil people have become powerful.
A virtuous person who is free from worldly ambition is indeed a source of contempt for others.
Disputing regarding the vow, doubting solitude, suspecting the truth, being corrupted in discipline,
pride regarding virtues, and rejecting the wholesome— these are [the faults].
The virtuous person does not create opposition toward the Dharma.
He is to be venerated by men and celebrated by the gods through his acts of accumulating compassion and merit;
he has attained the very essence of cyclic existence.
The body is an ornament for assisting others.
He worships without distinction, whether from the bees staying within the interior of a night-lily or those approaching from an opposing lotus;
no one else is so capable as he in the practice of serving both himself and others.
This is the continuous tradition of the virtuous, sweet in its lack of ulterior motive.
Those intentions which, when voiced before people, become like a whirlwind; which cause some kind of internal pain even when not uttered;
and which throb within the heart, clinging to the throat—what are they?
Those who possess merit obtain here a friend whose excellence is beyond description.
The earth is bounded by the ocean, and that storehouse of waters is but a hundred leagues deep;
Pūṣan, ever the traveler, declares the measure of the sky.
Thus, for the most part, all things are sealed with the bud-like closure of a manifest limit.
Furthermore, this boundless blossoming of wisdom of the virtuous prevails.
They do not become angry even at those who cause them harm; out of compassion, they provide assistance.
Capable of uplifting the entire world, they do not desire awakening for themselves alone.
It purifies the vessel and does not diminish its virtues;
it does not destroy the moisture, nor does it produce impurity;
beautiful at the end of its faults, it possesses no flickering instability.
Association with the virtuous is some kind of lamp within the abode of well-performed deeds.
Even a minute jewel is capable of saving the lives of those who have swallowed poison;
even a lion cub, in its fury, challenges elephants;
and even a tiny spark arising from the trunk of a tree consumes the forest.
The innate radiance of those who are great by nature does not depend upon a physical form.
Homage to the wicked! Or rather, who here would not pay homage to them if they wish to live,
since they [the wicked] inflict harm upon those who are like the preeminent sages, even though no fault has been committed?
They lead men to the subterranean realm (rasātala) by means of a curse.
The wise do not speak falsely when they say that a wicked person is even more treacherous than a venomous snake;
for he hates the mongoose clan, he hates the serpent clan, and he is ever a slanderer.
The intellect of the wicked is indeed exceedingly clever when it comes to performing what is utterly defiled;
for the vision of owls perceives form only in the darkness.
The wickedness of the base becomes exceedingly foul when they destroy the virtues of others;
even the clouds, though they obscure the light of the moon, possess a greater darkness within.
