Just as a hand soiled with dust covers a mirror, so does a wicked person treat a virtuous man; yet, the more he attempts to defile him, the more that man’s stainless radiance shines forth.
Bowing down when their lives are seized, yet rising again once they have been taken up—
Are these the younger or the elder buckets of the water-wheel, these wicked ones?
Homage to the one who is always fit for threshing, whose interior is filled with husks,
who possesses many seeds, and who is like a mortar for the wicked!
One who defiles the true vessel with the tongue, seeking alms while intent on quarreling, is always impure; such a slanderer bears a resemblance to a dog.
Alas! A wicked man, though foolish and unlearned, becomes a master of speech; he is a mere vessel for proclaiming his own virtues, yet a lord of eloquence when it comes to reviling others.
The wicked man, intent on slandering the virtuous, has eyes, heads, and faces everywhere;
possessing ears in every direction, he stands encompassing the entire world.
When there is praise for the virtuous, the tongue of a fool— afflicted by the disease of envy—
does not move at all, even when pulled by the beak of a heron.
By its very nature, this world is like an illusion, agitated by passion, hatred, and pride;
it deludes even the great, just as a wicked person deludes others through the cycle of existence.
Even a magician creates a painting with ease as a mere sport;
yet he is considered a "khala" (a base person) because he stands lightly amidst the great.
Alas, O subjects! Where will you go when you are ruled by one who is base, intoxicated with wealth, powerful, malicious, and entrenched in his position?

A hundred deeds done for the wicked are lost; a hundred well-spoken words are lost on the ignorant. A hundred speeches are lost on one who does not act upon them; a hundred insights are lost on the insentient.

A gift given to an unworthy recipient is lost; benefit is lost when it is disregarded by one who lacks the sense of its fruit. Virtue is lost upon one who does not recognize virtue; courtesy is lost upon one who is ungrateful.
With hands raised from afar, eyes moist with affection, offering half his seat and intent on firm embraces; giving answers that linger upon inquiries about pleasant topics—
he is like one whose inner venom is concealed while his exterior is full of honey, being exceedingly composed of illusion.
What indeed is this unprecedented method of drama that has been learned by the wicked?
Those straightforward-minded people who strive to remove the great merit long accumulated by the noble ones are to be honored; such wicked men are like virtuous ones.
Oh, how difficult it is to grasp the minds of the wicked, whose intellects are crooked!
One thing is in their speech, another is in their throat, and yet another resides between their lips.
While there were wicked people, we set out to acquire virtues;
this is that mockery of purchasing jewels in a village of thieves.
Both of them grow as if in competition through success that has a hundred branches:
the sprout produced from a refuse heap, and the man born of a noble family.
Being burned by the extremely sharp fire of the fame of others,
those base individuals, being unable to reach that same state, then began to engage in slander.
That very thing by the mere remembrance of which the virtuous undergo a continuous succession of intense suffering,
the wicked indeed treat with utter contempt, even as they laugh.
How can a person who does not know the treatises distinguish between virtues and faults? Does a blind man have the capacity to perceive the various differences in forms?
Generally, one who is impure comes to light through the affliction of the virtuous;
for had the sun not been swallowed, who would have known the son of Siṃhikā?
A wicked person is generally and constantly intent upon harming others;
because it is something they feel compelled to do, they do not require a specific cause.
With a slight thing it rises up, and with a slight thing it goes down;
oh, how similar is the behavior of the scale-beam and of the wicked man!
Oh, how similar is the nature of phlegm and that of a wicked person!
Phlegm becomes provoked by sweet things and is pacified by bitter ones.
Just as a weary lord of elephants, seeking shade, takes refuge under a tree, yet having rested, destroys that very tree— so does the base person destroy his own benefactor.
A wicked person should be avoided even if they are adorned with learning;
can a snake ever cease to be terrifying, even if it is decorated with a jewel?

Beauty for the sake of another's wife, wealth for the sake of tormenting the world, and power for the destruction of the virtuous— these qualities in a wicked man are even more wicked than his wickedness itself.
For those who subsist on the mere acquisition of knowledge gained by harming others,
the gathering of virtues is like the gathering of lines for a net by rogues who act as fishermen.
Even the sweet words spoken by a wicked person produce terror in me, like untimely blossoms.
The wicked man feels no shame even for the crooked conduct of a serpent, which is avoided by the virtuous; he possesses a mind that is unrighteous and devoid of compassion.
For a wicked person considers only his own cleverness to be wisdom.
He highly prizes his own conduct while harboring grief in his heart due to words of compassion;
the man of limited intellect clearly disparages his own fitness while offering praise for himself; he speaks of resorting to censurable means while claiming that misfortune is stable.
Having heard this heart-piercing suffering, an ordinary person spreads forth intense agony.
If it is argued that this is for the ripening of merit, then why did he not take it even earlier?
If it is for his own sake, why does he not share it with the poor and his own kinsmen? If it is because of fear of those who watch for his flaws, then why would one who is greedy abandon it?
Thus, a person who has performed a service generally harbors expectations for a reward.
How marvelous is his unimpeded valor in battle, which has humbled Indra;
how the Blessed One, the Lord of Fortune, was made fortunate by him with his hands held high in the *pāñca* gesture;
how sovereignty over the seven worlds was attained by his own hand, and fame that reached the further shore of the ocean was won.
Everything belonging to Bali was suddenly and clearly destroyed through association with wicked people.

Fame pacifies the afflictions; it produces [the desire for] fame, leads to an inauspicious rebirth, generates distress and weariness for people, and brings about ridicule. It causes the mind to wander, destroys pride, and diminishes one's lifespan.
Association with the wicked casts away the entire multitude of virtues.
Although the study of knowledge serves to pacify those ignorant of the grounds of discipline, for one who is naturally crooked, it leads only to an increase in wickedness;
yet may this [study] be capable of cutting through the darkness of those who harbor the fear of serpents.
The light from the jewel on the hood of a venomous snake, however, causes intense fear.
Even when being honored, the wicked person, dedicated to the ruin of the world,
causes terror at every sight, like a snake in the house.
Even an atheist trembles before a man who has fallen from truth and righteousness as if before an angry venomous serpent; how much more so, then, a believer?
Those for whom the slaughter of living beings is a sport, whose words cut to the very vitals,
and whose purpose is the torment of others— they are the death even of Death itself.
Alas! What great suffering! This world is utterly perverse, in that the virtuous man is treated with contempt, while the wicked man is gratified by it.
The wicked, possessing evil minds, do not desire to perceive the virtues of others as much as they desire to know their lack of virtue.
A wise person should avoid a wicked man in both friendship and enmity;
like a dog, he causes injury whether by wagging his tail or by biting.
Therefore, nothing else in the world is found to be more ridiculous than when a wicked person calls a virtuous person "wicked."
A virtuous person should be content with the wicked even when they cause harm;
it is no gain at all for a serpent to be coiled around one if it does not bite.
Obtained [as ruler], he will be arrogant, dishonest, foolish, and an exclusively cruel master;
this wicked man, having caused many virtuous people to die, shall himself perish.
What rivalry can there be between a malicious person and a self-respecting virtuous man,
for whom terrifying speech and the reviling of the good are considered ornaments?
Thorns pierce with a single point the foot of one person;
but the wicked, with a thousand faces from afar, take the lives of all living beings.
Having created the tip of the wicked tongue that takes the lives of all living beings among men,
why did the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) pointlessly create weapons, poisons, and fires?
Just as a virtuous person is ever vigilant regarding the benefit of others,
so too does a wicked person remain constantly on guard against the harm of others.
The base person fears the slanderer who is skillful at exposing faults, yet the one with a deluded heart does not fear his own blameworthy actions.
For the wicked person whose fire of anger blazes in vain and who speaks harsh words,
there is no remedy whatsoever other than the Unsurpassed [Dharma].
For the wicked and for thorns, there are exactly two remedies:
either wearing shoes, cutting off their tips, or avoiding them from afar.
Even while living, a good person is not able to do as much for others as a wicked person,
once dead, can do for their benefit.
Whatever is most dear to oneself, that indeed should be given to one who possesses virtue;
for this very reason, a wicked person bestows his own faults upon the virtuous.
Disease, a tumor, a sprout, fire, poison, a mule, wood-boring insects, and worms,
as well as a person who is ungrateful by nature— these flourish without destroying their own substratum.
A wicked person does not find delight without reviling others;
for a dog, having tasted all kinds of flavors, is not satisfied without excrement.
It is better that a virtuous person be utterly fruitless yet pleasant to associate with,
than that a wicked person be sharp and lethal like an arrow, even if he bears fruit.
Whom does a wicked person not wound? For he is sharp by his very nature; even when taking up a partisan, like an arrow released from its string, he is devoid of virtue.
A wicked person cannot be made into a good person even with great effort;
who, even by means of refinement, could make garlic fragrant?
Like a lowly man who has risen up, inevitably failing to find support elsewhere, he finds pleasure through a flaw; the illustration here is the one born from the loins.
In debate he was like the ten-faced Rāvaṇa; in searching for the faults of others, he was like the thousand-eyed Indra;
in seizing the conduct of the virtuous, he was like Arjuna with his thousand arms—a base man indeed.
Those men whose minds have been corrupted by the wicked place no trust even in a virtuous person.
A child who has been burned by milk-porridge will blow upon it and eat it, even if it is curd.
In the beginning, it causes shame; in the middle, it brings contempt;
and at the end, it leaves one empty—this is the case for one who speaks even a single word well-placed while associating with the wicked.

Who indeed could relax their suspicion toward those wicked men, who by nature conceal their enmity while appearing as divine seers who pierce the vital secrets of others, and who are devoted to deceit?

An ignorant person is easy to please; one who possesses specialized knowledge is even more difficult to please. But a man who is puffed up by a mere fragment of knowledge does not delight even Brahmā.
One who is obsessed with what is impossible is generally a fool, not a wise man;
for who other than a child would wish to grasp the shimmering reflection of the moon in water?
For even when he has attained his rise, a wicked man first brings distress to his own kin;
like a rising fire, he utterly consumes the very wood from which he was born.
One who has heard but a tiny fragment generally displays an excessive abundance of eloquence;
for it is the poor actor alone who everywhere most excessively mimics a drama.
Only the wicked, having seized the burden of those possessed of virtues, drag them forward before them;
for it is only straw and wood that float upon the ocean, not jewels.
That which is placed upon the heads of the great, the wise regard as mere straw;
the wise bow to the insignia, while the crow treats it as its own seat.
Even for those who dwell together, if they are wicked, there is no intimacy, like that of a lotus and water;
but even for the virtuous who dwell afar, there is affection, like that of the night-lily and the moon.
Even when relying on a completely pure livelihood, a wicked person causes distress to others;
even serpents that feed only on air do not refrain from harming others.
Whatever purpose an ignorant person accomplishes, that for him is a mere coincidence, like the "crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya);
for even a wood-boring insect, by chance, somehow carves out a syllable within pieces of wood.
Generally, those of a base nature do not become beneficial unless they have been humiliated;
the *aśoka* tree blooms even more profusely when struck by the feet of a courtesan.
The skill that a wicked person possesses in piercing the vital organs of others is not employed for their welfare;
the potency that poison has in causing destruction is not for the sake of benefit.
Even when treated with great honor, the treacherous never abandon their innate nature;
indeed, was not the moon held upon his head by the Great Lord, yet it remained curved?
Like the wind, these common folk generally take on the form of others through contact;
but the virtuous, like the rays of the sun, remain unattached even when in conjunction with both the good and the bad.
Even a most ignoble person incites another toward the oppression of the world, just as even a poor man might incite Śakra;
and a stone, though itself incapable of cutting, sharpens the edge of a sword.

People are keen to perceive the transgressions of others even when they are far away, yet not their own even when close at hand; one does not see one's own wound, but scrutinizes the spot on the moon.
The wicked reveal their own true nature by inflicting excessive wounds upon the virtuous; hunters kill deer even when they are dead, but they do not seize the lion.
It is for this reason that the ignoble constantly afflict the virtuous man, even though he is unchanging:
what has the lotus done here to the frost, that it always burns it?
The wise are unable to speak of the faults of others, even when they exist, just as they cannot speak of their own virtues;
whereas the wicked, however, proclaim the faults of others, even if they do not exist, just as they boast of their own virtues.
A virtuous person feels shame even when [an error] is pointed out by another; whereas a base person, having not done it at all, proclaims it himself. Fie upon such meanness!
Even when facing his own destruction, a wicked man does not account for the suffering and misfortune of others;
indeed, when a thousand have perished at the front of battle, the headless torso often dances.
Due to their innate wickedness, even the virtues of the unrighteous cause distress to the world, just like their faults;
even the fragrance of poisonous flowers, though sweet, bewilders the minds of men.
One who has gained height, though once lowly, overcomes his master most quickly;
for the dust on the road first covers that which raises it up.
Garlic, though perfumed with the scents of musk, camphor, agallochum,
and sandalwood, does not relinquish its foul odor, just as a base person does not abandon their innate, natural disposition.
"There has been a service rendered by this one to my heart"—such a consideration never exists among the wicked;
like fire that has flared up along with the *hotṛ* priest, it burns its own very support.
Indeed, doing a favor for the wicked becomes the cause of even greater harm;
for by acting in accordance with their wishes, they become excessively provoked, like diseases.

Indeed, nothing else bears fruit; rather, it is the thorny plant alone that brings about misfortune, until—like a poisonous tree—it suddenly kills the very person who relies upon it for relief from fatigue.
For the wicked, inflicting injury upon others regardless of their own interest is nothing but a calamity;
even when hunger or thirst ceases, a venomous snake does not stop from biting.
Just as water and milk that have become one, or like the minds of friends,
the power of swans and of wicked people lies in their ability to separate what has been mixed.
Even a poisoned arrowhead, smeared with deadly *hālāhala* venom, can be endured by the steadfast when it strikes within;
but not the false and wicked speech of a villain provoked without cause.
In this world, hunters, fishermen, and slanderers are enemies without cause toward deer, fish, and virtuous people, who sustain themselves with contentment upon grass and water.
Vast at its beginning yet extremely thin at the end, causing division and stained;
as crooked as a buffalo's horn, the affection of the wicked brings fear to a person.
The friendship of the wicked turns a worthy vessel into an unworthy one; it burns away virtues and swiftly destroys affection. It bestows impurity upon the pure, like the flame of a lamp.
To whom have faults not been surrendered by that wicked man, nor virtues forcibly seized?
Nevertheless, he is not separated from his own faults.
Even when touched by a single quality, it is not variegated.
That one who is being propitiated in many ways does not actually become propitiated— what is surprising about that? But this unprecedented excellence of intuition is truly marvelous.
That which, when cultivated, turns into an enemy.
Having encountered reproach for his faults, the wise man turns away from them and is deeply distressed, thinking,
"I am known to have faults in every respect."
An evil person commits even more evil.
In this very way, one cannot even survive among the wicked; what then can be said of those who are favorites of the king? For even Nala was previously difficult to endure.
How much more so, then, when it is driven by a powerful wind?
The gods did not drink the nectar from the ocean, nor did Hara consume the fierce *hālāhala* poison; indeed,
it was deposited by Fate within the speech of the wicked.
These two are external; the other is internal.
For he who becomes angry on account of a specific cause will certainly become placid when that cause has passed away;
however, for one whose mind harbors hatred without cause, [there is no such relief].
How will another satisfy him?
That which is otherwise is called outward-facing;
yet that which throbs within the heart is indeed other than that. This conduct does not lead the undisciplined across.
Like the reflection of water on a yoke, they are non-existent for those who lack [wisdom].
Where is the path of the slanderer obstructed?
He bites even that which is seen and heard;
it is exceedingly difficult for one whose vision is not detached.
Furthermore, this [world] is [afflicted] by those whose hearing and sight possess the venom of poison.
Let fools travel by means of hundreds of elephants and horses; let the wise travel on foot, devoid of wealth. Even a row of crows perched upon a mountain peak—
It does not equal the royal swans resting upon the sandy banks.
One who puts you to shame with pleasant words while feigning respect, and who belittles you while exalting himself— such a foolish friend should be avoided in every way.
This assembly of virtuous people, greedy for even a fraction of merit, does not conceal a fault even when it is manifest;
they remain exceedingly harsh toward those who are devoid of faults.
The time comes for the barking of the dogs of slanderers who are enraged.
When one engages in dispute, then fame is destroyed;
when one practices loving-kindness, then virtues are corrupted.
Having observed the state of affairs in both ways, the discerning person examines them closely.
He treats ordinary people with contempt and strikes them down.
Whether cherished, or caressed by hundreds of good deeds, or embraced, or protected from hundreds of calamities—
an evil person never produces anything but misconduct.
He sleeps with confidence in the middle of his lap like a serpent.
It cries out harshly and becomes enraged without cause;
it defiles through touch and prevents entry;
it bites in a shameful manner and is never satisfied.
And what indeed is the difference between a dog and a wretch?
A snake kills that which it strikes with its foot, or that which it crushes with its firm staff, or indeed that which it bites with its fang; yet today,
there is another entirely who, like a serpent, acts as a slanderer.
It touches one ear and destroys the other along with its very root.
It is indeed fitting that some, relying upon that wisdom which has attained uninterrupted activity, should restrain the spreading darkness of conceit in this world.
Alas, they extend this blindness of egoism with its hundred branches!
O Kālakūṭa,
by whom was this sequence of ever-increasingly superior stations taught to you—
first in the heart of the ocean, and then to the bull-bannered Śiva?
Now you dwell in the throats of the wicked, and moreover, in their speech.
Generally impure by nature, a wicked person staying near the great inflicts injury upon those who seek their aid;
even though he brings happiness to the entire world, he is like one afflicted by the cold.
While smoke remains, fire cannot be enjoyed with ease.
Smoke, having somehow attained the position of a cloud, quenches the heat of a fire with showers of rain; likewise,
one of impure nature, having by chance attained greatness—
For the most part, it disregards even one's own kinsmen.
Of this man who hates virtue, who has by fate obtained power, who is unrestrained and has exalted all the wicked, and who has forgotten his own base course of action born in a previous life;
By whom can one dwell in happiness when entering the range of experience of the lowly?
It is no wonder now that,

through the stroke of ill fortune, this base man of little stature stands so high, while he who is truly great does not; even though he is crowded with hundreds of impurities and filth from the streets.
On the back there is refuse, but not a treasure-trove.
One might forcibly extract a jewel from between the fangs of a makara’s mouth;
one might cross even the ocean, agitated by garlands of surging waves;
one might carry even an enraged serpent upon one's head like a flower.
But one should not seek to please the minds of foolish people who are stubbornly attached [to their views].
One might obtain oil from sand by pressing it with effort;
one afflicted by thirst might drink water from a mirage;
and one wandering about might perhaps even find the horn of a hare.
But one should not seek to please the minds of foolish people who are stubbornly attached [to their views].
I have wept in the wilderness; I have massaged a corpse;
I have planted a lotus on dry land and rained down upon barren soil for a very long time; I have tried to bend a dog's tail and whispered incantations into the ear of a deaf man.
The ignorant person has been sprinkled with the cosmetic ointment applied to the face of one who is blindfolded.

In vain was the ox milked; for a long time the cow, burdened by the weight of her udders, was embraced as if she were a young woman; and hope for beryl was placed in a fragment of glass shimmering with rays.
By me, a fool, bowing down to you who are pitiable and ignorant of virtue.

An arrow, even while remaining on the path of the heart of a bow, meets with one of these fates: the severing of its own side, the loss of its properly gathered fruit, the breaking of its own form, a fall into impurity, or total destruction.
Indeed, from the clinging of the crooked to the straight, evil clearly arises.

That power of virtues brings calamity upon those very virtues; had the Creator not united me with them, I would have been despondent due to my misfortune, seeing the virtuous man possessed of qualities while I remained devoid of them.
In his own home, he certainly performs a festival of constant and abundant prosperity.
Having perceived his own self to be devoid of virtues, he desires those found in others; yet this does not bear fruit for him, for if he does not lament, there are no such virtuous ones here.
Consequently, he exerts himself to wipe them away, to curse them, or to treat them with contempt.
Alas! This lowly and delightful desire to conquer through qualities has been abandoned.
If you cannot endure the virtues of others, then strive to acquire them yourself;
for it is not possible to wipe away the fame of another under the pretext of disparaging it.
Cease, if you will not, from these mental pursuits driven by attachment and aversion.
With parasols in your hands, you shall dispel the fatigue caused by the rays of the sun.
In the intense association born of their very birth between the gem and the serpent,
the gem does not partake of the serpent's faults, nor does the serpent partake of the gem's virtues; indeed,
whether a person is wicked or virtuous, it is by their very nature.
Due to non-attachment, there is neither wickedness nor goodness in anyone at all.
Poison cannot be turned into nectar even by hundreds of efforts;
the neem tree does not abandon its own bitterness even when standing in a pool of milk. Likewise, a wicked person does not speak noble speech that is refined with virtues.
Even after a long time, how can there be the form of gold in iron that has been swollen by its own strength?
It would be better to place both hands into the mouth of a wrathful beast;
it would be better to drink poison and fall asleep in the abode of Death;
it would be better to cast one's body from the peak of a great mountain and have it shattered into a hundred pieces.
But one does not truly accomplish one's own welfare by means of wealth acquired through base people.
Established in outward appearance, he does not calculate the weight or lightness [of his actions], nor does he hesitate anywhere;
he does not examine form at all, nor the conduct of men—how then could there be news of him? Alas, he fears neither great infamy nor even the most grievous scandals.
Death, a foolish poet, a villain, a wicked king, and a thief—these are equal in their actions.
A lion took away the life of Pāṇini, the beloved author of grammar;
an elephant violently crushed the sage Jaimini, the founder of Mīmāṃsā;
and a crocodile killed Piṅgala, a treasure-house of knowledge in prosody, on the shore of the sea.
What is the use of virtues for those animals whose minds are struck by ignorance and who are filled with excessive rage?
He reviles those worthy of worship; he mocks the suffering; he afflicts his kinsmen;
he hates the brave; he treats with contempt those who have lost their wealth; he commands those who depend on him;
he makes secret matters public; and he strives to foster an attitude of enmity.
The wicked man quickly abandons what is unspeakable, yet accepts virtues while rejecting faults.
In the intense suffering of others, he laughs and plays out of joy;
yet, through delusion, he stumbles and falters at even a slight affliction of his own. This base man roars and speaks what is censurable toward those who are proud.
Having been made to hear even a small amount of harsh speech, he comes to strike.
If you will be devoted to the company of the virtuous, you will flourish;
but if you fall among the assemblies of the wicked, you will perish.
They whisper it into the ear with the sounds of drums; that which was proclaimed throughout the kingdom, they speak of piteously with bowed bodies so that one may become free from sin.
They praise what is uttered even by a debtor, for it is not a harsh word that strikes at the vital core.
Are those who are indeed treasuries of deceit and folly not the ones who captivate kings?
The merchant displays his prowess in the dance hall, the ragged poet in the streets of clever talk,
the village dog in the courtyard of its own home, and the rat clearly in the hole beneath the mountain peak; likewise, the rogue enters the palace of the king with the boldness of a glutton.
They go like turtles dragged from a pond; it is strange that they should go elsewhere than there.
In one who possesses modesty, dullness is counted as a fault; in one who delights in vows, hypocrisy; in one who is pure, deceit;
in a hero, cruelty; in one who is upright, perversity; in one who speaks kindly, wretchedness;
in one who is brilliant, arrogance; in a speaker, garrulity; and in one who is steadfast, incapacity.
What indeed could be the virtue of those possessed of virtues that has not been marred by wicked people?
A rat attempts to scale Mount Kailāsa; a crow, craving the flesh of Garuḍa, seeks to seize him;
a restless mongoose, wishing to kill the serpent Takṣaka, wags its tail at his base;
and a frog, desiring to reach the far shore of the great devouring ocean, even attempts to cross over a serpent.
Generally, one who is near death remembers their habitual actions, not their trivial deeds.
A speck of a fault and a heap of virtues—these two, by chance, have fallen into the mouth of a wicked man;
one spreads like oil upon water, while the other becomes as solid as ghee.
What refuge have they taken that kills them like poison? Why are riches not abandoned nor enjoyed by this wretched man?
A donor equal to a miser has never existed, nor will there ever be one:
he who bestows wealth upon others without even touching it himself.

That misfortune which occurs when wealth is lost— whether for one who possesses it or for a generous donor— is already attained by the miser even before that loss, due to the deficiency of his wisdom.
If those who possess wealth are wealthy because of that wealth which is empty of both giving and enjoyment,
then why are we not wealthy by means of that very same wealth?
If one delights in wealth buried in the middle of one's house,
why would one not delight in Mount Meru by following that same principle?
What could a hungry parrot do even if a *kiṃśuka* tree were laden with fruit?
What could dependents do even if their benefactor were wealthy but stingy?
If that wealth of men is barren of both giving and enjoyment, and is not enjoyed by friends,
then what indeed would be misfortune?
The wealth of those who have accumulated it with great effort becomes the cause for another;
by one it is gathered with exertion, and by others the honey is drunk.
Whatever you give to the distinguished and whatever you eat day after day—that, I consider, is your true wealth; the rest you merely guard for someone else.
Fortune is but a mockery in a man who is defiled by dependence on others;
what beauty could he display here, like the fashioning of bracelets upon a withered arm?
He who, having rendered a service, desires a return favor from that person, is wretched;
because he is subject to craving, he licks up even what has been vomited.
Giving, enjoyment, and destruction are the three destinies of wealth;
for him who neither gives nor enjoys it, the third destiny—destruction—is his.
If one is wealthy merely by the existence of wealth, even without giving or enjoying it, then why are we not also wealthy? For Mount Meru remains as our gold.
Even the wealthy, if they neither give nor enjoy their riches, are counted among the ranks of the truly great poor;
for since it does not quench one's thirst, even the ocean is but a desert.
Those who are pursued by the wise day after day through their comings and goings become utterly weary;
having encountered the proximity of wretched folk, they lie down as if asleep.
For those men who are timid regarding enjoyment and intent only on the accumulation of wealth,
riches remain in the house like a jewel of a maiden, for the sake of another.
Those in the world who possess wealth but lack generosity are the most foolish;
they experience only the sufferings of guarding their riches and being separated from them.
There are some who are exceedingly clever at enjoying even the riches of the wretched;
yet the abundance of water from the ocean constantly finds its end in the submarine fire.
Though they have attained them, these wretched ones, by virtue of their own past actions, are unable to enjoy their wealth;
for it is said that when grapes ripen, crows suffer from inflammation of the mouth.
The miserly do not relinquish their wealth from their hands, just as drops of oil do not leave dust; yet,
by some stroke of fate, they may eventually be spent by the one who employs them.
They desire to go forth together with the impurities.
That wealth which is hoarded and not employed in sacrifices, nor given to the virtuous when requested— that wealth guarded by a miser— [is of no use].
And he goes to the houses of thieves and kings.
Better these trees that dwell in the forest,
their beauty of fruit plundered by flocks of birds; not so the houses of the wealthy, which are as wretched as a [decaying] hood.
Their conduct was like that of serpents who have deposited their jewels.
For one who is well-restrained and carefully protects life as if it were their own, and who maintains self-discipline even toward their own body,
as they follow your path through the succession of existences—
With deceitful wealth, the five steps were not fulfilled.
Oh, how great is the cleverness of riches when they dwell happily in the house of a miser!
They neither reach the state of being given away nor the state of being enjoyed.
And they manifest a certain supreme state of nirvana.
His thirst for the inner peace [of liberation] was not quenched by the mingling of wealth with salt-water; his physical luster was impaired by long-term consumption of tasteless and parched food;
and he suffered from insomnia and weak digestion due to the fear of kings, water, thieves, and fire.
For the miserly, suffering is manifest as even more extreme than the suffering of poverty itself.
Each one is devoted to excellence, uniquely skilled in the knowledge of others' virtues;
these wealthy men are masters in all the arts, adept in the conduct of teachers.
Yet, alas, they tremble with praise even at hearing the words of a mere flower!
When the earrings were worn down by rubbing against the crown of his head during ascetic practices, they became diminished.
He does not manifest joy toward a friend for fear of the expenditure of wealth; being afraid, he is not drawn by service for fear of having to return a favor;
he speaks falsely for fear of being asked for his money, and he is not pleased even by praise.
How can a farmer live, terrified by the loss and depletion of his wealth?
If, by the turn of fate, the moon were placed upon one's head because it was considered the essence of all virtues— why was its waning orb not instantly brought to fullness? Thus,
for the sake of worldly devotion, they falsely proclaim their own integrity toward the virtuous with great ostentation.
The wealthy, their minds trembling at the expenditure of wealth, perform honorific acts that are empty of actual meaning.
What cause for greed is there for a wise man in the mere shell of the universe?
The great ocean is never agitated by the leaping of a small fish.
Those of unrestrained mind do not set foot upon even the slightest [virtue],
for even when they have attained the world, their desires remain boundless.
For men whose minds are haughty, these two things bring happiness:
either the cessation of all attachments or vast and extensive prosperity.
"This one is a kinsman, that one is a stranger"—such a calculation belongs to those of small minds; for men of noble heart, the entire earth itself is their family.
Let alone old age, death, poverty, and disease—
for why does even birth itself repeatedly cause such shame to the wise man?
In this revolving cycle of saṃsāra, who is there that has not died and been born again?
He alone is truly born by whose birth a lineage attains greatness.
Would that such a superior man could be seen upon this earth— one by whom the wealthy, with their faces swollen with pride, have never been looked upon.
The earth and the qualities of the earth are to be honored; there are kings who possess discernment.
Why, then, do those of exalted intellect fall into the state of defeat?
It is fitting for a blind man who has never seen the face [of his benefactor] to beg;
alas, what great misery it is that even one with eyes begs!
The torment of the fire of poverty has been extinguished by the water of contentment; who indeed could witness the internal burning of the frustration of a supplicant’s hopes?
He alone possesses the majesty arising from the full enjoyment of perfected virtues;
for he has no desire even for wealth that is coveted by the three worlds.
For those who are intoxicated by their very learning and yet remain miserly despite possessing wealth—
for them, cursed by fate, fire has arisen from the water.
What is the use of that fortune which is like a bride kept for oneself alone,
and which, unlike a courtesan, is not enjoyed even by common travelers?
Generosity is the virtue of the wealthy; wealth is the virtue of those who practice generosity.
But when wealth and generosity are separated from one another, they are a mere mockery.
Like a cluster of blossoms, the conduct of a wise person is twofold:
either it stands at the head of the entire world, or it withers away in the forest.
He alone among men bears the foremost burden who, with the hand of generosity,
wipes away the dust of supplication that has grown grey upon the faces of those who seek his aid.
Blessed are those who do not hear the piteous words of their supplicants, having fulfilled their desires through mere mental representation alone.
That intellect which is devoid of courage is considered mere womanhood;
and that courage which is not endowed with discipline is bestiality, not manliness.
Wise men may indeed relinquish even their dear lives,
but they do not desire even great honors from their enemies.
I consider this nature of the mindless one to be most wonderful:
that even when being benefited, it neither feels joy nor undergoes dissolution.
The mind feels shame even toward one who has previously returned a favor or performed a service;
yet, a benefit bestowed upon one who has already rendered a service is greater than death itself.
Even one who returns a great favor does not become equal to the original benefactor;
one merely imitates what was done, whereas another acts without any motive at all.
For he who brings life to his kinsmen, his dependents, and his friends, his domestic prosperity is truly fruitful; fie upon the abundance of wealth that cannot provide for others!
Even a cloud, though it consists of water, becomes beloved to all the world;
yet the sun, though its rays are constantly extended, becomes unpleasant to the eye.
That which has not been attained by anyone, from which even their desires turn back—even that is not obtained; what, then, is the fruit of the pride of other high-minded men?
The joining together or the breaking apart of actions occurs through the application of destiny;
whether in appropriate or inappropriate action, my engagement and withdrawal depend upon that.
Though one’s life may endure for an eon, neither vitality nor sovereignty is attained, nor even that which is desired;
yet the world still performs what ought not to be done—what purpose does it have in view?
Abundance of wealth is no cause for pride; some are naturally open-handed.
In the rainy season, whose abundance of water is greater: that of the clouds or the ocean?
If she was begotten by herself, then she is his own daughter; if by her father, then she is indeed his sister, Śrī;
and if she has had union with another, then she is another's wife.
Those of wise intellect become fixed in their minds upon the relinquishing of that [attachment].
The toil born of acquiring wealth,
even when it has borne fruit for this person, is tasteless;
for the acquisition of wealth is for one's own satisfaction.
The acquisition of virtues in order to win over others to the supreme [state].
When there are boon-granting deities present, that man of deluded intellect who praises one man over another while craving a mere fragment of wealth—
I consider him to be a cruel man, the very first of his kind.
Just as a body, it is said, appears like a piece of wood when deprived of life,
even so do I perceive my own life when devoid of shame.
It is empty of the supramundane that has been manifested.
Even though they are peaceful, where could they scatter their splendor?
Where could they not blaze? And where indeed would they not be renowned?
For surely the Creator himself has obstructed them by confining them within [the body].
Within the shell of the Brahma-egg, they are like lamps inside jars.
For even when one whose conduct is steadfast is treated with contempt,
their quality of being a true being cannot be erased;
it is like fire that has been turned face-downward.
The crest never goes downward at all.
It is illogical to say that those who have been born will not perish;
for arising itself is necessarily the cause of destruction.
And this remains true even when there is equal affliction by the calamity of death.
Death is better for one whose intention is dedicated to the welfare of others.
Even in this boundlessly vast expanse of time, only these two or three virtues have reached the state of being fully matured;
oh, how worldly is the people, for they find no supreme satisfaction in these!
Stiff with pride, he considers even this entire blade of grass as something significant.

These wise ones do not experience even a slight torment within themselves merely by reflecting on their own minds, for no harm has yet been done by that [reflection]; yet those who, day and night, here and now, act solely in accordance with the minds of others—
They carry themselves with a desire for victory; how can they be objects of compassion?

In the past, some with vast hearts created the world; others maintained it, and still others gave it away as if it were a blade of grass. Indeed, here in this world, other steadfast ones enjoy fourteen realms.
What is this fever of pride in men who possess only the lordship over a few towns?

Since not even a single moment of this earth has passed without being enjoyed by hundreds of kings, what great esteem can there be for rulers in the mere acquisition of it? They are merely lords over a fraction of a fraction, over but a tiny portion of its parts.
When sorrow ought to be felt, fools instead display joy.
O heart, why do you not venture day after day to lead the minds of others— who are turbid with afflictions— to great clarity?
For when you yourself are serene, you possess the qualities of a spontaneously arisen *cintāmaṇi* jewel.
Is that thought, being secluded, not nourishing what you desire?
Even without wealth, the steadfast man touches the state of being highly honored;
yet the wretched man, even when embraced by wealth, falls into a state of humiliation.
For the vast attainment of a multitude of virtues that arises from one's own nature—
Even a dog wearing a necklace of gold cannot attain the majestic splendor of a lion.
Those two alone truly live whose wealth is enjoyed comfortably by supplicants as if they were in their own homes,
and whose sharp intellect serves to dispel the darkness [of ignorance];
whereas he who is concerned only with himself, even if he possesses great power, is wretched for lack of wisdom.
For that which possesses a form like a painted jewel, its existence is indeed non-existence.
The earth serves as a support for the act of providing space; space serves for the act of seeing;
and the sun serves for the act of establishing its own greatness—such are certain other qualities.
Thus, toward this group of benefactors that is ever difficult to abandon, [one should remain devoted].
How can the minds of those with great intelligence cast off the stain of despondency and shame?

That which is always enjoyed by teachers, servants, kinsmen, and good friends, but not according to one's own whim; which enemies do not covet when it has been acquired through valor; and whose existence arises only through the depletion of wealth or the loss of friends—[such is the nature of sovereignty].
What kind of joy is that for those possessed of virtue, compared to which the joy of a two-legged being toward a four-legged one is not even a fraction?
For the virtuous who do not abandon the path of justice, misfortunes may arise by chance;
let them be like those that befell Bali while he was personally bestowing the earth upon the Primal Being,
or like those of Śakra through his many loathsome and censurable deeds.
May I not even possess sovereignty over the gods, for that would be a cause for my downfall.

The bed is the grassy meadow, the seat is the pure rock, and the dwelling is beneath the trees; the drink is the cool water of mountain streams, the food is tubers, and the companions are the deer. In this forest, where all these things are obtained without being sought, there is only this one drawback: Subhūti 0540-1: The bed is the grassy meadow, the seat is the pure rock, and the dwelling is beneath the trees; Subhūti 0540-2: The drink is the cool water of mountain streams, the food is tubers, and the companions are the deer. Subhūti 0540-3: In this forest, where all these things are obtained without being sought, there is only this one drawback:
O seeker of what is difficult to attain, you remain in vain, though your efforts for the sake of others' welfare have never been fruitless.
For the wise, there is no negligence in abandoning even a very small birthplace; jewels do not lose their value when they depart from their original location.
The heads of kings [are taken] by crows; frogs [take] the mouths.
Brave, learned, and beautiful women will establish their dwellings wherever they go.
Rudra has fled to Mount Rudrādri, Hari to the ocean, and the gods have taken refuge far away in the sky;
even the mighty lords of serpents remain at the very bottom of the netherworld.
The lotus-dwellers have hidden in the lotus groves—I suspect it is out of fear for the multitude of supplicants.
In the Kali age, virtuous persons are solely devoted to the upliftment of the distressed.
The base do not indeed begin their work out of fear of obstacles; the mediocre, having begun, desist when thwarted by obstacles;
but even when struck by obstacles multiplied a thousandfold, [the noble] do not falter.
Those who possess supreme virtues do not abandon what they have begun.
How can this moon, which is a mine of defects, possess eternal fullness, when its true virtues do not blossom even as its rays spread forth?
As the moon wanes, it draws near; as it waxes, it moves far away. Since it is ever subject to impurity, its behavior toward friends and others is but what is fitting.
How was such a sun, a treasury of splendors, not ashamed,
having reached a mere fragment of the cosmic egg and yet stretching out its feet?
The rising of the sun alone is praiseworthy; what is the use of grasping at the rising of others?
For when he has risen, there are neither darknesses nor [other] lights.
What was not sufficient in this loveliness of the moon,
that even the lotus, though intensely scorched by it, placed its trust in him?
By stretching out its rays as it lingers toward the southern quarter,
the sun has lightened not only itself, but the day as well.
The zodiac sign through which the sun moves for two years and six months is not traversed by the moon in even three days.
Even though the moon is borne upon the head by Śambhu, who is himself the moon, it nevertheless undergoes waning; alas, dependence on another is indeed a hardship.
Whether he falls into water, goes to another direction, enters fire, or goes into the earth— how can that toothless sun be called "Sūrya" (the Piercer) by the wise?
He who, having just finished the sign of Pisces, is now prepared to enter Aries.
Let him fall into water, let him go to another region,
let him enter fire, or let him go to the earth; or let him be carried by the sun,
the moon, or the wind— what can they do regarding his virtues?
There is destruction among all the wonders of the world.
The splendor of the moon remains great only so long as the orb of the sun does not approach; but when that treasury of all light has risen—
What difference is there between the moon and a fragment of a white cloud?

Behold how those who follow the six modes of conduct and who discern between the real and the unreal describe this [body]: what the thieves, unchaste women, and others say of it— [They say: "This is a mere heap of skin, sinews, bones, marrow, flesh, blood, mucus, tears, pus, urine, excrement, phlegm, and the like. They say that this body is composed of such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for various diseases, such as leprosy, abscesses, consumption, epilepsy, and jaundice; it is a vessel for hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and fatigue. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair; it is a vessel for the suffering of the three realms of existence. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the hells, the animal realm, the world of Yama, and the states of poverty and wretchedness; it is a vessel for the suffering of being born in the various evil destinies. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of being separated from loved ones, being joined with the disliked, and the pursuit of what is desired; it is a vessel for the suffering of the cycle of rebirth. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the aggregates, the elements, and the sense-fields; it is a vessel for the suffering of conditioned existence. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the afflictions, karma, and birth; it is a vessel for the suffering of saṃsāra. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three poisons, the four floods, the four graspings, the five hindrances, the five aggregates of clinging, the six internal sense-bases, the six external sense-bases, the seven stations of consciousness, the eight worldly dharmas, the nine abodes of beings, and the ten bases of non-virtue; it is a vessel for the suffering of all the outflows. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three kinds of suffering, the eight kinds of suffering, and the hundred and eight kinds of suffering; it is a vessel for the suffering of all phenomena. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three realms, the four modes of birth, the five destinies, and the six classes of beings; it is a vessel for the suffering of all sentient beings. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three times, the four truths, the five faculties, the six perfections, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the nine successive absorptions, and the ten powers; it is a vessel for the suffering of the path to liberation. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the five eyes, the six supernatural knowledges, the seven treasures, the eight liberations, the nine unobstructed knowledges, and the ten powers of a Tathāgata; it is a vessel for the suffering of the attainment of Buddhahood. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three jewels, the four reliances, the five powers, the six roots of merit, the seven limbs of awakening, the eight branches of the holy life, the nine successive meditations, and the ten stages of a Bodhisattva; it is a vessel for the suffering of the Mahāyāna. They say that this body is a vessel for such things as these. Furthermore, they say: "It is a vessel for the various sufferings of the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma, the four methods of attraction, the five types of knowledge, the six supernormal powers, the
If that which is perceived were something created, then it would have been created by the sun.
There exists that certain digit of the Moon, composed entirely of nectar, exceedingly priceless; by it alone has the Supreme Lord been invested with [the status of] a knower of qualities.
The fault of its dark spot was not even counted when it was considered as a crest-jewel.
These many great lights arise,
and even the moon is sufficient to adorn the circle of the world;
yet, apart from the sun, none of them rises or sets.
By its rising, day is made; by its setting, night.
He who does not desist from delighting the worlds even as he is wasting away— indeed, while he remains established in heaven, the dawn would never have been renewed;
such was the nature of fate, by whatever means, that it sustained him alone.
My friend, he passes his time distractedly; look, here is that very moon.

The moon, having waned, enters the orb of the sun month after month; having regained some small portion once more, it follows at a great distance. If it should somehow become full, it rises in rivalry with the sun.
The fool does not desist from wickedness out of malice, nor did he refrain from wretchedness out of pity.
Having placed his footstep upon the summit of Sumeru, the mountain that supports the earth,
he by whom darkness was destroyed traversed the middle realm of Viṣṇu;
now that moon falls from the sky with but few rays remaining.
It is difficult to ascend, and even for the great, it culminates in downfall.

The falling of the vessel of Kalaśaka brings no great calamity to Pūṣan; for who has not gone to their setting in due time? Others have gone, and others will go—who can avert such a sign of destruction from one whose splendor is so blazing with majesty?
Where is this defeat more incongruous than from the head of Rāhu? By the decree of fate, this is appropriate; yet it causes pain that he, devoid of shame, still wanders in the sky before his friend.
The setting of the sun does not lead to great distress, because—who has not gone to their setting by the power of time? Others have gone, others are going, and others will go.
Only this causes affliction: that one is surrounded by darkness, excluded from light.
Having found space in that very same vast primordial sky.
That very earth which, from the beginning of creation, was nourished and sustained day by day with hundreds of flavors, is now, at the time of the end of the aeon, consumed by its own rays;
thus, having performed some action of its own, it is overwhelmed by the prior and subsequent [effects] of necessity.
Alas, even that sun, its rays vanished at the end of the day, has gone to its setting.
By that Lord of fierce radiance, who has truly made the entire world possessed of sight by uprooting the thick,
flesh-like darkness, how cruel and wicked is the person when that Vivasvat has set?
Just as the sight of a crescent moon or a lamp provides stability, so does it bind one to steadfastness.
First, the Lord of Umā is to be pitied, for by virtue of his sovereignty he bears upon his head both a flawless human skull— washed by the Ganges— and the moon as equals;
yet the moon is even more to be pitied, since such a humiliation still occurs despite him.
With a body as pale-white as the blossoming smile of moonlight, he cultivates supreme joy.

The ocean, having become the father of the waters, embraces the moon with its surging waves when it is full out of the joy of its own increase; yet, when it has waned, it releases it from afar. But by means of that very wealth which was lost, it gradually brings about its rising once more.
And since perfection remains so far away—oh, homage to that Friend!
Who would not desire the rising of that King of Planets, who stands afar, bound by darkness, yet brings joy to the virtuous circle? Alas,
now that he has risen, he has acted in such a way as to cause further suffering!
Thinking, "This world is harsh," people do not look him directly in the face.
As soon as they see him, whose thousand hands have dispelled the darkness,
hundreds of *piśācas* flee daily out of fear;
it is a marvel that when the moon has waned, they are severed by Hari.
A single cloud-demon seizes that jewel of the sky.
The sun is ever-striving to protect the entire world seized by darkness;
yet not even a single being in the world is capable of protecting that very sun when it is seized by darkness.
That the lotus flower attained splendor at night from the night-blooming lily of the Treasure of Virtues— that greatness certainly belongs to the King, the treasury of dullness.
A night devoid of the moon never shines; likewise, the moon devoid of the night is indeed shorn of its splendor.
What is the reason that, of these two, only one [is present] each month?
Born from the state of transcendence, it is the union of embrace.

The moon leaves the night as it rests upon its bed in the sky during the bright fortnight, but during the dark fortnight, the night departs; for when the moon withdraws from its sleeping place in the vault of heaven—
If that [marriage bond] is severed between the two, how can they still be considered husband and wife by that much alone?
He who, having shattered the darknesses, illuminates the quarters; who bestows awakening upon the eyes and is desired for his manifold virtues;
and whose wandering about in acts of service to others never leads to weariness.
The wise person pays homage to one who is praiseworthy, not to one who is base.
Whether his investigation be true or false,
nevertheless, there arises a great clamor from the people regarding one of such exalted station;
for even when he has ascended the scales, his greatness is celebrated and his darkness destroyed.
"Indeed, such radiance as this does not belong to one who has gone to a maiden."
The moon, though surrounded by a host of stars, though the leader of medicinal herbs, though its body consists of nectar and it is endowed with beauty,
becomes devoid of rays upon reaching the orb of the sun.
Who, when seated in another's assembly, does not fall into insignificance?
"O dull-witted one, arrogant with pride, do not harbor rivalry with your own father, the Sun, on the grounds that 'just as he is high and yields excellent fruit, so am I.
From afar, all those like you have been utterly destroyed by his splendor of their own accord."
This treasury of splendor, who is a friend to the virtuous, does not desire to conceal his transgression from anyone.

"O Prince, do not harbor rivalry toward your own father, who is the cause of your birth and the source of your play, thinking, 'His state of happiness is equal to mine. For he, O delight of the royal line, is [the refuge] of all the world— "
He who brings an end to darkness, his own self purified by the hand of Giriśa.
The Sun, having recognized his own fitness for the dissimilar fire that abandons its grasp through stinginess, withdraws its radiance, intent on the pacification of its laughter;
let him who does not know fate be called a "peacock" (śikhin) by others, for such is the origin of that name.
There may even be lamps by whose power the world forgets the sun of fierce rays.
Those lotuses that are devoted to me suffer exhaustion when struck by frost;
and those days, which take refuge in me alone, undergo extreme emaciation.
Thus departing toward a distant quarter, as if out of affection for the people who have taken shelter with him—
In the winter, the Blessed One, the Lord of Day, has departed from the world; let him be served.
No consecration and no ritual preparation is performed for the lion in the forest;
for one who has acquired his prowess through valor, the sovereignty over the beasts is his own by nature.
"I am alone, I am without companion, I am emaciated, and I have no retinue"—
such a thought does not arise even in a dream for the king of beasts.
With claws as hard as thunderbolts that shatter the temples of rutting elephants,
the lion attains lightness of fame by his very name as the "Enemy of Deer."
The sharp claws of the lion do not descend even upon leaping deer,
though they are eager to split the frontal globes of elephants.
What can we do, and who is to be blamed, for this inconsistency?
Not even a single *kākiṇī* is the price of a lion; yet ten million is the price of an elephant.
How could deer fearlessly tread upon the path of even a sleeping lion, who effortlessly crushes the frontal globes of audacious elephants?
How can this wretched deer compete with the lion, whose paws are crimsoned with the blood from splitting the temples of rutting elephants?
The elephant, languid with the weight of rut, roars in the forest as long as the lion has not yet arrived with his tail tucked over his head.
Can men live in comfort after having torn out the mane of a lion that shines with cheeks quivering from the pride of its own valor and strength?
What great distraction could there be for Hari, who possesses rutting elephants that fall at the mere touch of his hand, as he engages in a fight with a lion?
As long as the lion’s claws remained stuck in his bones,
the life of that forest-dwelling herd was sustained for that moment.
His stride was one of terrifying valor that shattered the cheeks of herds of trumpeting elephants,
and he brought to rest the endless conflict with the deer.
How can Hari accept this undesirable consequence?
Even as a cub, a lion falls upon elephants whose temples are stained with rut;
this is the nature of those possessed of courage, for age is certainly not the cause of their splendor.
To the lord of beasts, who dwells alone in the forest, who bears no royal insignia, and who is unversed in the science of policy,
yet is exalted among beings— the title "King" is applied.
A lion displays his prowess against an elephant whose trunk is marked with the deep *alijhāṅkāra* sound,
but not against a mongoose that dwells in the mountain caves scratched by its own claws and mouth.
Who would venture to place the palm of their hand upon the face of a lion whose mane is smeared with the mud of rutting ichor from the bursting temples of elephants in a state of frenzy?
While hundreds of young elephants, unrestrained by their drivers, were leaping about out of delusion and wandering heedlessly before him due to their folly,
he whose mental disposition was accustomed to splitting the frontal globes of rutting elephants—
For a lion, it is only appropriate to close his eyes.
Upon seeing the lion, who resembled Death himself as he approached with his mane and shoulders quivering under the influence of rage,
and who was surrounded by flocks of birds that had come desiring to devour his flesh—
He wandered among the heads of herds of elephants blinded by rut.
That lion, whose thirst was quenched by the fresh mass of blood arising from the frontal globes of the enemy elephants torn open by his fierce hands with claws like saws—
He was always wealthy; alas, today he is a beggar for even a blade of grass!
A body that is emaciated, an intellect intent on the slaughter of others,
and a discernment between good and evil expressed only through animal-like behavior—
thus, there is nothing at all virtuous about this king of beasts.
But that radiance flashes forth by which the wretched world is illuminated.
The lion may be the enemy of the elephant or the lord of beasts;
yet I do not consider even that to be a duality.
For by the blow of his quivering claws, like the point of a thunderbolt—
[He is like] a moving mountain from which intoxicated elephants have been toppled by a mere playful blow.
In the cave of Hari, where the herds of elephants are renowned for being struck by the tips of his swaying rays that fall like claws, a jackal—
his vision destroyed by the sight of the lowly offspring of Saramā— [perishes].
"Alas! It is a tragedy that we have seen today that audacity has taken root here."

Where in this world is a lion— a treasure of pride— compared to a blade of grass, when its tusks are restless and agitated by the splitting of the temples of intoxicated elephants, and its thundering claws strike like the points of vajras?
Even when his life is at stake, he maintains the sustenance of his own body.

O lion, do not attempt to leap upon this cloud, which roars loudly from its position as the archer for the stability of the universe; you whose mind is spoiled by the pride of having subdued rutting elephants—
lest it strike you with hailstones from this mountain split open by the thunderbolt.
From the falling that arises due to his habituated state of leaping, the breaking of his limbs occurs spontaneously and is inconceivable.
Does the herd of deer harbor enmity toward Indra in battle, as the surface of the earth is adorned with pearls falling from the frontal globes of tall elephants pierced by his sharp, harsh hooves?
Even when gathered together from all sides for a single purpose, it remains entirely so.
Hari effortlessly subdues the fierce-tusked elephants, whose broad temples are adorned with mountain-like swellings and who resound with the dense *guṅguṃ* humming of swarms of wandering bees.
In the three worlds, majesty alone is revered, not a deformed appearance.
O Lord of Heroes, let not the lion— the king of beasts, whose natural majesty is unfeigned and whose prowess is truly formidable— be provoked while he dwells in mountain ranges and cave-dwellings;
for he is solely intent on drinking the fat produced from the frontal globes of elephants.
Whatever has been gained by your own mind when it was agitated by calamity—let that alone be reflected upon.
To King Mīra Shāh, who desired to go to Kaśmīra,
the sovereign Śāhābuddīna dispatched a messenger with this message:
Why do you, so free from fear, desire to wander with the fickle gait of a young deer? Desist! This forest is by no means empty;
here stands the blood spurting from the slaughter of the lord of elephant-herds—
The lion, possessing a magnificent mane brilliant with a mass of shimmering, flickering flames.
The lion, his magnificent mane stained with blood as it lay scattered upon the frontal globes of elephants struck by his fierce claws,
[is heard] through the cries of those who are most distressed and terrified by his deep roar.
He feels ashamed to stand upon the field of battle alongside the Patañjarikas and Naikas.
O bulls, roam fearlessly through the thickets of Jālimāṃsa as you desire;
O buffaloes, drink the clear water once more from the edges of the lotus ponds;
O elephants, again bear the splendor of rut upon your temples.
Because he could not endure it, the lion fled far away.

O lion, that you leaped up from afar upon seeing a thundering cloud in the sky was enough to weary the minds of the great; for now, out of fear of the essence-less [cloud], you are seeking refuge in the caves.
Upon seeing that, we were overcome with shame; what else could we do but go to the very depths of the underworld?
He who, through his play as Time— the Malla wrestler whose sole delight was the sport of shattering many intoxicated elephants, jars, pots, and earthen vessels—
now rivals the dense clouds bent low under the weight of thundering rain.
A lion, its body huddled from falling into a cage, assumes such a state as this.
Though emaciated by hunger, though wasted by old age, though his vital strength was failing, though he had reached a state of great suffering,
and though his intellect and fortitude were impaired even as his life-breaths were perishing—
he whose thunderbolt-like claws were swinging to split the temples of the elephant-king puffed up with pride.
What, does the lion, the leader of those possessed of great pride, eat withered grass?
His body is not bulky, nor are his tusks, nor is his trunk exceedingly long;
truly, O elephant, this is not a lion cub competing with you in mere outward display.
An unbearable seed of splendor was placed within his heart by the Creator in the past.
Because of such a nature, he regards even that which is most fit to be eaten as a mere sacrificial animal.

Pervaded by the foul stench of the abundant fat from the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants, formidable with rows of filaments shimmering amidst fragments of pearls clearly released through attachment,
he was the bringer of disease and widowhood, who seized the splendor of the powerful by the intoxication of his own arm-strength.
Who has ever seen a lion that is constantly unable to endure a herd of trembling deer?
Who, who, where, would not grunt with a roar as terrible as a grunting boar?
Which elephant would not strive to strip every lotus pond of its blossoms? And which wild buffaloes would not uproot which forests, since [the world] is thus [in turmoil]?
The lion dwells there, bound by the affection and playful charms of the lioness.

How could the hand of one who, even from childhood, was fond of pearls and rice-grains as warm as blood flowing from the interior of the frontal globes of rut-maddened elephants that he had split open, ever stretch forward in a state of distress?
When Hari was about to seize the life of a rabbit that had fallen into and was tumbling within a pit.
Flocks of birds, resembling the tips of claws smeared with blood, fled even from the palāśa forest;
such was the miserable condition of that aged lion.
There is not even enough for the scavengers to subsist upon its remains.
Having violently slain elephants in battle that were like clouds tossed by the wind— roaring toward the rain-clouds as if they were the Vindhya mountains themselves—
and having leaped from tree to tree upon a small-bodied monkey, he stood over it.
Alas! Even you, though enraged, have fallen into a state that is the laughingstock of lions.
With *huṃ* sounds cleverly imitating the roar of thunder,
having brought the pride of the mountain peaks to humiliation, and leading herds of elephants swollen with rut,
that lion, through his majestic power, [overcomes] the ten directions as they are tormented by his irresistible fangs.
Why does even a jackal exert itself when its prowess is already well known to all?
O young elephant, abandon your restlessness;
walk with the vow of discipline, head bowed low,
as fragile as the tips of the claws of the king of beasts.
The heavy end endures above, but not the light end.
Play and enjoy the lotuses;
plunge into the waters of the mountain cascades,
your body caressed by the trunk of a female elephant devoted to you.
O Mātaṅga, release your longing for the battle with the king of deer.
By that elephant, unrestrained, indifferent, and maddened, this [city] was thrown into total disorder; yet,
by the young elephant-driver, a foot was placed upon its head.
How was this weakling forcibly brought under their control?
He who was once a lordly elephant, served by herds of elephants and whose trunk was honored by the heaps of pollen falling from the flowers on the trees of the Vindhya mountain peaks,
has now become that very same lordly elephant, carrying out the commands of men.
How was he born, or for what purpose? Or is Time the master here?
O bull among elephants, whose limbs are scorched by the intense heat of the fire of grief arising from within, abandon your sorrow;
these lines were inscribed by the Creator’s own hand upon the tablet of your forehead.
Who is capable of wiping away these letters?

O lord of elephants, how many days must you spend here in this desert before you can go elsewhere? [Will it not be enough] with the waters of the Revā, applied by the trunks of your own female elephants?
Furthermore, you shall bring about tranquility during the summer heat.
"In this dull world, who indeed could be an elephant with such large ears? Surely he must be a vessel for misfortune!"—
thinking thus, he struck down even that ascetic who had approached him.
Why is he called a Mātaṅga? What more can be said than this?
In the water where the filaments of fresh lotuses bloom, he does not take a mouthful; he finds no delight in the fragments of half-chewed lotus stalks smeared with mud;
nor does he tolerate another female elephant, even if she sports near him and is moist with affection.
Remembering his beloved, who had fallen from his heart, the lord of elephants [wept].

The elephant, though bearing the form of a trunk, does not take the water cool as a crescent moon from the edge of the creepers; nor does he avoid the lovely lotus plants frequented by wandering bees, for he has become separated from his mate.
Drawing out his breaths, alas, he finds no delight even for a single moment at the end.
Having broken through river embankments and uprooted trees like tender sprouts,
having conquered rut-maddened rival elephants with his trunk, feet,
and tusks, he has now reached ignoble old age, which engenders hatred in the hearts of the young.
This very same elephant now endures the insults of young elephants.

O leader of the elephant herd, it would have been better for this unmarked wound from the goad to have fallen upon your head out of a desire to discipline you, than for this final blow from the tips of my claws, which are like thunderbolts.
Like the sharp claws of a forest lion that has suddenly sprung up in fury.
Having abandoned that mind which was under your own control while you were in the forest on the slopes of a mountain ridge, your mind has now fallen upon city-dwellers who are empty of true being;
this [state] consists of the exhaustion of the activities of binding with firm ropes and the infliction of death.
O intoxicated elephant, this is the fruit, corresponding to passion, that has ripened from your own karma.
Where is this form like a mountain, and where is that gait with its speed and grace?
Where are those eyes half-closed in playfulness, and where is that trumpeting of yours?
Where is the joy of charging against embankments, and where is that trunk—alas, that such a being as this!
Having mounted you, the child, being under another's control, makes you move about at his command with his foot.
The earth was shaken by the stamping of his feet; the birds were sluggish with fear;
the lakes were marked with mud; and the trees were scarred by the friction of his flanks.
Having reached this forest, which was now empty of tigers due to the power of fate, he was accompanied only by young elephants.
Each of those names was given because it could not be uttered without restraint.
Even while eating sugarcane and sweet potatoes, consuming food mixed with ghee, meat, rice, and the like;
even while wearing various rugs and carrying garlands of stars;
and even while holding a chowrie-tassel in his ear—such was the elephant; yet remember him thus.
Now he dwells forever in misery in the lands of the Indhyas, amidst thickets of sallakī trees and forests.

Having seen that elephant— whose trunk was being devoured by circles of bees sluggish with intoxication— who as a calf had been nourished by mouthfuls of handfuls of the finest wild rice, and who had drunk the milk remaining from oblations in cups made of lotus leaves;
Standing at a distance, the ascetic looked on repeatedly with longing and fear.
Placing your trunk upon your tusks, with your head hanging down and both eyes closed—why do you, O elephant, suffer because of a courtesan? Who indeed has not been deceived?
Take your fodder with a peaceful mind; let sorrow now be forever abandoned.
Those who are intoxicated, lacking discernment, and of wavering intellect, fall into calamity.
That she sustained her life with the morsel of food left over from her husband’s mouth,
that she drank the water turbid from his hand-dipping and only what remained after he had drunk—
having long since surrendered her own life, this is the fruit now obtained by the female elephant.
The distressed face of the elephant, who was terrified at being bound and offered as a sacrifice, was not seen.
"O young elephant, take a mouthful of fodder and abandon your bond of affection for the female elephant;
now apply the mud-paste that is desired for the wounds of your fetter-knots.
Those beautiful women of the Śabara chiefs, charming with their playful allure, have become distant from you."
The foothills of the Vindhya mountains are grey with the pollen of flowers from the trees on the banks of the Revā river.
A dog wags its tail, lowers its hindquarters,
falls to the ground, and shows its mouth and belly to one who gives it food;
but a preeminent elephant does not act thus.
She gazes steadfastly at him and enjoys herself with hundreds of endearments.

Where there is Mount Vindhya, and within it the Pippala tree beloved by the Pīlu bird; where the doe rushes forward with longing at the sudden arrival [of her mate], and the female elephant likewise; why does that elephant not remember this out of his own goodness? For fate indeed grinds everything down.
But this is even more unbearable than death itself, that this fool has been placed at the head of the task.
This very elephant, which once grew to maturity amidst the Vindhya mountains— where the Mallika buds were tossed by the gusts of wind from the Narmada river’s surging waves—
is now, by the power of fate, deprived of his mate and emitting only hissing groans.
Helplessly caught by the sinking vajra-rope noose, alas, what action can he possibly perform?
O scent-elephant, O rival of the elephant of the great mountain, do not even now remember with eyes closed in playful pride; abandon your arrogance now and resort to the present.
It is a crooked goad above the command of Fate.
O lady with eyes like those of an elephant in rut, do not cast aside the rivers of clear and sweet water to quench your unbearable thirst; do not cast it into the pond-water drawn up by autumn.
Even when this entire water has been drunk, your thirst will find no relief in that water.
Since this village has but a single exit, there will certainly be doubt regarding one's life.
Blessed are those deer in the forest, Father, who feed on dūrvā grass and sprouts,
for they do not behold the faces of those whose minds are intoxicated by worldly power.
Lifeless, devoid of breath, with its internal dart removed and its wound healed,
the doe remains motionless and unbound, like a statue, as the deer stands still.
The quarters are stretched out with ropes, the water with poison;
the earth is bound with snares, and the forest edges are ablaze with fire. Hunters, holding their arrows, follow his tracks.
To what region does the leader of the deer herd resort?
