Go from here with all possible speed, O deer; you shall be parted from your life. Why do you stand there again and again, turning your neck to look back?
It does not cause even the slightest softening of heart in those hunters who have slain you.
For those with cruel minds, these are but the flickerings of their eyes.
Chasing a mirage over parched ground,
the deer, afflicted by thirst, does not desist even when its mind is exhausted;
not knowing the reality, it seeks no other lake.
In the stage of the Śrāvaka, there is no hope for [the Mahāyāna], nor does it bear fruit, but rather creates an obstacle.
O deer, eat grass and sustain your life with water,
or else become one who feeds on air; even that would be a manifestation of your vital breath,
by which this [beauty] of yours possesses the lovely luster of a cluster of blooming blue lotuses.
The gaze of a fool, arrogant with the intoxication of wealth, does not reach his own mouth.
Where even a slight stumble leads to a fall, where progress upward is achieved with great difficulty,
and where the process of entry through the gate is arduous due to the dense thicket of cane creepers— O deer, why have you abandoned these delightful forest lands in search of something superior?
Why were your hooves needlessly clipped by one who was intent on dwelling in the mountain fastnesses?
These are not the grounds of the Malaya forests with their clear, flowing waterfalls,
where the thirst of embodied beings is quenched by the mere sight of them; rather,
this is the parched Bharu region, inhabited by harsh crows and filled with expanding delusions.
O deer, these are merely mirages; this is not water, so depart.
The forest of my birth was abandoned like a patch of young grass; the clearing was left behind like a mother;
the trees, which provide a refuge for dwelling in confidence and are like kinsmen, were not counted as such;
and that doe, distressed by the pain of separation from her young offspring, was not looked upon with pity.
Even as they search for his tracks, these pitiless hunters still do not release him.
Having severed the snare, cast off the trap, and forcibly broken through the net,
the deer emerged from the forest thick with a mass of flickering flames;
leaping with speed beyond the range of the hunters' arrows, it ran away.
When one has fallen into a well, what human effort can avail against adverse fate?
O Lord, you wander about at will; you lust after the wives of others and do not feel distress.
You do not look upon the face of those who speak with crooked words due to sudden, causeless anger; nor do you spare even a single moment for your beloved wife, whose love is made manifest.
O Sāraṅga, by whom was this exceedingly beautiful vow of yours taught?
By chance, a deer wandering at will has encountered a fresh cluster of rice blossoms, from which drops of milk-like sap flow as they break;
it reveals its inner agony like tender grass scorched by the fire of its sighs.
Meditating upon that very [truth] every day like a sage in the forest, he withers away.
That deer does not take delight in the vine-arbors, nor on the dusty ground,
nor even in the cool, lovely green shades at the edge of the forest;
day after day, he meditates incessantly upon that very same long-eyed beloved.
With his mind fixed upon the caves within the belly of the king of mountains, he remained there, dressed in the attire of a lover.
With its horn, it scratches its body to gain familiarity with those who are free from desire;
wandering slowly and at will, it avoids the dwelling of the herd-leader out of fear. Seen, it stands unnoticed, yet it is instantly struck by the sidelong glances of the female deer.
The deer, having entered another herd due to the power of adverse fate, dwells in misery.
"Taking all my flesh except for my breasts, O hunter, release me and go; show me your favor. Even now, I am still unskilled at swallowing mouthfuls of fodder."
My son is intent on beholding my path.
Before him lies the Revā river; on the opposite bank is a mountain with peaks exceedingly difficult to climb;
to his left is a lake, and to his right is the calamity of a forest fire;
behind him, a Śabara hunter with bow in hand pursues him most fiercely.
This young deer is unable either to go or to stay.
Where does he play, where does he roam, and where does he find his sustenance?
Where indeed does he drink water, and where does he sleep? Thus [he questioned] the innocent deer, who was not causing him any harm.
A hunter pursues him for the sake of killing, wielding his bow.
"This is the moon, the one with nectar-like rays, the son of Atri, the lord of the twice-born;
through my merits, he has been obtained as a refuge"—with such thoughts, O innocent fawn, take joy; abandon this sinful [thought] and do not leave him.
Having suddenly devoured a fish, he has made it into the form of a ram.
O young camel, if by some stroke of fortune you should ever, through the power of fate, find honey from a swarm of bees—
desist, desist from them! There is young grass in the forest.
Those who are sweet-tongued at first will surely wither away in the end.
Just as a young camel, having abandoned the forest land dark with emerald gems— adorned with lakes of blooming lotuses and full-blown water-lilies—
remembers the trees of the desert sands; so too does he remember them.
That delight in familiarity is difficult to restrain; it is not an enemy to virtue.

O beloved Karabhaka, why do you cry out in longing because you have not obtained that honey, so difficult to find, which was once drunk by you while in the forest? Maintain your composure with the familiar leaves of the *pīlu* tree in this desert region.
In this entire world, who has attained uninterrupted happiness?
O beloved Karabhaka, that *pilu* tree which you, greedy for honey,
abandoned without regard when its flowers and shade had vanished— now even that tree has sprouted new shoots and its young leaves are trembling.
It is enjoyed with happiness by groups of beloved female elephants and others.
"O young camel, why do you exhaust this little body of yours with such long sighs?
Desist, O rogue! For whom, my friend, has ultimate happiness ever truly arrived? Move about in health upon the tender shoots; abandon your longing for the honey of the *pīlu* tree."
Furthermore, you will once again become a vessel for wholesome things.

O young camel, alas, you desire to cry out impetuously; indeed, it is a fever for your ears. Or rather, your own long neck shall be your refuge, as it emerges from its mouth, exhausted by the passage through the wide opening of the cave.
When it is given at such a time, who knows what will happen to whom?
Thus contented with water, *vṛṇa*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, and *badara* fruits,
wandering happily in the forest, the young camel was rendered free from sorrow; yet,
by the deluded power of fate, his heart was made prone to the taste of honey.
Just as he eats nothing else, drinks nothing, sleeps not, and takes no pleasure.
He who was once satisfied even with a mouthful of nine *pīlu* leaves and jujube fruits,
whose path could not be followed even by his own companions on the long journey— he,
that very same young camel, now goes about with his vigor exhausted and fallen into a state of emaciation.
I think that this wretched creature of fate must surely have tasted the honey of the bees.
Remembering how, in the desert, you once chewed the fruit of the *pīlu* tree— free from bitterness—
and ate its lovely branch-tip with affection as it was placed in your mouth by the female camel,
and remembering the long, sorrowful moan uttered by that camel when she was overcome with grief; [how could I not weep?]
To those living beings, that very sound suddenly became like the trumpet-call for departure.
One who desires soft things despises the camel, while the camel, which is fond of thorns, despises him;
yet when both have attained their desired food, their pleasure is equal.
Maintaining neutrality means not mocking either side.
There is but one proud bird that dwells in the forest, the cātaka;
either it dies of thirst, or it begs from Indra.
O startled and innocent *cātaka* bird, why do you run fruitlessly with your neck outstretched across the desert?
This is a *tāpiccha* tree enveloped by a forest fire in the summer heat; it is not a cloud.
Even when thirsty, the peacock awaits his mate who drinks like his own life; surely his gaze is fixed by the bonds of affection for his beloved.
One sees only a very small amount of water in rivers.
Let this young *cātaka* bird now offer its petition with its head bowed low, for it is afflicted by the calamity of excessive height;
indeed, it desires this, for [the water] does not exist within these vast quarters of space.
Where indeed are those waters that are so clear, cool, and sweet?

This beautiful majesty of the plumage of this peacock, acting as the tilaka ornament of the forest lands with its sweet cries, is indeed difficult for crows and other such birds to perceive in the sky.
Even though he was crushed, he did not become like a sparrow in his gait.
Having abandoned the clear masses of water that surpass even the essence of nectar, yet are reddened by the pollen from heaps of blue lotuses,
the cātaka bird drinks only the drops of rain from the cloud.
I think that he is arrogant because of his head, out of fear of bowing down.
O Cātaka bird, who could be deluded by your restriction of drinking only divine water?

Even a fault takes on the nature of a virtue for those who possess conventional understanding; yet if you wish to drink the water standing upon the ground, you would merely reveal a sore in your throat and your own unworthiness.
Whom could the rule of drinking divine water not delude?
Even a fault assumes the nature of a virtue for those who possess a conventional understanding.
Are there no reservoirs of water adorned with fresh lotuses and encircled by rows of swans? Alas,
what a formidable obstacle this must be for the cātaka bird!
Just as one might desire a stream of water from the cloud belonging to Indra.
Why are the clouds so far away? Why are other birds not heard crying out above?
Have their wings—those wretched things due to their own sin—perished within their bellies? Or is it that wandering in the sky is no longer pleasant for them, because of that row of fierce crows?
Out of fear of the slowness of understanding through various synonyms, the peacocks remain established on the ground.
Not by the *tāṇḍava* dance, nor by the cascade of nectar for the eyes;
not by the cry of the peacock, nor by that elixir for the ears;
even by your plumage, which possesses the luster of a celestial bow—your [beauty]...
The fire is not satisfied without its fuel.
O dear Cātaka bird, how great a peerless sin have you committed,
that not even a drop of water falls into the hollow of your beak from the fresh rain-cloud?
Deprived of the gift of water droplets and manifesting a white, cloudless appearance, O Cātaka bird, why do you cry out in vain? This is merely an autumnal cloud.
There are wells of shimmering form all around, and auspicious rivers;
nevertheless, for the cātaka bird, only the rising of a rain-cloud yields fruit.
You utter sharp and flattering cries like the notes of a peacock,
and you dance with your tail fanning out to please;
O *cātaka* bird, you thus strive toward the rain-cloud.
You obtain not even a drop of water, and yet you feel no shame.
Having made the son of Īśvara (Śiva) your vehicle,
your own plumage has withered away;
have you not worshipped that Supreme Person?
May he who would quench their thirst with showers from clouds of hair.
Due to the extraordinary joy of dwelling in a state befitting his mind,
the very nature of a swan is attributed to a swan even when it is in the water of a pond.
Bees, grey with pollen, drink honey from the lotuses;
swans eat the *śaivāla* moss—fie on this perverse fate!
Even if, by the turn of fate, the world were ever to become devoid of lotuses,
would a swan ever scatter its own mass of refuse like a common cock?
Where the sharp-tongued *ṭiṭṭibha* bird nearby caws harshly,
for the swan there, either retreat or silence is the only refuge.
Even if water adorned with lotuses were present everywhere,
the mind of the swan does not find delight except for Lake Mānasa.
Even when hungry, the swan avoids the lotus filament covered in dust;
for one who has taken a side with the virtuous, the stalk of the lotus is highly esteemed.
Why do you dart your gaze so restlessly, O one cherished by the dwelling of a mind as tender as a budding flower? Descend,
O kalahamsī, into the pond!
Once again, you shall go to the abode of the mud-born.
O swan, having abandoned the delightful river of the Himalayas, whose waters are reddened by the pollen of lotuses and whose enchanting songs captivate the hearts of female bees—
"Ha! Ha! You of ruined hope, tell me, toward which direction are you so eager?"
O swan, where has your discerning intellect gone now, you who were once capable of separating milk from water?
For when a mere fraction of the moon’s light falls upon the waters of a pond—
Out of a desire for lotus shoots, you wish to take [this] from the root.
Having wandered for a long time through the waters of the celestial river— the meritorious, world-purifying, and enchanting tresses resting upon the head of the moon-crested Lord— by fate...
Having obtained them, you wish to abandon them here; you are not a swan.
Having remained for a long time in the sky with his stars motionless,
he gazed upon the lotus pond defiled by contact with elephants; then, with a roar deep as the sound of rising rage, he spoke.
The swan, turning back with tears, departed without faltering.
This very bird, O Fate who strikes us down, has by your machinations abandoned that lovely fragment of lotus stalk— white as frost or a conch shell— which was once brought to its mouth by its mate.
It brings about a state of attachment to the stalks of water-weed.
Why do you caw so harshly and loudly out of rivalry with me, O wretched bird, you crow whose mouth and interior are stained with excrement?
You agitate the waters by flapping your broad, white wings.
Dwelling in the lotus grove, I am a swan, not a crow.
At the end of the day, the swan, flying through the air, entered the forest of kāraṇḍava ducks, crows, cranes, and vultures to dispel his fatigue;
they mocked him, saying, "This one is mute," and plucked at his wings.
For a lowly status is indeed a ground for the contempt of the great.
Where is the hard leaf of the *pīlu* tree, and where is the tender lotus sprout?
Where is the bitter, salty water of the well, and where is the nectar of the *tāmarasa* flower?
Where is the heart-pleasing pollen of flowers, and where is the harsh dust of the salt-waste?
Where is the desert region, a domain for crows, and where are those like you, O swan?
"O royal swan, why have you come here?
That crane who was previously known here as a swan—
depart from there with all haste at dawn."
"Until they say, 'This is a crane,' you fools do not understand."
O swans of the lake, do not cry out here, signaling the contraction of your own dwelling upon seeing these birds flying in the sky;
for these are deer who maintain vows honored throughout the world.
To these beings who are free from effort, even the oceans become like blades of grass.
Somewhere on a tree growing by the bank, with your body concealed by leaves,
pass this difficult rainy season with its falling torrents of rain;
but when it has ceased, [spend it] by a lake where lotuses are in full bloom.
You are that very same swan; those playful graces of yours are here once again.
Its depth has vanished, and even its waters are covered by hundreds of webs;
friend swan, rise up first from this burnt lake, before he,
his body fouled by mud and water, begins to lament aloud.
A chattering crow does not place its pair of feet upon its head.
The crane does not touch the lotus stalk with its beak, for it has been repeatedly broken;
it does not drink the water, nor does it go to sleep upon the mass of moss;
the crane does not engage in the sport of breaking the buds of the lotuses.
Seized by grief and distressed by separation from his beloved, he wailed piteously.
In the lakes, the swan, who at night is unobservant as he repeatedly mistakes the reflections of the stars for lilies and searches among the stalks of water-lilies,
does not, however, bite the white lotus even during the day, fearing it might be a star.
The world, wary of deception, looks for faults even when they exist.

O swan, in every region here, though the terrain is uneven and marked by mud, there are waters bright as pearls, lotus stalks shimmering with breaking waves of milk, abundant wine from the *tāmarasa* flowers, and sandy banks fit for your playful wanderings.
O crane, why do you take up residence in this old pond where the fish are bold, parched, and few?
"May this reservoir of water be filled once more with shimmering waters, teeming with schools of sardines and waves, and may we again behold its lotuses in full bloom"—
with such a heart bound by hundreds of threads of hope, my wretched mind dwells thus day and night.
On the shore of a lake dried up by the sun, an old crane withers away.
With his body radiant with a yellowish-red unguent from the pollen fallen from swaying lotuses,
he experienced a festival of joy while listening to the warbling of the bees; yet, even when his beloved offered him a morsel of lotus-root from her beak, he was unable to accept it.
Now this very swan, having gone to the desert, piteously longs for grass.

Those who, having remembered her, immediately abandoned Lake Mānasa in their desire for something superior, and with minds full of longing, see that very same lotus pond inhabited by cranes and sink back into it once more— lightened now that their pride has vanished.
They are not swans, though as white as swans; they are likely nothing but cranes.
Embracing which, the cranes cry out harshly with their necks extended in long gasps;
upon whose slopes these water-fowl leap, splashing the water against their shoulders;
she who is constantly frequented day and night by even the foul-natured cranes.
It would be fitting if that lotus were abandoned by the wise swan.
Form is their captivating, heart-stealing companion; the lotus-honey is for their drink;
sport is in the waters among the lotuses; dwelling is within them; pollen is their ornament;
their livelihood is by means of the lotus-fiber, which is esteemed by the virtuous; and the sweet-sounding bees are their friends.
Free from servitude, wretchedness, and humiliation, the swan lives in happiness.
Even fish know how to distinguish milk from water;
the fame of the royal swans is well-established, for it is attained through merit.
Even when their wings are falling away from the claws of a furious owl, certain other birds— those whose bodies are nourished by dung— do not abandon their own refuge.
But as for those royal swans who have been nourished by even a mere fragment of the lotus-stalks from the celestial river, how could they ever abandon even the turbid water of the Gaṅgā?
Why do you utter such exceedingly tender words, O male cuckoo,
in this abyss that is terrifying with the deep, heavy resonance of dull stones?
The notes of a cuckoo raised among crows remain melodious; how could there be harshness in one whose nature is inherently auspicious, even when in the company of the wicked?
O sweet-voiced cuckoo, who here hears even a fraction of your sound— a herald for the union of those whose bodies are love— amidst the hollows of thick trees and trunks scorched by forest fires?
In the forest glades where harsh cries were resounding, the sun was appearing.
Becoming silent, O cuckoo, wait for that very spring, your kinsman, whose favorable breeze carries the fragrance of *mālatī* flowers tossed by the playful wind;
for it is there that these eloquent words of yours shall attain fruition, while these [others] merely flash—
The summer days, bearing up clouds of dust and maintaining a state of intense heat.
"Brother, enough, enough with the warbling of the cuckoo, for virtues are not valued because of it;
remain silent here in some hollow, covered by a mass of withered leaves,
amidst the harsh cawing of flocks of crows in the garden groves."
"O friend, this is now the time of winter; this is not the festival of spring."
In one place the chirping of crickets, in another the incomparable clamor of crows; in one place the cry of herons, and in another the tumultuous noise of monkeys;
in yet another place this terrible howling of jackals—alas, what a play of fate!
How can the young cuckoo, startled, utter its shrill cry?
Even when being tormented, the bee frequents the ketaki flower;
what indeed can faults do to one whose mind is captivated by virtues?
Even after performing the drinking of the wine-vat right before the lotus plant, the young bee still longs for the *bakula* bud; O dark honey-drinker, where is there truth in you?
Having observed that the blossoming of the bandhujīva flowers is fruitless and subject to impermanence,
the bee has now approached its teacher and become intent upon chanting.
O bee, wandering through the various quarters of the world,
tell me truly, setting aside all partiality: have you ever encountered, seen, or heard of such a thing anywhere?
If the flower resembles a *jātī* flower.
The lotus is his dwelling, the pollen its dust and passion;
honey is his drink, and the sweet speech of beloveds his song;
the soft filaments are his pillow upon which he lies.
What royal grace is there for a bee in the water?
Falling and rising, standing still and motionless; its plaintive cry of compassion, coming and going;
the lotus, soiled and struck by the frost.
For there is nothing that, having been observed, was not performed by him.
The lotus plant, though once dark with beauty, cannot endure being frequented by its beloved in his absence;
yet now, it is filled in its heart with that very spring.
She remembers the essence of delight day and night.
If a bee, seeking a drop of honey, does not desire intoxication,
it will not meet its death by falling upon the tip of an elephant's ear;
yet one who approaches others out of a desire for a mere fragment of pleasure [is like that bee].
Such a person indeed becomes a vessel for defeat.
O honey-bee, you have repeatedly rejected many flowering creepers whose tips were beautifully blossomed as if they were mere grass; now experience the fruit from those [creepers] enveloped in thorns.
This, then, is a source of shame compared to the ketaki vines.
Behold today, at the departure of autumn, that very bee who once sported within the hearts of lotuses in full bloom and dwelt amidst the buds of mango trees.
The days pass with difficulty through the hollows of the bamboos.
Having drunk the fragrant floral nectar, its pollen acting as a dye, the bee sat upon a lotus among the creepers;
now bound by the rays of the moon, it cries out piteously.
What person in this world do misfortunes not afflict who is devoid of contentment?
O bee, for now, divert your restless mind toward other flowering creepers that can endure being crushed; do not,
out of season, sip the pollen from the buds of those whose faces have been plucked away.
O fool, why do you mistreat the young jasmine?
His body was stained tawny by the pollen of lotuses clinging to him as they were struck by droplets of water from the rutting ichor of Airāvaṇa’s face;
his wings were shattered by frost driven by a fierce wind.
Exhausted on the ground, he lies here helpless like a bee.
Why do you wander about so full of longing, your fortitude cast down, warbling piteously like a bee seeking the nectar of flowers? Fix your resolve upon other trees and creepers.
For that blossoming mango creeper has indeed been broken.
When the lotus bud— perfuming the entire expanse of the quarters with its own fragrance,
red in hue, possessing a charming face, and delicate in form—
became fit for enjoyment;
At that very moment, he was led by the ritual procedure to another region, Madhupura.
In the lotus, radiant with its natural brilliance, two bees entered simultaneously, their movements graced by sweet and tender speech; of these two,
one had its body filled and overflowing with a great abundance of nectar.
In this difficult situation, there is no second person who is even touched by passion.
The swarm of bees, having left the mango tree, went to the jasmine;
then it went again to the red *aśoka*, and from there to the *kadamba* tree.
Having stayed at those as well for a very long time, it departs from them for the lotus.
The world, hating the virtues it has long cultivated, seeks ever something new.

What indeed was not done there by the bee, who, having wandered about with his soul utterly captivated by the beauty of the painted lotus, longed for its honey? Having experienced its flavor, that bee of little intelligence did not turn away from it even slightly.
But it has been placed at the head by discerning people for those blinded by craving.
The bee wanders slowly among the *bakula* trees; it finds no rest in the *kunda*.
It does not attain freedom from sorrow in the naturally fragrant red *aśoka*;
its mind is distracted by the longing for the scent of fragrant flowers in the forest.
A bee, remembering its former garland, becomes thin upon its body.
Kissing her gently, he touches her with his limbs and exerts pressure;
he even strives to break the seal by falling at her feet,
unable to wait for the appropriate moment due to the agitation of his mind.
Through merits, a young bee obtained a fresh jasmine flower after another.
Seeing the lotus pond withered by frost and its lotus stalks destroyed, the bees have suddenly become friends to the temples of elephants.
Alas! Fie upon this nature of living beings, which causes such lack of trust.
No one who has exhausted their purpose reckons even the first scent of virtue.

O bee, why do you wander for so long in the delusion that this is fragrance? Indeed, O bee, you do not know the truth: the summer season is scorching intensely. Behold the forest; its branches are laid bare, and it stands empty of flowers.
He has gone; he is rich in cows, naturally beautiful, and possesses the splendor of the month of Caitra.
By whom has its noble flower been smelled? By whom have the filaments been kissed? By whom has its nectar been drunk? By whom has it been stirred by pollen, or by whom?
O, O deluded honey-bee, go quickly to other flowering trees!
O Subhūti, is anything at all obtained from a *pippala* tree by merely reciting its name in vain?
"Fresh honey should be drunk at one's pleasure"—
thus, with a heart deceived by the agitation of thirst and longing, and lacking the realization of reality,
one does not desist from the lotus-pool of painting, despite being weary and one’s efforts being fruitless.
Though he is of evil intellect and addicted to vice, the honey-bee still wanders about, driven by the desire for nectar.
That sandalwood creeper, for the desire to enjoy which ponds with blooming blue lotuses were not even counted,
and embracing which with an eager mind one attained supreme bliss—
that very creeper, now seen broken by a bee, is what the bee continues to live for.
Let that be called his fortitude; he has not, however, acted in accordance with affection.
By whom honey was drunk at will from the bud of a *kesara* flower in the grove of Āmodinī;
by whom nights bright with the moon were spent within the heart of an autumn lotus;
and by whom wandered upon the temples of elephants, stained by the flow of rutting ichor.
How then can this young bee find satisfaction in clinging to a *karīra* branch?
Let it not be that my death occurs by his hand through some stroke of fate;
yet, if my life were destroyed by thirst for him, then why would the world be devoid of flowers?
For by that very same merciless one, my beloved Padmākara has been utterly uprooted.
Alas! The fickle bee, longing for the water of his gift, pursues that very same elephant.

O bee, you have already experienced the reversal of your sense of taste, the fickleness of your ears, that gaze of yours which—intoxicated and forgetting self and other—loses all sense of direction; what more need be said?
O bee, you have ascertained everything, since even now you still seek to consort with the elephant.
"Brother, what is this obsession that you practice the 'inner-void-maker'?"
O bee, you whose body is exhausted by the toil of being tossed by the wind from the flapping ears of elephants blinded by rut— why do you endure this suffering in vain?
For here is the beauty of a lotus bud, its calyx hidden by a swarm of humming bees.
Full of joy and with their intentions made manifest, there are indeed lotus-pools at every step.
A bee, having left the fragrant *navamālikā* flower, went to the *yūthikā*;
having left that as well, he went to a sandalwood tree, and from there he went to a lotus.
There, captured by the moon, that dull-witted creature cries out for a very long time.
Without contentment, a greedy person undergoes hundreds of defeats.
"The night will pass; a beautiful dawn will arise;
the sun will emerge and the lotus pond will bloom"—thus does the bee think while it remains within the calyx.
Alas, alas! An elephant has trampled the lotus pond.
Wandering among the forest clusters at the edge of the woods, the bee did not smell the fragrant *gandhaphalī* flower;
was it not beautiful, and was he not a lover?
The will of the Lord alone is more powerful.

The fish, with its entire body grown large within the womb and embraced by its infancy, remains motionless as it is incessantly drunk in by bees who, having attained their desire, have their mouths wide open in the intense joy of embracing its beauty.
From afar, with eyes devoid of blinking, he gazes intently at the lotus.
While living, the crane is seen to swallow fish like a sage; yet the vulture does not even devour the dead. Fie upon this "lordship of sages" in appearance!
Standing on one leg upon a lotus stalk with his neck curved,
the old crane creates the illusion of a water lily for the young fish.
This crane has suddenly perished;
alas, where indeed has its flesh gone?
O Fate, it is well that someone has [offered it] to you.
He is not capable of being deceived by anything whatsoever.
O crane, although you wish to abandon the conduct appropriate to your own kind and desire to attain the state of a swan, nevertheless, you must still observe your own vow.
This very thing bears fruit for those men who strive with diligence.
They did not have the warbling of cuckoos,
nor did they have gait like that of swans with graceful movements,
nor did they possess the variegated plumage of peacocks.
Even so, there is virtue in the crane's vow within the crane.

O crane, let alone that cleverness of yours in discerning the true nature of the water and milk that have been mixed together, and let aside that charming grace of yours in placing your soft steps; if you know even a little of this, then perhaps you may hope for some relaxation of your desire.
O friend, why do you not remain silent like me? Why are you not a swan to me?
"Who are you, with red eyes, face, and feet? From which Mānasa lake have you come, O swan? Is there there a forest of golden lotuses and water like nectar?
Or is there a bed of pearl-oysters and heaps of conch shells, and are there anywhere beds of lapis lazuli?"
"Are there indeed *chambūka* birds here, or not?"—thus the cranes cried out "Hīhī! upon hearing this.
Having a plumage of identical color and black as the cuckoos with which it is associated,
by what means is a crow recognized if it does not speak for itself?
Even when they cry out in competition with the peacocks, making sounds from their own throats,
do these wretched crows know how to produce the *kekā* call?
Let the male cuckoo bear a dark body, let it kiss the excellent fruits,
and let it wander through the lovely interiors of mango groves; indeed,
let it perform all the behaviors of its kind.
Indeed, in the matter of making a sound, a crow is surely nothing but a crow.
Having attained close proximity even by force through the lovely voices of flocks of cuckoos of enchanting beauty, what can this wretched bird do when fate has become adverse?
The crow did not succeed in imitating their [sounds].
This village is surrounded on all sides by Bhilla hunters who delight in unaccustomed violence and are fond of arrows as deadly as poison; therefore, O parrot,
spend your time quietly upon the trunk of this tree.
Or rather, since there is no eloquent speech, silence alone is the refuge here.
With his toes he scratches the faces of the gods, their excrement smeared with the remnants of food they have eaten;
and with his pride destroyed, he wanders fearlessly among the heads of the virtuous.
What indeed will a wretched crow not do once it has reached the sky?

Misfortune in speech, impurity of body, and alas, fickleness in actions—these are known to be born of doubt; yet its true nature is indeed inexpressible. Nevertheless, like the abundant fruit of the tree of evil deeds, one remains thus afflicted.
Alas, the crow repeatedly faints at the brilliance of the cuckoo’s plumage.
These peacocks are dancing and these parrots are reciting charmingly to be heard;
yet they are not merely being watched here, for indeed they are being driven away in anger by this traveler,
who has gained a connection [to them] by announcing the discovery of his beloved’s house.
Now this [world] is being devoured without restraint by the deceitful one who feeds on offerings.

O crow, let there be harshness in your speech; your one-eyedness is forgiven. As for this greediness of yours—what account can be taken of it? Indeed, this meanness is your very ornament; for all this, ordained by your nature, is endured by us like the heat of fire.
But that you, who are thus devoid of virtue, should even have a neck—that is simply not tolerable.
A crow, having driven away the cuckoo, enjoys tasting the fruit of the mango tree; a osprey, warding off the royal parrot, sports with the pomegranate;
and an owl, together with his mate, sleeps comfortably upon the crest of this tree, displacing the peacock.
Alas! Today, while the hawk is out of sight in the forest, that which was born has become perverted.
Is he one whose body is adorned with a crest like a peacock? Is he a reciter like a parrot?
Is he sweet-voiced like a male cuckoo? Is he of noble gait like a swan? Or is he a source of playful diversion like an ordinary fledgling bird?
By what quality was the crow confined in a golden cage?
The birth of the Lord of the Maruts on the day of the Yuga, celebrated as a festival for the whole world; the great renown during the proclamations of auspicious days; full youth and manliness;
a conflict with rivals equal to that of Rāma; and such-like skill in astrology—[these are the shared qualities].
Because of that quality, the crow was placed in a golden cage.
This was the initial onset of the Kali age,
which arrived having eclipsed the multitude of *tiraskṛta-bahūdaka* swans;
on the final day of his asceticism, [the Lord] summoned him with great reverence.
Alas, even a one-eyed brahmin is honored in every house wherever he goes!
Just as the name "moon" is applied elsewhere to something that resembles the moon in its function,
so too the name "firefly" was given by someone pleased with a certain insect.

O jewel-insect, that you shine in the night when the ten directions are soiled by thick and total darkness is one thing; but now, during the day, it is quite another, as the beautiful white rays [of the moon] are obscured by the hands of the sun.
Not burning even the tip of a withered blade of grass and not revealing even a single grain of mustard seed,
the firefly shines forth, proclaiming its own independence as a mere insect.
The fireflies, having dispelled much darkness in the sky,
shine with a brilliance that is great yet faint; their light is bound only to their own bodies,
while the intense and heavy splendor of the sun is clearly manifest.
The seven-horsed sun does not rise until that [time] has passed.
That night, in which even worms like you, O wretched ones, once shone, has passed into total darkness;
now this day has come, with the ten directions illuminated by the blazing rays of the sun.
Even the moon does not shine here; O firefly, how much less so you?
The moon shall depart and the splendor of the stars shall perish; the jewel-lamps, having licked away the darkness, shall no longer remain;
O firefly, the entire world shall become blind.
"You will go to Dunmeṣa"—this is far off.

May there be no well-being for that mere fragment of light, which flickers within beings or is hollow with superimposed qualities and the like, and which deludes the timid— [that fragment] by whose shimmering shadow this [world] is studded with the name "firefly."
We are mocked even by a worm that, out of malice, mistakes us for a moving jewel.
A tree is adorned by the very clusters of fresh leaves it produces;
that it casts off those same leaves when they have withered—what is so surprising about one of low birth?

O Mother, where have those trees gone—those rich with sprouts and flowers, those abundant with blossoms and fruits, and those possessing such excellence of fruit and such noble growth? Alas! Where have they come from? Where have they vanished?
It is indeed fitting that the Creator did not labor in vain in fashioning him;
for what is the use of sandalwood fruit that does not correspond to its own nature?
Driven by a craving for jujube fruits and ignorant of the trees, I, while in the forest, mistook a *khadira* tree for a thorn and clung to it.
Either a great tree perishes along with its roots,
or the sprout of a *nyagrodha* seedling does not undergo the process of becoming a sprout.
Blessed are those trees whose flowers, leaves, fruits, shade, roots, bark,
and wood do not turn away from those who come in need.
Whether falling amidst a rain of embers or when the wind of universal destruction blows,
the palm tree that was once rigid perishes along with that very rigidity.
Trees by the roadside that provide shade, are free of predatory beasts, possess noble growth, and yield fruit, exist for the welfare of others alone.
Indeed, for those who have no recourse, suffering does not arise from being humiliated;
for the most part, even when kicked by the foot, *aśoka* trees put forth new sprouts.
Even if a sandalwood tree is ordained by fate to be devoid of fruit and flowers,
it nevertheless dispels the suffering of others by its very form.
When the spring month arrives, all the forest ranges attain growth;
that there is no leaf on the *karīra* tree—how can that be the fault of spring?
While the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) shines with its thick branches laden with fruit, shattering the brilliance of the sun,
what creature— even a beast— would seek shade from withered creepers?
When a tree by the road stands nearby, its hundreds of branches radiant with fruits, flowers, and new shoots, and its mass of rays from the sun obscured, what traveler would experience fatigue?

Those trees which have cast aside even a fraction of their own self-interest and are dedicated to quelling the suffering of people upon this earth— we do not know how they have come to be without any other recourse.
Herein lies but a small fraction of Prajāpati’s intention.
We endure venomous serpents even upon sandalwood;
for how could a beautiful object remain unprotected? Tell me, what is it that you wish to protect—the excellence of your own self?
You have gathered together the thorns of the khadira tree.
This great block of sandalwood (malayaja) has been bound together by snakes with mutually-linked coils; having climbed upon it, they have made it their own,
while the jasmine flowers (sumanas) do not resort to it.
For this very reason, it is not joined with a fruit.
Whatever is even slightly improper, if it is followed by what is proper—
what flower or fruit has not been produced by the sandalwood tree?
We feel great shame that it should depart in such a hasty retreat.
Having taken up a large axe, he approached him.
O young *campaka* tree, whose beautiful blossoms are accustomed to the pleasure of kissing the loveliness of a young woman’s cheek— why do you put forth flowers? Abandon here this blooming smile!
This desert land is filled with throngs of wild and uncivilized people.
Where is there any thought of blooming for a campaka tree whose roots are being scorched by the parched sands of the desert?
Generally, such things do not occur for those situated in an unsuitable place.
It is better to do no more than simply preserve one's own life.
The Creator has manifested the ultimate wickedness within himself by depriving the birch tree of its fruit;
for what use are its barks, which have been sliced by hundreds of sharpened weapons?
He does not fulfill the hopes of the succession of those who seek his aid.
O friend, what is the use of one who delights only in thorns and hates the fruit; what is the use of one who finds pleasure only in the limit of bitterness;
what is the use of one who is averse to the graceful play of shade? What indeed is the use of such a person for the sake of the virtuous?
"O student, this khadira tree has indeed been created by a wicked person."
"Has this been obtained after a long time like nectar? Will it lead to immortality, or will it grant a long life like an elixir?
This is its fruit—that this traveler, scorched by the curse, [is restored]."
The palm tree, being rigid, bears fruit only after a hundred years.
O tree, adorned with the splendor of a great burden of fruit,
renowned throughout the world as the sole producer of relief from hunger and heat—
how could this have been cast down by me from you?
One fruit, bitten by a bird, was obtained in small measure.
O you whose very nature is auspicious due to your extreme coolness,
truly there is no tree whatsoever that is equal to you;
for even those seeking shade [flee] from the double-tongued serpent.
Through attachment, even sandalwood is no different from a poisonous tree.
How is it that in this forest no one remains alone, yet there is not even a single noble tree so tall and rich with flowering vines and fruit?
By the command of the Destroyer of the world’s happiness, whose elements have been consumed by fire—
Only the Dhava, Khadira, and Palāśa trees possess growth.

O travelers, behold indeed the course of destiny for that very tree whose shade you have repeatedly sought when your distress from the heat was assuaged by you— now that its continuity of branches has been severed and it occupies the expanse of the sky, it perishes in time.
Now that it has dried up, its bed is scorched by sand and embers, and it burns intensely.

That very tree by the roadside, whose branches were so broad that the ten directions seemed to converge within them, where birds of many colors would circle and gather to rest, sleep, eat, and dwell in comfort upon its bending fruit-laden limbs— now that it has been uprooted by a wicked elephant.
The cowherd boys scratch their skin, which is parched and rough from the cow-dung ash.
Is it contentment? Is it incapacity? Or perhaps a lack of appreciation for him? Or is this dwelling in the forest merely a pretense? Or is it even hatred?
Let it be, O Fickle Fate; let it rest with this fruitless beauty of flowers that is so ill-suited to you.
Why have you not formed a connection even with something that is not a worthy match for sandalwood?

"Rooted in goodness, expansive, with dense and radiant shade, standing upon the path of the virtuous—it must be resorted to by the good. Reflecting thus, Tālodhvaja took refuge [in the Bodhi tree], thinking: "A man's power is only this much; whether it bears fruit today, or tomorrow, or even later—"
Whether it be at a specific time, or at some point, or perhaps never—regarding this, the Creator is the sovereign lord.
Since you were born at a crossroads, you possess a dense and beautiful shade; what need have you for shade?
Since you are laden with fruit, what need have you for fruit? Since you are full, why must you bend down? O noble tree, my friend, endure now the pulling of the tips of your branches.
They cause agitation, crushing, and destruction among people by their own wicked deeds.
O you whose entire body is pervaded by the quality of spreading fragrance, O you who possess the form of a *gopī* with slender and beautiful breasts,
this certain fault now manifested through contact with a serpent has been proclaimed.
O sandalwood tree, because of this, travelers pass you by from afar, avoiding you.
The sandalwood tree, which was your beloved friend, has been cut down; you have fled away,
and those pleasures derived from the habitual enjoyment of luxuries have been forgotten by you there every day—
if you do not repay that striker with the poisonous flame from the tip of your fangs.
O serpents, why did you not yourselves go to your destruction along with him?
At your feet, this human lifespan has passed away as time withered it;
even for a moment shorter than that, from what power could one have lived beyond? Therefore, may you be well; attain great prosperity, for even now, what haste is there for us?
O daughter of the Tāla tree, you have borne auspicious fruit in your sons and grandsons.
Is it necessary to speak of the virtues of sandalwood? Its very shadow is dense and fragrant; its very touch removes the heat of distress; its very qualities are what constitute its excellence.
Yet, from its very roots, it is defiled by serpents that dwell within it, forming a continuous barrier.
I know that it would be better for you to go to a *dhava*, a *khadira*, or some other tree, but not to this one.

There are no fruits worthy of praise, nor is there even a desire for the shade provided by sprouts; there are no flowers that are beautiful to the mind, nor are there birds that pour forth the nectar of song—
for this impure self, whose form is like an old statue filled with the excrement of a flock of crows.
Alas, how is it that you were created by the wicked Creator beneath this tree that is free from pride?
"It has no sweet fruit, nor lovely blossoms, nor creepers with glossy leaves; it offers no shade to relieve fatigue, nor do its birds warble melodious notes.
Is this a khadira tree, or have you mistaken it for something else, O traveler?"
O traveler, why then do you seek to wound your limbs with the mouths of these harsh thorns?
May those trees— glossy, leafy, which dispel the fierce heat with their abundant branches,
bending low with sweet fruit and severing the hunger-pangs of those who take refuge in them—
be consumed by fire; and may these travelers go upon those very paths.
The trees have become rough, thorny, and overgrown with many tree trunks sprouting from the holes where serpents dwell.
Shadow does not belong to the self; how could it belong to another? It is devoid of grasping.
When the heat of summer descends, why is the ground cool? From where does the wind come? The report that fruit will appear after a hundred years is merely a report.
Alas, for how long have we fools been robbed by the palm tree of our youth?
"Who are you, sir? "Know me to be a wretched man, cursed by fate, a Śāhoṭaka. "You speak as if out of dispassion; well said! Why is this known? Tell me.
"Here, on the left, there is a banyan tree which the travelers serve with their whole being."
Even the shadow of one standing on the path does not exist for the sake of benefiting others.

By their fragrance you have provided rest for the winds; by their sprouts, for the deer; by their hanging bark, for the ascetics; by their flowers, for the bees; by their fruits, for the birds afflicted by the heat; and by their shade, for those distressed by the summer sun;
and by their trunks, for the scent-elephants—thus have you constantly distributed relief to all.
O Druma, you have attained the rank of a Bodhisattva; truly, others are of low birth.
In those places, where the ground is shaded and fragrant with the honey dripping from flowers bent low under the weight of wandering bees,
crowds of travelers rest as if in homes; there,
their thirst is forever quenched by the water of mountain torrents, and they find satisfaction through the fruits of the trees.
May those trees rejoice, bear fruit, and attain the highest excellence.
O you who adorn the path, O you who provide sustenance for the trees along the way, may you remain equal and eternal!
Even now, cover the horizons with your branches and kiss the sky with your *sāla* trees;
for it is not only at your root that you have rolled about with the intent of providing rest.
Those afflicted by the heat were liberated, and we were satisfied with hundreds of fruits.
That tree, whose growth was sought with hundreds of desires by those full of hope,
has now been born from the lake as one who bestows fruit upon travelers and serves as a refuge for all who depend on him;
it is crowded by other birds gathered from various lands, unknown to one another.
Although he had obtained the opportunity, the old bird remained at a distance and watched.
Even though they have encountered the suffering of being scorched by forest fires, the distress of harsh winds and water, the heat of the sun,
the dragging of elephants, and even grave calamities from thunderbolts, [trees] still provide wood,
shade, fruit, bark, flowers, clusters of blossoms, or sprouts.
Oh, how excellent is the conduct of these trees, for they do not withhold their fruits from those who seek them day after day!
Swans [come] with the hope for lotus groves; crows and vultures with the hope for meat;

travelers with the hope for sweet fruit; and bees with the hope for fragrant scents—to this lofty street, which is devoid of essence and filled with clusters of red flowers that bear no fruit, they approach from afar.
O Śālmali tree, who has not been deceived by you every single day?

O traveler, do not rely upon this sandalwood tree for rest, thinking it to be one that has reached the further shore of the activity that pacifies the exhaustion of wandering through the terrifying desert;
for those dwelling in its vicinity are terrified by the rows of dense, poisonous flames.
How many travelers, having been revived, were then led by venomous serpents to the state of mere memory?
There was a place where flocks of female bees, their minds greedy for sweet nectar, sang aloud; where birds arrived from distant lands had built their nests;
and which was frequented by hundreds of travelers seeking relief from the exhaustion caused by the summer heat.
Now this shady tree has been crushed by an elephant in rut.
We have eaten sweet fruit and made our bed from the shoots and leaves growing at the tips of the branches; we have drunk water cooled by your shadow, and our fatigue has been dispelled.
Having rested there for a very long time, we have attained supreme peace through the mind.
May you be the tree of the true path and we its travelers; may there be a meeting again.
Even if a cloud were to shine upon the summit of the mountains or in the sky,
though it be consumed by the winds, would it ever sink into the netherworld?
A cloud that has taken its place in the sky,
filling the ocean with a flood of water,
is nonetheless incapable of filling even a cow’s footprint.
How can that which is unreal be spoken of in this way?
Look at this great lake, the sole life-sustenance for the traveler here, how it is drying up! Fie upon you, O cloud, who have foolishly blocked its path to the ocean!
Has the street of merchants here been made to prosper?
Those clouds that pour forth rain are ever-risen for the sake of pacifying the people, regardless of their own interests; yet those who seize them do not allow them to rain.
Indeed, there are some of great power among them.
Where has it been seen that the blind Bālāhaka could smell the grass that was not grazed by the cow?
[He is] like a great tree, a kinsman to travelers—
One who is impoverished by illusions, dewdrops, and particles of dust.
Some [rivers] become surging with fierce waves by taking refuge on the heights of lofty mountain peaks;
others, however, are mere droplets of water, falling upon grass and clods of earth.
The waters do not reach exhaustion for those who are free from deceit.
There, where you have dwelt for a long time without possessing anything,
free from debt and without the burden of accepting gifts or contracting loans—
there, even on the shore of the ocean, you roar shamelessly.
O Cloud, no one has ever been seen who is as bold and majestic as you.
Having opened its mouth and laughed for a long time with rumbling sounds, O cloud, you pour down rain upon the body of the cātaka bird,
whose neck is stretched out and curved at the tip of its beak.
Your life is at stake; this is merely a joke.
Having ascended to dwell upon the lofty summits of the high mountains,
and likewise having drawn water from the ocean for the sake of soothing the world’s distress,
they cast their long shadows across the vast expanse of the sky, which is great by its very nature.
"O Megha, who indeed does not envy you? For such is your commitment to this vow."
Having ascended, they dwell upon the lofty summits of high mountains;
they draw water from the ocean for the sake of quelling the world's distress;
and they cast long shadows and form vast expanses in the naturally immense sky.
"O Megha, who indeed does not envy you? For what reason do you thus desire such a vow?"
Excellent, O mass of clouds that rise so well! Excellent, O you who are to be cherished by the wise upon this earth!
Who else but you is capable of performing such a difficult task?
For while there are only a few fields suitable for everything else, therein lies the thunderbolt.
In all those deserts of scorched sand where no means of subsistence exist, may there be showers of rain.
In that dried-up lake, where frogs dwelling in hollows and tortoises made it appear as if dead beneath the earth,
and where large fish wallowed in heaps of thick mud until they repeatedly fainted— there, an untimely cloud arrived and performed such a deed.
Where the water is drunk by herds of wild elephants whose trunks are submerged in it.
Even though it was firmly rooted by the light qualities of the mountains,
the heads were suddenly brought low by the grasses of the raincloud that pours forth abundant and unrestrained showers.
And that movement is due to the nature of water, which is difficult to grasp.
One cloud, having grown large, thunders with great impetuosity after receiving only a few, sparse drops of water with difficulty;
yet another, a ground worthy of praise for its incomparable greatness, dances— truly, I do not know [how].
Is it perhaps a cloud, with its vast heart, that has emerged from the midst of these two? Or is it a cātaka bird?
Those clouds have departed, their bodies dark as a shimmering swarm of bees,
whose splendor once eclipsed even the distinction between land and water in the world.
O young *cātaka* bird, blinded by futile thirst, why do you wander about so distressed?
In this autumn, when the clouds have vanished, where could even a single drop of water from you be found here?
"Let us see what he does," thought the ministers, who— though driven by powerful actions— had out of pride neglected him from afar while his minor magical feats were being accomplished; now,
having gained full scope and being unable to restrain him, they released a thunderbolt.
Alas! This prosperous mountain village has been utterly consumed by its dense enemy.
Having roared loudly, completely obstructed the sky, and shrouded the circle of the quarters,
and having assumed a body as beautiful and dark as a fragment of crushed sapphire,
the cloud released its water even when the arrival of the rainy season had come.
And the entire beak of the young pigeon was drenched by him, though he himself did not do so.

There, in that village— where the sky was pervaded by portentous clouds, where the ministers were absent, and where bold acts suited to one's own nature were practiced— it manifested itself in such a way that it bridged the gap between those whose inner selves were exceedingly pure and clear and the mud flowing through the streets.
Nor was it even noticed by the people, just as [the movement] of the currents of floodwaters and river streams is not perceived.

O clouds, have you not heard of the Buddha’s fame, so heavy with the gift of his own body? Or have you never anywhere heard the story of the Pārijāta tree? For by giving this water which is so easily obtained, while you roar aloud, [you bring about the destruction of all beings].
No shame arises for those who, out of impetuosity, run wildly through the sky.

It rains in the proper place and does not thunder in vain; it swiftly removes exhaustion and brings security to the surface of the earth for fields whose luster has been withered by the heat. Whatever excellence it holds deep within its heart, it manifests as something else that causes delight.
May this cloud of the Sugata, with its skin as dense and glistening as an unfailing rain-cloud, continue to grow.

The ocean does not roar, for its fame is vast due to its activity in bestowing the objects requested by the Lord of the Three Worlds; it is filled with the priceless jewel of its shimmering crest of flames.
This ordinary water, by its very nature, is merely transformed by the removal of a tiny amount of that [ocean's] water.
Having cast its water into the void, the cloud roars with pride, disregarding its own destruction.
Just as the ocean does not maintain its boundary known as the shore,
nor does it provide assistance to those who are parched with thirst, so too [the Bodhisattva] does not maintain this other boundary.
In the case of cows and other animals, milk turns into curd either on the next day or immediately;
but even today, there has been no transformation of the Ocean of Milk—how much less so for the Great Ones?
Although the ocean reveals its jewels through its clarity,
nevertheless, do not think in your mind that it is only knee-deep.
Alas, even he who is an ocean of water is called a mere river if not even a single drop of water falls into the mouths of those who seek it.
May that greatness of the ocean, renowned upon the earth, go to destruction— that ocean by which not even a single person afflicted by hunger and thirst was ever satisfied.
When the ocean has rescued the gods from death by pouring forth a stream of the essence of nectar,
whose heart on earth would still throb for wretched summer ponds?
That this moon-crested Hara is [the Lord],
that this Hari is the sovereign of Śrī, and that these immortals are indeed gods— [all this is due to his power].
Thus, these are but mere droplets of his majestic power.
Indeed, your very saltiness is a virtue, O sea-monster,
by which no one approaches you;
you bear a terrifying form.
O Ocean of Wheels, for what purpose are you here in front?
Setting aside the enmity arising from the seizure of his fortune and disregarding the churning of that mountain,
the great ocean gave refuge to Hari.
For the conduct of those with wise minds is indeed free from envy.
May the Lord of the Waters, who bears the brilliance of the moon and whose crown-jewels lead the way, carry the blades of grass upon his head; for in reality, there is no lord superior to the Lord.
Jewels are indeed jewels, and likewise, grass is indeed grass.
Let those miserable ponds, whose very nature is distress, hate the summer and long for the arrival of the clouds; but as for the ocean—
[how could it be moved] by the flickering of a foolish minnow or the shifting of the king of mountains?
The milk in her womb was unwavering; both of these things were inconceivable.
The boulders are jewels, the aquatic creatures are green, the goddess Lakṣmī is personified in the water, the heaps of pearls are its sands, the coral vines are its moss, and the water is nectar.
On its shores stand the wish-fulfilling trees; what more need be said? Its very name is "Treasure-Mine."
From afar it is an elixir for the ears, yet even when close at hand, one's thirst is not quenched.
Let alone the removal of fatigue by the waters of the ocean for those whose minds are scorched by forest fires far away;
let this much suffice: if their tongues are not [quenched] by even drops of water.
It burns, yet craving does not reach a state of doubling.
O abode of sea-monsters, do not despise these jewels; for what indeed has not been bestowed upon you by the Kaustubha through its harsh blows against the stones tossed by the surging waves?
Even the Supreme among Men extended his hand in supplication.
Alas,
we are deeply ashamed that many of these merchants enter the vast ocean with their cargo-laden boats placed upon their shoulders.
Just as dogs and water-birds are driven by intense thirst.
This ocean must be kept at a distance by women, children, and those who are thirsty, precisely because it is undrinkable;
for it is made terrifying by the rows of fierce makaras with their gaping jaws.
Why do you fear the succession of further waves?
Fie, fie, fie upon this ocean of the shameless one,
in which travelers are utterly exhausted like those in a desert land,
their throats parched by the fever of thirst and their long tongues protruding!
Dejected, with their eyes cast down, they proceed along the riverbank.
Even if it were churned by the hosts of the armies of gods and asuras,
or filled with the waters of clouds and rivers,
or even if it were consumed by the fire of the submarine mare’s mouth—
The ocean was not agitated, nor did it diminish in its extent.
Wherein Maināka and other mountains dwell, trembling with fear of Maghavat;
from where the Lord of fierce rays rises and where he sets;
and wherein the Lord of the worlds lies hidden in some corner of his belly—[that is the ocean].
Who is able to weigh the profound majesty of this ocean of merit?
By Śrī, Ratna, and Abhyāṃ for Hari;
by Śaśilekhā for the Enemy of the Mind-born (Kāma); and by Pīyūṣa for all the inhabitants of heaven—how else could he remain so slow with the weight of his fame?
If the ocean were not to endure the exertion of being churned, [it would not yield its treasures].
Released toward the uneven [shore], the fierce [waves] took refuge in the ten directions;
by means of moonstones, jewels, and pearls, they generally employed seduction.
What indeed did the deceitful ocean not do at the commencement of its labor?
Even that was not tolerated by the skillful gods, who were without the nectar of immortality.

O Ocean, since this time has passed with such profundity and greatness, even though it has not yet commenced its accustomed display of virtues— what follows after this? Alas, O Sea, why do your waves remain without reaching their completion?
Desist from this; not even a drop of water remains in these rivers.
Even while dwelling for a single moment upon the lap of this [world] with its face turned away,
his body momentarily ablaze within,
he does not dispel his thirst for the submarine fire of craving, even though his wealth has increased.
Let that cruelty of the ocean go to destruction; let its greatness vanish.
Alas! This is the ultimate ignoble state of the Lord of Rivers:

that he has allowed these jewels of brilliant luster—whose qualities have been long cultivated—to find their place within dull, useless things that have come from elsewhere and taken up residence there.
Having suddenly attained a state of identification with that, he incessantly casts [the object] away with powerful [impulses].

In this world, there was once a certain one who became a crest-jewel [of pride] because, though he possessed all the waters from jars and other vessels, he was unable to hold even a single mouthful for his thirst;
yet he roared loudly on all sides with deep and heavy thundering, praising his own greatness.
Having become corrupt, O Ocean, why do you defile the cavity of our ears?
In this place, the water is harsh and alkaline, unfit for drinking; having found it, one suffers greatly.
Even the mere act of plunging into it is not undertaken by one who is healthy, due to the fear of predatory serpents.
O traveler, why then have you become so deluded by thirst in this desert named "The Ocean"?
You run in vain after a multitude of stainless jewels that have been destroyed by being hidden within.

This support for all the waters in the three worlds is yours; this splendor within your watery abode is yours; this state of being a Great Being is yours—having served you alone, the shore-mountain whose form is terrifying with its many breakers.
O Evil One, that quarrel which causes torment is extinguished wherever there is a stream of stones.
Let this ocean scatter the great mountains with its surging waves rising from the play of the shore;
let it deafen the quarters of the sky with its roars and assume vast proportions.
Yet, may it cut through the excess of thirst for travelers whose bodies are scorched by the heat of the sun.
What can even the ocean, though it has made its roar, do for the sake of equality with the vast expanse of the sky?
Alas! By him who gave to a suppliant out of great compassion for beings an incomparable treasure of nectar,
as well as the abode of Śrī, the great jewel, the wish-fulfilling tree,
and the cow— by his very curse, the ocean has become a sea of salt water and incurred infamy.
Regarding this world as worthless as a blade of grass, he focuses his mind one-pointedly on grasping at faults.
"Alas, what misery! Even those dwelling on the bank, seeing me with my burden of water rendered fruitless,
these creatures go elsewhere every day,
as if their exhaustion had arisen from carrying this useless excess of water."
I believe that the ocean daily offers its own form as a sacrifice into the submarine fire.
By the protection of the established order and by safeguarding the great lords of the earth,
Viṣṇu attained some measure of rest for a very long time;
yet, due to the agitation caused by the pain of churning the ocean, he was unable to maintain his own characteristic depth.
Alas! As they quickly offered the nectar to the gods, it was all vomited back up.
How wonderful is that Blessed One, the submarine fire; how wonderful is the ocean!
Upon reflecting on the excellence of his karma, a trembling arises in the mind.
Though he drinks the waters of a single vessel that devours its support, no satiety has ever been born.
Not even the slightest fatigue arose in the body of that other great-souled being.

O Ocean, if you do not feel agitation and lend an attentive ear for a moment, I ask you something; having reflected upon it, give me an answer. For you are seen sighing with a breath sharpened by the excessive regret of despair.
For thirsty travelers, how much greater would that [suffering] be than the burning heat of a forest fire?
Here sleeps Keśava; here lie the kinsmen of his enemies;
here rest the virtues of the mountain-dwellers seeking refuge;
and here lies the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction.
Oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight is the form of the ocean!
He gave the goddess Śrī to Vaikuṇṭha, the fresh moon to Bhava,
and even Uccaiḥśravas to the wielder of the thunderbolt— how could those be counted?
But that he gave even his own body to a sage afflicted by thirst for it— that is what truly defines him.
Who else in the worlds could become such a Bodhisattva, who is like an ocean?

If the ocean, its waves scattering jewels that blaze with light, were turned back toward its own shore by the winds— if such a thing could happen— it would surely be the fault of those seeking gain who have met with a reversal of fortune.
Yet, for the donor, there is not even the slightest sense of being a donor.

The ocean clearly transforms those countless drops of water that are constantly tossed within it into the state of precious pearls; having received them from the clouds as they fall, it embraces them with its circling waves and takes them in.
Generally, even one who is humble is honored by masters if they have shown respect.
May there be well-being for the coral vines, the flowers, and the gems; may the row of pearl-oyster shells be auspicious.
I have obtained every single fruit of the ocean.
That I have not been torn apart by fierce aquatic creatures.
Having taken water from all around the mouths of the rivers,
what has this wicked ocean actually gained?
It has merely turned it salty and offered it as a libation into the submarine fire.
And it was cast into the hollow depths of the subterranean realm.
The foolish person who does not grasp a great jewel when it has come at the right time,
seeing it later in the hands of another, will afterwards be consumed by regret.
When it is split and enters within according to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) as desired,
what kind of purity can there be for that insentient crystal stone?
That which is a quality of crystal becomes a defect;
for it assumes the reflection of even those things that are stained, due to its own transparency.
That the price of a fragment of stone is so small compared to the earth is the manifestation of that splendor whose essence has not yet set.
He who, out of a desire for wealth, seizes the tips of dry grass or blades of straw belonging to another,
is a fool whom even others employ as a foot-protector against a "jewel-grass" (a mere blade of grass mistaken for a gem).
Born of a noble lineage, possessing virtuous qualities, well-rounded in conduct,
and embraced by virtues that rival the heat of the sun—
behold, O observer, how even such a necklace is pleasing to the eye.
She was pushed outside by her pair of high breasts.
If a jewel, worthy of being set in golden ornaments, is fastened into lead,
it neither cries out nor does it shine.
There is blame for the one who incites [the offense].
It would be better for an emerald to remain stained than for it ever to abandon its own nature; fie upon the innate purity of crystal, which [attains] its stainlessness so easily!
He who clings to form when it has reached its end.
O friend, in this world where there is such great abundance of jewels, O wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*), do not become a mere stone; do not fail to be a jewel!
For today, such gems as these appear in the world.
For those whose very skill in grasping a blade of grass is their ornament.
Even if he falls to the ground, even if he is covered in dust,
even if he is disregarded by the wicked who are like those blind from birth,
he possesses within himself the great majesty that is venerated by the three worlds.
For the wish-fulfilling gem never indeed abandons it.
O Cintāmaṇi, if you have not been borne upon the head by any lord on earth, do not despair because of that; for indeed,
the seed of merit required to install you does not exist [in them].
In this world, the head of someone is worthy of such good fortune.
By what creator was this common quality of being a "jewel" bestowed equally upon both the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and the grass-gem (*tṛṇamaṇi*)?
For one does not grow weary while granting the desires of those who seek them.
Another, however, was not ashamed while grasping at a withered blade of grass.
Surrounded by hundreds of desires, though worthy of being the crest-jewel of the lords of the world,
he has treated even grass as sufficient and has set his foot upon stones;
yet he who has taken such a path still falls within the range of the vision of those possessed of true discernment.
In the mountain caves where the rocks are crumbling, this wish-fulfilling gem lies desolate.
He grasps it with longing, gazes repeatedly at that delicate thing,
and conceals it within a surge of incomparable joy, thinking, "What a great jewel!"—
yet he has merely obtained from somewhere a piece of glass that possesses a luster like a cosmetic ointment.
Alas, that wretched and vulgar man undergoes excessive torment!
O brother, filling the circle of the quarters for a long time with your mass of rays, why have you shone here in vain through this dense cloud?
Who here truly knows your ultimate and natural worth?
When a village has been burnt down, the common folk lose their regard for emerald gems.
To some this [gift] is far away; some of unrefined intellect do not understand its inner significance at all.

Some proud person does not beg, while another of meager intent seeks only a tiny trifle. Thus, for one who is addicted to the vice of giving what is requested, the bright lines of magnanimity do not shine forth.
Born as a touchstone for those places difficult to traverse due to their subtlety, you are like a wish-fulfilling gem.

Those who have forcibly grasped grass thinking it to be jewels, or lumps of iron thinking them to be gems, have been seen for a long time in every house with their jewels burnt away and their number diminished;
I do not know whether this is due to their non-existence or by the power of fate that such is heard here.
Even the name of such a jewel does not exist here for one who picks up common gems.
When pearls are cast from the depths of the ocean by the great waves and roll along the shores, appearing like clear bursts of laughter due to their stainless luster,
that occurs because of the exhaustion of that very ocean for those who have reached other continents.
But there are indeed sea-faring merchants who are addicted to the acquisition of jewels.
"This ruby is of great value, honored upon the surface of the earth, radiant, and of noble birth;
surely, having seen it from afar, some wretched state of misfortune has fled far away.
Thus, for the sake of removing calamity, was this [image] established by someone through a proliferation of delusions.
In the infinite [space], that very same piece of stone, harsh with hundreds of scars, was seen.

O Mount Rohaṇa, may you be well; do not even in your dreams harbor such thoughts as, "Now that we have fallen from our place because of you, how shall these jewels exist? For if we, the glorious gems, find our firm foundation through you, then [we shall endure].
Those kings, devoted to aesthetic splendor, will place us upon their crowns.
Let the peacock, having climbed a tree on the path, cry out loudly for a long time;
yet when the quality of sound pervades all directions, the conch shell becomes the ground of true estimation.

When the remains of Śaṅkha were cracked open after he had died, did he truly breathe again with the breath of life? Or rather, was it merely that this sound issued forth from him? It was not his voice.
That which is not worth hearing is that which does not proclaim the true meaning.

Having abandoned their lives, the conch shells— possessed of the quality of whiteness and having attained a special status as ornaments for the face of the world— resound with a display of great majesty.
Those whose hearts are possessed of such [qualities] are able to sustain that life.
The sound of a conch shell, though steady, pleasing to the ear, and truly a supreme blessing,
is like something else entirely when it resounds in some village courtyard during the twilight hours,
its long blast amplified by the straight necks of intoxicated, stout dogs.
The sound called *nāda* is produced by imitation, joyful rustic laughter, and striking.
Though being disregarded even by those born from the mine of jewels, though his body was reduced to mere dry bones and hanging loose,
and though he was struck by gasping breaths accompanied by wheezing sounds;
One of pure intention speaks only of auspiciousness, like a conch shell.
There are thousands of conch shells in the ocean, struck by the spray of its waves,
which roll along the shores with their hundred ridges staining the surface of the earth;
yet among them, there arose one certain Pāñcajanya, a marvel for the virtuous.
It is filled by the winds of the breath of the Enemy of Mura, which are capable of destroying the world at the time of its dissolution.
The utterance of "Huṃ" fulfills all hopes; his birth was from the ocean of milk;
his body, which kisses the face of Govinda, is more beautiful than the orb of the full moon;
this is his innate glory—what more need be said of these virtues? For they are as follows:
O Pañcajanya, crookedness resides in your heart; because of that, we are deeply ashamed.
"It would be better to remain without splendor than to possess a splendor equal to another's";
thus, when the night-lily blooms, the lotus closes its buds.
This defect of the lotus— its aversion toward the moon, the abode of a multitude of virtues— is certainly due to its association with worldly splendor.
With so many internal cavities and so many thorns on the outside,
how could the fibers of the lotus stalk not be fragile?
O Lotus, what is the reason for your covering yourself with these very long, white fibers?
If there were indeed something noble to be seen, you would not have covered them.
Like a frightened goddess of fortune, she does not set foot there.
O land-lotus, gather thorns;
joyfully proclaim your birth from the family of mud;
even so, maintain your steadfastness at the meeting of the waters.
You are departing for the state of being the abode of supreme splendor.
This is the ruin in the eyes and this density of passion in the heart, as well as this face intoxicated with honeyed pride;
yet even so, the lotus remains the supreme abode of beauty.
Indeed, it is said that their very wretchedness constitutes their misfortune.
Even lotuses and other things of great quality do not meet their destruction during the nights due to separation from the sun;
for that [destruction] arises from the dullness born of being produced in a pond filled with mud and water.
This manifestation of the Elder is renowned throughout the three worlds.
O lotus, surpass Lakṣmī who is marked by her skill with the *kuśa* grass;
abandon your blooming and relinquish your trembling slightly;
bring joy here to the swarms of bees that have come from afar.
When a friend is present in the proper manner, perform this as you desire.
O Kuśeśaya, listen always thus to my words,
which I shall speak to you out of affection;
for they possess this stainless luster, like bees drawn by virtues.
Are you going toward that which is most delightful, or toward a thicket of thorns?
"Shrink back, O lotus flower; abandon your beauty!
Behold, the maker of faults now rises. Having reflected upon this, it gradually gains power over its own crooked nature."
Concealment of one's virtues is appropriate for those who possess them.
Though its fibers are breaking, though it has become full of many thorns, though it is riddled with holes, and though it has arisen from foul mud,
the lotus nevertheless possesses a splendor to be enjoyed by the bees.
Upon the rising of the sun, it always attains full blossoming.
Granted, let the clusters of lotuses resound with a thick, humming drone from the swarms of bees greedy for honey; yet,
where the Creator himself sings with a melody most pleasing to the ear—
He is that certain bee, the lotus at the navel of the mountain-bearer.
O you who dispel the heat, who are sympathetic, beautiful, and awakened;
O you who delight in affection for friends and uphold a flood of excellent virtues; O you who have satisfied the six-legged bees by the gift of your own limbs—
It is fitting that your abode should be here, in each and every lotus.
O land-lotus, your birth was not from the mud, nor do you suffer the misfortune of dwelling with the dull-witted;
