your body is anointed with a luster that steals the brilliance of jewels. Had the Creator not fashioned such lightness of heart within you, [he would never have made you so].
You alone would have become the one supreme station of Fortune here in this world.
On the surface of the waters, many clusters of lotuses have arisen,
which serve as a comparison for the faces of lovely women who resemble the lords of the night;
yet, in the navel of the enemy of Bhauma (the Earth), there arose that one unique Great Lotus.
He who has become the father of the one who brought forth the manifestation of the three worlds.
O Puṣya, elsewhere an opportunity was skillfully snatched away by those lured by the fragrance;
even entry into its own interior was not granted, for it remained firm and tight due to its state as a sheath.
Having been thus led to despair, this dull-witted one, its movement faltering, [remains] at nightfall.
Behold the bee, who has been forcibly driven away from both sides even by the glorious lotus!
"Brother lotus, endure this contraction for a short while;
that same beauty shall be yours at dawn when the sun has shone forth."
Having descended into the depths and become stained by the mud, the lotus stalks—
though possessing excellent qualities— are dragged up by fishermen devoid of virtue, revealed only by their own sprouts.
Then those lotus buds, endowed with excellent qualities,
were borne upon their heads by the proud, while they themselves remained closed, dull-witted as they were.
In the desert there is no water at all;
even if it is obtained with great difficulty, it is bitter, scanty, and hot, and does not quench one's thirst.
Even a single drop of water falling from the beak of a restless cātaka bird is a source of intense joy to one suffering from thirst;
yet today, that very drop has been multiplied by the Friend who brings the arrival of the clouds.
Another was created by Jaladhara with waters.
O traveler, how is it that in this desert— well-named for its abundance of materials necessary for the success of friction-fires—
this very opposite is seen there?
There is a well there, and in it is water that is obtained without effort.
In this desert, what more remains unspeakable in words?
O traveler, do not abandon [this place] again and again; be one who is compassionate toward those who have sought refuge here.
For you, who are greedy for even a mere drop of water as if it were meat, [this is the only thing left].
A bed of sand was seen with its surroundings ablaze.

[He beheld] excellent trees, their bodies encircled by an abundance of vast shoots and clusters of flowers, bending low under the weight of their fruit; they were broad and sheltered by hundreds of birds warbling sweetly.
The deluded one searches for branches in the desert, for they do not exist there.

"Devoid of water, trees, and grass, alas, I am truly unable to provide even the slightest assistance to these weary travelers"— thinking thus, he does not cease to feel constant remorse, nor does he ever rest at ease.
He employs them for the attainment of the waters of the dance of the sixth Marut.
The traveler has wandered on, his mind bewildered by the speed of his journey; he has repeatedly raised the dust of the earth, and then, sighing for a long time, he stands there in dejection.
What indeed has not been done by this traveler? And yet, the desert remains cruel.
By its very nature repulsive, it has become painful; it does not attain even the slightest degree of tenderness.

On this side is a terrifying flock of crows; on this side, the work of owls; here are these vultures and the like; and here is this family of herons. In this cemetery, which is barren of all virtues, [we are] utterly ruined.
Moreover, there were even two or three birds whose voices were indeed melodious.
Are you confused, or are you mad, that you are observed in such a moment? Again and again, none of your actions are preceded by careful reflection;
for even though you know it yourself to be waterless, you have entered this desert expanse.
O traveler, that you desire to obtain water cool and sweet—

He who experiences suffering for the sake of others is sweet even in his destruction; indeed, every transformation of his is esteemed here by all. Yet, if he does not reach full growth, it is because he has fallen upon barren soil.
Is this a fault of the sugarcane juice, or rather of the desert-born [water] which lacks its virtues?
The heat is within yourself; those traveling on the road avoid the faults of the trees and creepers clinging there.
O desert, this intense thirst of yours is truly the source of such calamity;
for is this not a very great benefit—a master of drops of water who thunders with pride?
For it is for your benefit that even common clouds gird themselves with rain.
Thus, by this method, you have rendered yourself incapable of performing even the slightest benefit for anyone.
Therefore, do not offer any help; otherwise, O fool, you will be censured.
For you are merely creating from afar the deception of water-bearing clouds by means of a mirage.
Out of affection, you draw others toward yourself even though their minds are deluded by craving; therefore, you are to be pitied.

Are these mango trees beautiful, their heads bowed under the weight of their fruit? Are these plantain trees lovely, providing shade that dispels the heat? Are these campaka trees fragrant, covered in blossoms?
Alas, they have all been licked by fierce, unrestrained young camels and stripped bare once again.
O fool, why do you wander aimlessly in this windless desert, seeking in vain to die?
Let the intermediate waters remain in the chasms or go anywhere else;
the limit for the flow of the celestial river is the ocean, the mine of jewels.
Where is the hollow reed, and where is the sugarcane? Yet they both possess the appearance of being well-formed.
These two are conjured illusions for the deception of those whose minds are empty of discernment.
He has no strength for bearing burdens, nor does he possess the quality of a draft animal for plowing;
yet, like a temple ox, he nevertheless eats sumptuously.
A crocodile, having reached its own domain, can drag away even a lordly elephant;
yet that very same creature, fallen from its place, is treated with contempt even by a dog.
Better a kick from a lion with its tail raised high and terrifying as it shakes its mane, than mounting upon a jackal.
The sandalwood tree, though its essence is solely fragrance, is served even when it bears no fruit;
serpents, whose food is air, serve it as well—such is the nature of destiny.
Where has the deer gone? It does not live, though it eats various kinds of grass day after day. But for the lion, who feeds on elephants slain by its own strength, sustenance is difficult to obtain.
Even Viśvakarman himself would not be able to straighten out a piece of bad wood that is crooked, full of internal cavities, and riddled with many hard knots.
Not even slightly imitated by that [lake], nor was its water cooled by long service;
rather, my eyes have been blinded by smoke from wretched lamps.
When shall we behold with stainless eyes this ruined marketplace,
where the wish-fulfilling gem and the glass trinket are perceived as having inverted qualities?
If one touches a lamp, suspecting it to be a radiant campaka bud,
what else can happen to him but the burning caused by the stain of soot?
The ocean, with its peaks like a mountain and its mass of flickering submarine fires,
and this heap of refuse from the city— neither of these is to be stepped over by anyone.

On Śeṣa, who possesses many heads, each heavy and capable with the brilliance of jewels upon his hoods— who else but he would venture to bear the burden of the earth, while wretched little insects merely crawl about?
Who could perceive, even with effort, the path by which peacocks take their food,
were it not for those very fools who, delighted by the roar of the clouds, would dance?
In autumn, the night— its mass of darkness destroyed by the hundreds of rays of the full moon—
does not even equal the luster of the day, though the sun is hidden by clouds.
Even for one who possesses a soft and lovely retinue, this alone is unseemly for the God of Love:
that he has placed upon his banner a sea-monster with a mouth made terrifying by its fangs.
O wise goldsmith, homage be to you,
who repeatedly examines even in difficult circumstances whether a golden ornament is equal to a mere stone.
That which you are now placing upon the scale.
That jar-like blind well has indeed been filled;
it is incapable of removing your grace,
for its base conduct has been sealed by you.
Receive those drops of water from his mouth.
If a centipede, though possessing a hundred feet,
cannot even cross over a cow's footprint,
how much less can Hanuman, the two-footed one, do so?
We dispute regarding the crossing of the ocean.
There is no proficiency in upholding the lineage of the gurus,
nor any regard for the accumulation of great virtues;
even discourse on the production of fruits does not exist in their search.
O foolish hunter, what is there now for you here in this house?
Regarding the grass-gem and the man who possesses it,
why is it said that both have a vast intention? For those two, [the gem] is minute by comparison with even a tiny fragment on the tip of a blade of grass.
The explanation of apprehension and its establishment is concluded.
"O brother goldsmith! Cease your labor today regarding this golden vessel, which is already adorned with the effort and craftsmanship of various figures fashioned from gold."
For one who applies an inferior color, there is the gain of great value.

Who here has not long been carried away by the suspicion that it is a pearl because it rests upon the tip of a slender blade of grass? Therefore, he who perceives this drop of water in such a distorted way—
In this world, we here are endowed with consciousness.
O biting serpent, it is improper [to say] that the Lord leads you to the place of anklets out of favoritism;
for the bees, intoxicated by the honor of being drawn toward [the lotus], [do not seek such things].
Why do you make such tinkling sounds? Is it appropriate for you to do so?
"Goldsmith, you have come here to sell items suitable for the ears;
even now, it has not been heard here in this village."
He was surely the village chief Aviddhakarṇa.

Surely we shall destroy those haughty mountains by means of our form; for when their strength has been crushed during the conflict that destroys their wings, is it not fitting for the submarine fire to be provoked?
Even the radiant [deities] were unable to withstand the churning of the ocean.
How wondrous is this ocean, so vast because it is filled with the floods of clouds and the currents of rivers! Yet you, as a mere small well, provide benefit to those who seek your aid.
For by compressing the cavity of the belly, this greatness [is achieved].
Fie on the submarine fire, which, though a foe,
approaches out of desire to fill its own belly; fie even more on the ocean, which acts in such a manner toward one who is likewise.
One should not satisfy even the enemy's desires with one's own waters.
Desiring to protect her young who had entered their nest in a tree,
the female dove, having quickly scooped up water from the river with the hollow of her wings,
is said to have repeatedly sprinkled the forest fire.
An affectionate person indeed does not consider their own suffering.
A crow, though naturally fickle, maintains a pure conduct;
having obtained an offering, it calls upon its own kin and others alike—
even toward the carcass of an elephant, though it is full of skin, bone, and flesh.
A dog hates and strikes others, being of a miserable nature.
The cloud that takes up water only to release it once more in that very same place is the foremost among the dull-witted;
but he who desires to take back exactly what was vomited forth— [he is even more so].
He is the master of the stream, a caravan leader free from shame.
Even though we conceptualize in many ways, we do not understand them; by what names shall we designate those of great intelligence,
for whom gold is the ornament of the entire world?
To discern reality, stones are the supreme authority.
The faces of those who possess all splendor have not withered; darkness has not set, nor has the benefit of the world been performed. By what quality, then, am I the son of the Sun, that the worlds—?
You shall cause him to return gradually, without an oath.
The farmer performed his labor in order to protect [the field];
look at this straw man, a mere likeness of himself!
Because it is stiff and inactive, it is indeed free from fear.
The herds of fish and deer will once again feast upon the grain.
Whose eyes are these, wide and unblinking, other than those of a celestial being? For even they, having grasped them,
have opened their mouths over the mass [of water]— what is this?
O fool, you have not seen the hook clearly within.
O you of base birth, tell me the truth: from the time of your birth until now, have you ever performed even the slightest virtuous deed? For what purpose was this fire raised by the charioteer?
O wicked one, do that which will defile this entire world!
Even if one should fall from manhood, even if one should go to the lower realms, even if one should become great through the exercise of power—
such is this resolve that one would uplift the entire world.
The direction has been made manifest by some Supreme Person.
The merchant-demon of glass, who possesses a meager disposition and stumbles while imagining only the conceptual constructs of his own family’s craft,
is seized by that jewel which rivals the sovereign Kaustubha gem.
[He was] filled with envy toward the skillful jeweler who effortlessly weaves [the gems] together.

Where is the Goddess Bhavānī, the sister who removes misfortune? Where is Lord Hara, the brother-in-law and kinsman of the afflicted? And where is the wretched state of those who have sought refuge in the ocean?
"O Maināka, you must not speak of this to us."
The lofty nature of the sun’s peak is in vain when it does not support him as he desires to set;
yet even that quality of the lotus stalk is praiseworthy for the Daitya.
Out of fear, the Lord of the Maruts approached him and took hold of him.
O Kubera, Lord of Wealth, you feel no shame: your home is a cemetery, your garment is an elephant hide, your ointment is ashes, and your vehicle is a bull.
This poverty belongs to you, your dear friend.
There is no cessation of capacity anywhere; all things possess degrees of perfection established by their own intrinsic nature,
even when being consumed by a fire that blazes for an entire eon.
Agastya drank the ocean with a single handful.
The Lord Viṣṇu supports the entire earth; the serpent supports him, and the ocean supports both him and the serpent; yet the pitcher-born Agastya indeed swallowed even that ocean with ease.
It is true that there is no limit to the greatness of the great.
Placed upon the broad slope of a young woman’s hips,
firmly grasped by her vine-like arm around his neck, and pressed tightly between her high, full breasts— this [man].
The jar enjoys the fruits of the burning of cow-dung.
If a dog, its shoulder-blade covered with bound-on artificial manes, is made to mount the path of the Lord of Beasts, it is merely a sham,
for it lacks the natural prowess of one who is intent on splitting the temples of rutting elephants.
How will the lord of deer let out his roar?
Even his remaining face makes the sun— the source of brilliance—
and the moon into vessels for its morsels;
for if indeed his entire body were to manifest, [what could remain?]
What indeed, what indeed would Rāhu not have done at that time?

O parrot, because you are deluded by the perceived similarity between this and the flowers, sprouts, and fruits [of the pomegranate], you do not know whether your own state is one of stability or instability;
therefore, you do not abandon this pomegranate tree out of hope for its fruit.
One who is distressed by a matter does not take account of the fault of disparagement.
Is it better for you here to have been crushed by the heat of the sun, O thicket? Or why were you not consumed entirely by forest fires?
Since you have been spared by the multitudes of heartless people who do not even recognize a stalk or a leaf—
Among other flowers, you, O Mālatī, have been placed in the center.

Is this appropriate for one who is pure, clearly intent on the elevation of his own side, and fit to attain the ripening of the fruit of his devotion to virtue? For you have approached the ear of another while standing before those present.
O cruel and wicked one, that you strike from afar with a falling arrow!
Adorned with golden ornaments, that king— whose royal splendor was once worthy of praise on the heads of monarchs— was reduced to such wretchedness by the dust clinging from his fall to the earth,
that he was indistinguishable from a common clod of earth, his discernment obscured by the confusion of his circumstances.
Having observed him, the world avoids him out of fear of injury to its feet.
When birds are summoned, even a gnat is not prevented from entering;
yet a grass-gem, whether placed in the midst or at the head, assumes the luster of precious jewels. Even a firefly does not tremble to move among those who possess great brilliance.
Fie on this insentient generality, which, like a master whose inner essence has not been scrutinized, [presides over things].
If its very nature is thus full of sap, why is it so dull? If there is indeed natural straightness, why is it so knotted?
If its root is swelling, whence comes this reputation of being a "mud-born" lotus? If these qualities are present...
"Friend lotus stalk, we do not believe that these holes of yours are real."
O friend, serpent! If you are a possessor of wealth, if you wear earrings, if you bear a crown set with jewels—what does it matter to us? May you have well-being;
we have no desire for such things if you discard your skin-cloak in an improper place.
But why, O brother, do you burn me with the fierce flame of your poison? What is this obsession of yours?
In one place, there are excellent jewels upon the head, a home in a mountain cave, and the abandonment of the skin of one's own body;
livelihood is provided by effortless winds, and such is the conduct in that one place.
In another, the path is crooked, speech is accompanied by deceit, and poison is seen in the very look.
O friend, connoisseur of enjoyments, what is this that the lamp burns according to its kind?
He possesses many faces, and his status as a Great Being is indeed well known;
for Kadrū’s first offspring was born here, and one must consider how this world came to be when she was provoked.
Such is the wondrous conduct of Śoṣa throughout the three worlds, by which she [was overcome].
Just as a foul color is removed even when one has knowledge of the venomous snake, so too is she turned back as if wiped away.
Of what use is that mountain of gold or that mountain of silver, when by their support trees remain merely trees?
We consider only the Malaya mountain to be truly so, for it is upon it that [fragrant] plants depend.
The śāhoṭa, nimba, kuṭaja, and even sandalwood trees as well.
Those who have already prepared a treacherous path with poison, whose number is beyond counting,
and who, double-tongued, lie in wait at vulnerable points intending to destroy the innocent world—
even these serpents, being deluded, place jewels upon their heads, confounding the true and the false.
For those endowed with virtue, there is no lapse whatsoever due to impropriety; enough with such anxiety.

It was maintained as an antidote to that [enemy], but it was not properly raised into independence out of fear—lest, being healthy, it might strike them back; thus it was not nurtured according to its desire. Let this cat wither away; let it remain here even if it is mute—what does it matter?
"Householder, what more need be said? At this moment, thieves are prowling about in the house."

If you do not give away the jewels on your own hood, do not give them for the sake of others; why do you, with such a wicked intent, guard whatever treasure or hoard has been deposited? This alone is enough; I ask you another thing: O serpent, why [do you act thus]?
With his hisses, heavy with the force of poisonous fire, he scorched these people.

Lacking substance and exceedingly light by nature, these fragments of withered grass and the like are unfit for any purpose; fie upon this wind that, turning its back on inner essence, has now reached those things that exist independently!
Behold how, by means of the utterly unsteady [mind], the paths of the great ones have been elevated into the sky.

O friend, look at those who are light by nature and have never been counted anywhere— those who for a long time lay hidden upon the earth, trampled daily by feet alone, yet now tossed into the sky by the fickle-minded wind.
These particles of dust, remaining atop the lofty mountains, cause them to appear like kings.
If my listeners are free from envy, I shall speak these words. One should fear much from one's own side, but not so much from a powerful adversary;
for when darkness has completely enveloped everything, how little can even a possessor of light do?
Just as the stars shine by their own power when the sun is present, but not otherwise.

Indeed, the pair of eyes of the Lord of Consciousness— which are rich in the vision of the entire multitude of objects present before him— are truly stainless; therefore, having abandoned contact with other limbs,
the nose, which delights in fragrance and is as pleasing as a bamboo flute, remains fixed in the space between the two eyes.
It is not eternally withdrawn within this [heart]; do not search for it with your eyes; release your sighs, O weary one!
This is but a small portion from his mouth: that fool, hearing this, thought a drop of water upon a lotus leaf was a pearl,
even as it was being slowly picked up and vanished by the slight movement of a fingertip.
When he has flown away from there, one does not sleep day after day with inner sorrow, crying out "Alas! in grief.
Ah! How great is this embrace of contentment in this very lake! This swan’s mind does not turn even slightly toward a lotus, the abode of splendor;
though he has slept, he still remains awake—let us wait for him for a while longer.
At dawn, the beloved bees are indeed able to endure the hour known as *velā*.
The world was devoured by venomous serpents who subsisted on air alone; they, in turn, were swallowed by peacocks practicing the severe vow of consuming only drops of rain from the clouds;
and those peacocks were brought to destruction by hunters clad in the skins of fierce deer.
Even though he recognizes it as a manifestation of hypocrisy, a foolish person still strives for virtues.
The name of one of the two [traditions] had been closed; it was now reopened.
The hand of Fate, which had stumbled on its own path, was taken up by others. And this world has been rescued from the calamity of a vision that perceives what has never been seen before.
"O woodcutter, it is fitting that you have cut down this dark row of mango trees, which provide fruit out of season."
By whom the great burden was carried alone upon a most treacherous path;
by whom the sound of the intoxicated bull in his own pen was never once tolerated;
and who was the very ornament of the herd of cattle—oh, it is he himself now!
Alas, what a tragedy! The price of this white ox, now that it has reached old age, is being proclaimed for sale.
That a frog, emitting a harsh and angry croak,
raised its hand without fear to slap the face of a black snake;
and that a serpent, with its head hanging down, remained there while closing its eyes— [these were the wonders].
All of that was merely the playful manifestation of some Blessed One who is a master of poisons.
Always dwelling at sacred fords, her nature exceedingly tender and innocent,
her conduct— by the grace of fate— moistened by pure droplets of water fallen from the sky;
having observed all this clearly here in the world, O Moon, she is regarded as a simple woman by the foolish folk.
Your excellence has been demonstrated; by whom were these thorns seen, both outside and inside?
The bow is drawn wide like the gaping mouth of Death; these arrows are like venomous serpents.
Even that training which surpassed Arjuna is terrifying, and his gait causes all limbs to sink.
Oh, what cruelty lies within! Alas, the treacherous one has a sweet and captivating song on his lips.
I think that this forest will become devoid of deer, just as it will be for this hunter.
Let the greatness of the sky go to hell, let its lofty station be split into fragments,
let it suffer the contemptible course of fate, or let that void become non-existent— by which [sky] the sun,
with upraised hands, his luster lost, exhausted and tormented, is left behind.
Even for a friend who lacks support, no basis for stability has been established.
O you who cause a conflagration in every direction and bring an end to the forest, your flames do not please me;
people do not desire the growth of one who is intent on consuming his own support.
This fire was created by the ill-fated one to tear up the very roots of this mountain.
O wicked one, who would not have doubts about you, you who bring such distress to the world, like a forest fire?
Wasted by hunger, somehow or other constantly supporting his emaciated body, he wandered from house to house among householders seeking a scrap of leftover food; yet,
finding only a fragment of bone fallen by chance, he beheld these three worlds as empty.
Thinking thus, he said: "Alas, fie! That very son of Saramā now acts like a lion!"

A dog, having obtained even the dry sinews, marrow, and blood-stained bone of a cow—though it be devoid of flesh—is satisfied; yet that does not serve to appease its hunger. A lion, however, abandons a jackal even when it has come into his very lap and slays an elephant instead.
Every person, even when fallen into distress, desires a reward that corresponds to their own nature.
Seeing the turbidity of the waters, the swans have slowly flown away; the lotuses, their filaments crushed by the rain and their luster dimmed, have sunk into the water;
that path which provides access to the bliss of all seasons is now covered with fresh grass.
Alas! Even such a lake, naturally pure, has been destroyed by its very growth.
For those whose minds are awakened by the happiness of contentment, that state is not difficult to attain; yet for those men whose intellects are agitated by greed for wealth, it remains far away.
Thus, for whose sake was such a station of perfections ordained by Fate?
Mount Meru, whose greatness as gold is fully realized within itself alone, does not please me.

The overturning of high and low among the wealthy; the carrying away of seeds from those whose hopes are shattered; and the seeking out of one's own natural vulnerabilities by those who, free from fear, arrange their defenses while the innocent child sleeps.
Alas, having found an empty dwelling infested with mice, what—indeed, what—has not been done by them?

When the great elements have utterly dissolved into one another as if out of fear at the end of the eon, that single tree alone expands with its mass of trunks; it is the tree within whose belly-cavity the God places the three worlds and dwells.
Like a child at the tip of a branch, languid from the playful grace of water-sports he has enjoyed.
Born in the lineage of the mountains, she who delights the gods with her excellent qualities became the beloved of Lord Śambhu— of Trivikrama, whose mind is intent upon benefiting the three worlds.
Ambikā, intent on granting the desires even of the Mlecchas and the source of her own abode, increases the height of the Vindhya; what kind of power is this of destiny?
Bhā. Amṛtadatta said:
"O foolish-minded plowman, why do you strike at fruit that has already been lost? Do not, do not wield the plow; the field is no longer there, nor have you seen any hardness here."
Not even a trace arises here; the result is merely the cessation of afflictions.

Have you not constantly seen or heard of many who have gone forth without seeds? O Wind, what kind of delusion is this of yours, that you [speak of] that which has arisen from a place of dense refuse?
Since you cause this mass of dust to find its footing in the sky— a realm frequented by hosts of radiant deities—
let alone the fact that it obstructs the path of people's vision while being raised up;
by what means can this defect of soiling your own body be endured by you?
Born from Amṛtadatta, he became that one Tortoise who offered his back for the support of the broad burden of the world;
and there the praiseworthy birth of Dhruva revolves, wherein the circle of luminaries is held in check.
Having developed useless factions, they do not act for the benefit of others, neither above nor below;
other beings are born and perish like gnats inside a fig within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
O enemy of elephants, why do you cry out so harshly into my ears?
O you whose own intellect is well-known, what is there that is not understood?
By the tusk-tip of a single lion, which pierced the frontal globes of an elephant,
an entire herd of elephants was submerged in the cavity of a mosquito's throat— of whom [is this the deed]?
O Udra, you who are crooked and violent in uprooting the trees that shelter the banks— do not be so arrogant as to think, "I shall agitate the ocean with the flow of my river!
If you desire to preserve your own existence, O water, wander instead among the deserts or remain right there.
The submarine fire is far away, yet here it is swallowed by great beings as they enter it.
O Lord of Waters, you who possess firm stability and lofty peaks, and who rely upon the mountain that serves as the world’s boundary,
why do you vainly desire to cross over this ocean by means of the moon’s distant pull? For from that, nothing but the destruction of jewels and living beings would come to you.
Surely, having encountered a blow, you shall roll right there at the end of his footstep.
O virtuous one, you incessantly cause the sun in the sky to sway in your lap,
as well as the host of stars, the moon,
and other radiant lights such as the brilliance of lightning.
Even though it is so variegated, you nevertheless do not abandon the blindness within.
This is that Śaṅkara, whose self-restraint is renowned throughout the three worlds;
now, distressed by separation, he bears his beloved in his own body.
Thinking, "By him we have indeed been conquered," [he holds] the hand of his beloved—
Pressing with his hand, Smara, having burst into laughter, triumphs.
Those side-long glances of women—drawn and released from the bow of their brows, stealing the beauty of the blue water-lily, the bee, and the sky;

intoxicated, black-tipped like a deer, piercing the hearts of men with cruel arrows that are the pupils; feathered with long outer corners and made treacherous by the poison of smiles—these are the glances of women, thick with lashes.
May the arrows of the five-arrowed god, who conquers the three worlds, be utterly overcome by those whose vigor is supreme.
Go, O beloved, if you must go; may your paths be auspicious.
May my birth also take place in that very place where you have gone.
